AI.tldr: A new benchmark (DSB-IFEval) evaluates how full-duplex voice agents follow implicit instructions in real-time spoken conversations, testing eight assistant roles across five conditioning protocols, revealing architecture-dependent trade-offs in persona adherence versus explicit rule following.
AI.motivation: Existing voice agent benchmarks mainly test turn-management through explicit instructions, while real deployed agents often operate based on roles/personas from which appropriate conversational behavior must be inferred. There's a need to evaluate how well agents can follow implicit instructions in real-time spoken interactions.
AI.method: Introduced DuplexSpeechBench-IFEval (DSB-IFEval) with 1,038 test cases across eight diverse assistant roles. Evaluated five conditioning protocols: default behavior, explicit instructions, persona-implied behavior, combined persona-rule conditioning, and instruction conflict. Used deterministic Instruction Adherence Score (IAS) for real-time floor management and LLM-judged Persona Adherence Score (PAS) for persona-consistent content. Tested six real-time speech systems including F-Actor, PersonaPlex, GPT-Realtime, MiniCPM-o, and Fun-Audio-Chat.
AI.result: Found architecture-dependent trade-offs: Full duplex models (F-Actor, PersonaPlex) show significant drops in adherence (9.7% and 4.5%) under persona-only conditioning vs explicit instructions. GPT-Realtime, MiniCPM-o, and Fun-Audio-Chat strongly adhere to persona content but their floor behavior doesn't adapt across conditioning protocols and remains constrained on proactive actions. All systems struggle to override persona directives under safety conflicts even when following conflicting instructions reliably.
AI.conclusion: Inferring behavior implied by a role, executing it at appropriate conversational moments, and resolving competing instructions remain distinct challenges for full-duplex voice agents. The benchmark reveals that current systems face trade-offs between explicit instruction following and persona-based behavior inference.

title: Robust PAC Learning of Concurrent Stochastic Games
comment: Main text: 10 pages, 1 figure, 2 tables; Appendix: 22 pages, 2 figures, 1 table
summary: We introduce the first Probably Approximately Correct (PAC) learning framework for general-sum concurrent stochastic games (CSGs) with transition uncertainty, while addressing the challenge of Nash equilibrium (NE) existence. Our algorithm maintains data-driven $L^1$ confidence sets over transition kernels and solves a robust CSG to compute a social-welfare optimal $\varepsilon$-NE, using a robust MDP-based exploration mechanism to drive joint state-action coverage. Crucially, we introduce a Nash margin characterisation that enables principled reasoning about equilibrium existence: the framework either returns an $\varepsilon$-approximate NE whose social-welfare value is $\varepsilon$-close to optimal, or provides a sound certificate that no exact NE exists. Under a minimum reachability condition $p_{\mathrm{reach}}>0$ over relevant state-action pairs, the algorithm terminates after a polynomial number of trajectory samples, with sample complexity $\widetilde{O}\left( {R_{\max}^2 H^4 |S|^2 |A| / (p_{\mathrm{reach}} \varepsilon^2)} \right)$. Empirical results on benchmark CSGs demonstrate near-optimal performance, correct handling of equilibrium (non-)existence, and sample complexity consistent with theory.

AI.tldr: First PAC learning framework for general-sum concurrent stochastic games with transition uncertainty that provides certificates for Nash equilibrium existence or non-existence with polynomial sample complexity.
AI.motivation: Addressing the challenge of Nash equilibrium existence in general-sum concurrent stochastic games with transition uncertainty, where traditional equilibrium concepts may fail to exist or be computationally intractable.
AI.method: Develops a PAC learning algorithm that maintains data-driven L¹ confidence sets over transition kernels, solves robust CSGs to compute social-welfare optimal ε-NE, uses robust MDP-based exploration for joint state-action coverage, and introduces a Nash margin characterization for equilibrium existence reasoning.
AI.result: Algorithm terminates after polynomial trajectory samples (sample complexity: Õ(R_max²H⁴|S|²|A|/(p_reachε²)) under minimum reachability condition, returns either an ε-approximate NE with ε-close optimal social welfare or a sound certificate that no exact NE exists.
AI.conclusion: First provably efficient PAC framework for learning equilibria in CSGs with transition uncertainty that rigorously handles equilibrium existence questions, with theoretical guarantees and empirical validation on benchmark games.

title: Evaluating Graph Neural Networks for Change-Criticality Classification in Maritime Navigation Charts
comment: Accepted at IEEE International Geoscience and Remote Sensing Symposium (IGARSS) 2026
summary: Graph neural networks (GNNs) are a class of neural networks suitable for learning on graph-structured data. Their application to spatial data is a natural extension, however its relatively unclear which message-passing operations, architectural configurations, and graph representation is best suited for classifying changes to objects in electronic navigational charts (ENCs)--geospatial vector datasets used for marine navigation. Maintaining these datasets is a challenge, and categorizing changes to objects in the ENC based on their significance to navigational safety is of particular importance. Here, we propose to represent these vector navigation datasets as a graph structure where the spatial objects serve as nodes and their spatial and semantic relationships form edges. We encode both the old ENC dataset and new ENC dataset into a pair of graphs and frame the task as a graph-pair classification problem. Building on this representation, we investigate the use of GNN architectures to classify whether the encoded graphs constitutes a critical or non-critical risk to navigational safety. We train and evaluate several GNN architectures and model configurations on ENC changes reviewed by maritime experts. Our results demonstrate that graph-based representations improve the classification of ENC updates, providing a scalable approach for automating or improving ENC maintenance workflows.

AI.tldr: GNNs can effectively classify ENC change risks by representing vector navigation data as graphs and treating change classification as a graph-pair classification problem.
AI.motivation: Maintaining electronic navigational charts (ENCs) is challenging, and categorizing changes based on navigational safety significance is particularly important. Current approaches for classifying ENC object changes are unclear regarding optimal message-passing operations, architectural configurations, and graph representations.
AI.method: Represent vector navigation datasets as graph structures where spatial objects are nodes and spatial/semantic relationships are edges. Encode both old and new ENC datasets into paired graphs, framing the task as a graph-pair classification problem. Investigate GNN architectures to classify whether graph pairs constitute critical or non-critical risks to navigational safety.
AI.result: Graph-based representations improve ENC update classification compared to previous approaches. The study demonstrates that GNNs provide a scalable solution for automating or improving ENC maintenance workflows through effective classification of changes based on navigational risk.
AI.conclusion: GNN architectures effectively classify ENC changes for navigational safety assessment. The graph-based representation approach offers a promising and scalable method for enhancing maritime chart maintenance automation.

title: Do GUI Agents Know When Not to Act? Enabling Conflict-Aware Termination for Multimodal GUI Agents
summary: Graphical user interface (GUI) agents are increasingly used to execute natural-language instructions on user interfaces, yet real users may issue infeasible instructions due to benign mistakes. A reliable agent should not only know how to act, but also when not to act. In this work, we introduce CONFLICTGUI, a benchmark covering instruction-internal conflicts and instruction-GUI context conflicts to study conflict-aware termination. Our evaluation reveals severe execution-biased overcompliance: agents that perform well on feasible tasks often continue to execute blindly under conflicting instructions. To mitigate this behavior, we propose CONFLICTGUARD, an inference-time framework that aligns an agent's feasibility awareness with its action generation. CONFLICTGUARD contains two coupled components: a feasibility verification protocol that guides the agent to assess instruction logic and GUI-side evidence before acting, and a conditional action modulation mechanism that steers agents from over-compliant execution into termination-oriented behavior. Experiments across five widely-used agents demonstrate that CONFLICTGUARD improves average conflict task success rate significantly, while preserving normal GUI-task performance. These results validate that a lightweight inference-time intervention can substantially boost GUI Agent's competence to identify inappropriate execution scenarios and refrain from unnecessary actions.

AI.tldr: CONFLICTGUI benchmark studies conflict-aware termination in GUI agents, revealing execution-biased overcompliance, with CONFLICTGUARD framework improving conflict task success while preserving normal performance.
AI.motivation: GUI agents often blindly execute infeasible instructions due to user mistakes, requiring agents to know when not to act. Current agents lack conflict-aware termination capability.
AI.method: Introduce CONFLICTGUI benchmark covering instruction-internal and instruction-GUI context conflicts. Propose CONFLICTGUARD inference-time framework with feasibility verification protocol and conditional action modulation mechanism.
AI.result: Evaluation shows severe execution-biased overcompliance in agents. CONFLICTGUARD significantly improves average conflict task success rate across five agents while preserving normal GUI-task performance.
AI.conclusion: Lightweight inference-time intervention can substantially boost GUI agents' ability to identify inappropriate execution scenarios and refrain from unnecessary actions, addressing the critical need for conflict-aware termination.

title: Verify Before You Distill: Prompt-Level Teacher Gating for On-Policy Distillation
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) accelerates post-training by providing dense token-level supervision from a frozen teacher on the student's own rollouts. Vanilla OPD applies this supervision uniformly across prompts, without checking whether the teacher is reliable for each prompt. Because reverse KL is mode-seeking, a confidently wrong teacher can induce a strong yet misleading update. Distributional proxies, such as entropy or teacher-student likelihood agreement, measure uncertainty or agreement but do not directly verify outcome correctness. We introduce Teacher-Gated On-Policy Distillation (TGOPD), built on the principle that teacher reliability should be verified at the prompt level before dense supervision is admitted. TGOPD estimates reliability from a small set of verifier-scored teacher probes and routes each prompt exclusively to dense OPD when the reliability check passes or to verifier-grounded GRPO otherwise. Across 4B and 35B students in mathematics, code, and instruction following, TGOPD outperforms Vanilla OPD in all six single-domain settings and achieves higher seven-benchmark averages at both scales under multi-domain training. By using otherwise-idle teacher capacity for reliability estimation, TGOPD also reduces teacher-side compute waste in asynchronous OPD, increasing teacher-node GPU utilization from 9.8% to 78.9% in the measured 4B single-domain run.

AI.tldr: TGOPD improves on-policy distillation by gating dense teacher supervision with prompt-level reliability checks, using verifier-scored teacher probes to determine when the teacher is trustworthy, achieving better performance across multiple domains and scales while improving GPU utilization.
AI.motivation: Vanilla on-policy distillation applies teacher supervision uniformly without verifying teacher reliability for each prompt. This is problematic because confidently wrong teachers can provide misleading supervision due to reverse KL's mode-seeking nature, and existing proxies like entropy or likelihood agreement don't directly verify outcome correctness.
AI.method: TGOPD estimates teacher reliability at the prompt level using a small set of verifier-scored teacher probes. Based on this reliability check, it routes prompts to either: 1) dense OPD when reliability passes, or 2) verifier-grounded GRPO otherwise. This uses otherwise-idle teacher capacity for reliability estimation.
AI.result: TGOPD outperforms Vanilla OPD in all six single-domain settings (mathematics, code, instruction following) for both 4B and 35B students. It achieves higher seven-benchmark averages at both scales under multi-domain training and increases teacher-node GPU utilization from 9.8% to 78.9% in 4B single-domain runs.
AI.conclusion: TGOPD effectively addresses the problem of unreliable teacher supervision in OPD by introducing prompt-level reliability checking, leading to better performance across multiple domains and improved computational efficiency through better GPU utilization.

title: Beyond "Made with AI": Visualizing Provenance Density to Mitigate the Transparency Penalty
summary: As generative AI makes polished prose cheap to produce, users can no longer rely on fluency as a proxy for truth. We call this failure mode the Fluency Trap: users trust fluent hallucinations while also discounting accurate content once it is disclosed as AI-generated. Binary ``Made with AI'' labels respond with authorship disclosure, but they do not show what supports a claim. We propose Provenance Density, an evidence-visualization interface that shows the density of verified claims in a text. In a user study with 81 participants, an idealized Provenance Density interface produced a large discernment gap between truth and fabrication ($+4.15$ points, $d=1.82$), whereas participants given no signal showed no detectable discrimination. A technical audit with 200 samples shows that retrieval density alone is insufficient; unexpectedly, the Consistency Veto carries most of the discriminative signal on dynamic queries. As AI-generated content becomes indistinguishable from human writing, effective transparency must move from authorship disclosure toward evidence visualization.

AI.tldr: Provenance Density interface shows verified claims density in AI text, helping users discern truth from fabrication better than simple "Made with AI" labels.
AI.motivation: As generative AI produces polished prose, fluency can no longer be trusted as a proxy for truth - users fall into a "Fluency Trap" where they trust fluent hallucinations but discount accurate AI content. Simple authorship disclosure labels fail because they don't show what supports claims.
AI.method: Proposed Provenance Density, an evidence-visualization interface that displays density of verified claims in text. Conducted user study with 81 participants comparing the interface against no-signal condition, plus technical audit with 200 samples.
AI.result: Provenance Density produced large discernment gap between truth and fabrication (+4.15 points, d=1.82), while participants with no signal showed no detectable discrimination. Technical audit revealed retrieval density alone is insufficient - the Consistency Veto carries most discriminative signal on dynamic queries.
AI.conclusion: As AI-generated content becomes indistinguishable from human writing, effective transparency must evolve from simple authorship disclosure toward evidence visualization like Provenance Density.

title: Causal Foundation Models
summary: Causal inference is the practice of estimating the effect of a treatment or intervention from data. It traditionally requires a bespoke pipeline for every new problem: first proposing a causal mechanism, selecting a compatible estimator, and finally training it. Meanwhile, across diverse settings and modalities, much of machine learning has shifted to the paradigm of foundation models: networks pretrained once at scale and applied to new tasks without fine-tuning. Causal foundation models (CFMs) bring this paradigm to causal inference. CFMs are pretrained neural networks that estimate causal quantities, such as the average treatment effect, on entirely new datasets using in-context learning without requiring model updates. This work provides a practical introduction to this emerging area. We summarize the necessary background in causal inference and machine learning before discussing CFMs. Throughout, we include example code and Jupyter notebooks.

AI.tldr: Causal foundation models (CFMs) bring the foundation model paradigm to causal inference by using pretrained neural networks that can estimate causal effects on new datasets through in-context learning without fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Traditional causal inference requires custom pipelines for each new problem (proposing causal mechanisms, selecting estimators, training), while other areas of machine learning have shifted to foundation models that work across diverse settings without fine-tuning. There's a need to bring this paradigm shift to causal inference.
AI.method: CFMs are pretrained neural networks that use in-context learning to estimate causal quantities (like average treatment effect) on entirely new datasets without requiring model updates or fine-tuning. The paper provides a practical introduction with example code and Jupyter notebooks.
AI.result: The work introduces causal foundation models as an emerging area that applies the foundation model paradigm to causal inference, enabling more flexible and scalable causal estimation across different datasets and problems.
AI.conclusion: Causal foundation models represent a promising new direction that could transform causal inference by bringing the efficiency and flexibility of foundation models to causal estimation tasks, potentially making causal analysis more accessible and scalable across diverse applications.

title: AutoGraphForge: Towards Automated Graph Theory Discovery
comment: 17 pages, 1 figure, 3 tables. Submitted to ITAT 2026 (Information Technologies -- Applications and Theory), CEUR Workshop Proceedings. Code: https://github.com/JanPastorek/AutoGraphForge
summary: We report on our ongoing project to develop a computational pipeline, AutoGraphForge, for an automated graph-theoretic conjecturing-refuting-formalizing-proving system. Conjecture generation is counterexample-guided and runs in rounds: a Graffiti3 generator proposes conjectures over a small, evolving snapshot table $T$ (initially a few hundred graphs with their computed invariants) that grows only by counterexamples to its own conjectures. A novelty filter of $559$ classical and folklore relations, closed under transitive composition and linear identity substitution, decides via a linear program whether a candidate is already implied by known results. Surviving candidates are tested against a dataset of about $348,000$ graphs, unioning the complete House of Graphs invariant export, the exhaustive census of all connected graphs on at most nine vertices, several extremal families (strongly regular, minimal Ramsey, Cayley, cages, barbells, lollipops, spiders), and random models. Counterexample-search algorithms then attack the remainder. Run for several rounds on an HPC cluster, the loop yields $6,522$ conjectures that survived the refutation dataset, the novelty filter and every active-search run -- among them nontrivial relations between the annihilation number and the edge-cover number for bipartite and regular graphs, which we prove by hand. A subsequent formalization and proving stage deterministically translates each surviving conjecture into a Lean 4 statement skeleton; every candidate proof is kernel-verified against a pinned mathlib4 and our custom invariant preamble. This stage integrates two neural provers -- DeepSeek-Prover-V2-671B (served with vLLM) and the Lean-specialised OProver-32B -- behind the independent kernel check. It is implemented end-to-end and passes initial sanity checks, with the full pipeline currently running on the cluster.

AI.tldr: AutoGraphForge is an automated system that generates, refutes, and proves graph theory conjectures through counterexample-guided rounds, novelty filtering, and neural theorem proving with Lean 4 verification.
AI.motivation: To automate the process of mathematical discovery in graph theory by creating a computational pipeline that can generate conjectures, refute false ones, and prove true ones, reducing the need for manual theorem proving.
AI.method: The system uses a counterexample-guided iterative approach: 1) Graffiti3 generates conjectures over evolving snapshot tables, 2) Novelty filter with 559 classical relations checks if conjectures are already implied, 3) Testing against 348,000-graph dataset, 4) Counterexample-search algorithms, 5) Formalization into Lean 4 with kernel verification, 6) Integration of neural provers (DeepSeek-Prover and OProver) for automated proving.
AI.result: The system generated 6,522 conjectures that survived all filtering stages, including nontrivial relations between annihilation number and edge-cover number for bipartite and regular graphs (proved manually). The pipeline is fully implemented and passes initial sanity checks, currently running on HPC cluster.
AI.conclusion: AutoGraphForge demonstrates a working automated mathematical discovery system for graph theory that successfully integrates conjecture generation, refutation, and formal verification, showing promise for automating mathematical research processes with rigorous verification.

title: ObserverBench: Testing Mechanistic Estimates for Intervention and Control
comment: 28 pages, 4 figures. Code, benchmark, leaderboards, and submission interface: https://kwisatzh.github.io/observerbench/. Frozen artifact release: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22136091
summary:
Mechanistic interpretability is increasingly used to guide interventions such as activation steering, circuit removal, and safety monitoring. Yet an internal estimate that is accurate on average can still choose a poor action.
  We present ObserverBench, a benchmark framework for testing whether an internal estimator---an observer---is adequate for the intervention, control, or safety task it directs. Each task fixes the model, information boundary, allowed actions, decision rule, held-out cases, and loss. The benchmark reports estimation accuracy separately from the loss caused by the chosen action.
  Theory and experiments show why both are needed. In closed-loop control, observer errors matter at the starting point and along directions the allowed intervention can reach. On circuit-intervention tasks in GPT-2-small and Qwen2.5-7B, pairwise observers predict unseen effects more accurately without always choosing better actions; observers trained on action loss choose lower-loss actions. In safety triage, a score that perfectly separates violations can allocate a fixed intervention budget poorly when violations have different costs. Across Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B-it, and prospectively frozen Qwen3.5-9B APPS tasks, AUROC can rank monitors differently from deployment loss, and the best information source changes across models. Sparse SAE readouts also trail their layer-matched dense controls on the reported Qwen panels, under disclosed activation-density or checkpoint mismatches.
  ObserverBench provides fixed task contracts, runnable baselines, and table-based submissions for evaluating interpretability methods through the actions they enable.

AI.tldr: ObserverBench is a benchmark framework that evaluates internal estimators ("observers") used in mechanistic interpretability by testing whether they lead to appropriate actions in intervention, control, or safety tasks, rather than just measuring estimation accuracy.
AI.motivation: Current mechanistic interpretability methods focus on internal estimates that may be accurate on average but still lead to poor actions when used for interventions like activation steering, circuit removal, or safety monitoring. There's a need to evaluate whether internal estimators are adequate for the practical tasks they're meant to direct.
AI.method: ObserverBench provides a benchmark framework with fixed task contracts that specify: model, information boundary, allowed actions, decision rule, held-out cases, and loss functions. It reports both estimation accuracy and the actual loss caused by chosen actions, allowing for comprehensive evaluation of observers.
AI.result: Experiments show that accurate estimation doesn't guarantee good actions: pairwise observers predicted unseen effects accurately but didn't always choose better actions, while observers trained on action loss performed better. In safety tasks, monitors with perfect AUROC could allocate intervention budgets poorly when violations had different costs. Performance also varied across different models (GPT-2-small, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B-it).
AI.conclusion: ObserverBench provides a practical framework for evaluating interpretability methods through the actions they enable, emphasizing that both estimation accuracy and action outcomes matter, and that the best approaches can vary across different models and tasks.

title: Making Every Tool Call Count: Necessary Tool-Evidence Path Rewards for Agentic Vision-Language Models
summary: Modern vision-language models (VLMs) can directly answer many image-grounded questions, yet they often struggle with complex queries requiring fine-grained visual details or external knowledge. To acquire this missing evidence, agentic VLMs invoke tools such as image cropping, image search, and text search. However, existing training paradigms primarily evaluate tool-use based on final answer correctness, leaving evidence acquisition and utilization insufficiently supervised. This leads to two critical shortcomings: (i) models frequently issue redundant or off-target tool calls that fail to gather necessary evidence, and (ii) even when appropriate tools are called, models often fail to extract the necessary information from the resulting observations. To address these limitations, we introduce the NTEP (Necessary Tool-Evidence Path), a novel annotation scheme that explicitly specifies the essential external evidence and corresponding tool calls for each query. Building upon this, we propose NTEP-R (NTEP Reward), a supervision mechanism ensuring that each tool invocation strictly advances the reasoning process toward the final solution. Specifically, our approach rewards the agent for aligning its pre-call intent with a necessary evidence-seeking goal, and for ensuring the information summarized from the post-call observation aligns with the necessary evidence. Furthermore, we introduce a non-repeated-goal regularizer to penalize redundant calls that revisit satisfied NTEP goals. Extensive evaluations on seven image-grounded benchmarks demonstrate that our 8B-parameter instantiation, NTEP-8B, significantly improves both search-oriented accuracy and tool-use efficiency within a unified three-tool framework. These results highlight the critical value of fine-grained tool-evidence path supervision for training robust agentic VLMs.

AI.tldr: NTEP (Necessary Tool-Evidence Path) is a novel annotation scheme and training approach that improves vision-language models' tool-use efficiency by explicitly supervising evidence acquisition paths rather than just final answers.
AI.motivation: Current vision-language models struggle with complex queries requiring fine-grained visual details or external knowledge. While agentic VLMs use tools, existing training only evaluates final answer correctness, leading to redundant/off-target tool calls and poor evidence extraction.
AI.method: Proposes NTEP annotation scheme specifying essential external evidence and tool calls for each query, then NTEP-R supervision mechanism. This rewards agents for aligning pre-call intent with evidence-seeking goals, ensuring information from observations aligns with necessary evidence, and includes non-repeated-goal regularization.
AI.result: NTEP-8B (8B-parameter model) significantly improves both search-oriented accuracy and tool-use efficiency across seven image-grounded benchmarks within a unified three-tool framework.
AI.conclusion: Fine-grained tool-evidence path supervision is critical for training robust agentic VLMs, addressing fundamental limitations in how models acquire and utilize external evidence.

title: Learnable composition for neural operators
summary: Neural operators are fast, differentiable surrogates for physical simulation, but their accuracy often degrades when domain geometry, size, or operating conditions differ from training. Supervised adaptation can recover accuracy, but even a small target set requires costly high-fidelity simulations. We therefore ask how pretraining and transfer can be designed together to reduce this deployment cost. LatentDDM first pretrains a neural operator to predict fields on small subdomains. For a new setting, it freezes this operator and trains only a lightweight module that composes the local predictions. We evaluate our method on two complementary problems: steady Darcy flow, where long-range pressure coupling must extend across increasingly large porous domains, and unsteady incompressible flow around a pitching airfoil, where rollout errors compound as target pitching frequencies exceed the training range. Compared with the capacity-matched models that process the full domain at once, LatentDDM's error is 36-56% lower on larger Darcy domains after adaptation with 16 target simulations. It also improves 20-step field rollouts in fast-pitching airfoil flow, both zero-shot and after few-shot calibration. These results identify the co-designed local pretraining and composition-level transfer as a promising design principle for physical foundation models.

AI.tldr: LatentDDM: A neural operator framework that pretrains on small subdomains and adapts to new geometries/conditions via lightweight composition modules, reducing deployment costs while maintaining accuracy.
AI.motivation: Neural operators degrade in accuracy when domain geometry, size, or operating conditions differ from training. Supervised adaptation requires costly high-fidelity simulations, creating a need for more efficient adaptation methods that reduce deployment costs.
AI.method: LatentDDM pretrains a neural operator to predict fields on small subdomains, then freezes this operator for new settings while training only a lightweight module that composes the local predictions, enabling efficient adaptation without expensive target simulations.
AI.result: 36-56% lower error on larger Darcy domains after adaptation with 16 target simulations compared to capacity-matched full-domain models; improved 20-step field rollouts in fast-pitching airfoil flow, both zero-shot and after few-shot calibration.
AI.conclusion: Co-designed local pretraining and composition-level transfer is a promising design principle for physical foundation models, enabling efficient adaptation to new conditions while reducing deployment costs.

title: GrowPage: On-Demand KV Budgeting for Efficient LLM Reasoning Serving
summary: Long-output reasoning has made the key--value (KV) cache a critical memory bottleneck for efficient LLM serving. Existing KV compression methods usually rely on a predefined per-request budget and adjust only which KV states are retained, leaving the total capacity fixed throughout decoding. However, reasoning workloads exhibit substantial demand variation: different requests require different KV capacities, and the attention demand of an individual request evolves during generation. We introduce \textbf{GrowPage}, an on-demand KV budgeting framework that treats KV capacity as a runtime resource. GrowPage maintains lightweight dual-timescale query summaries to capture recent and long-term attention behaviors, and uses their relative attention working sets to estimate demand evolution. At each capacity boundary, GrowPage either compresses KV states within the current allocation or acquires an additional physical page when broader demand emerges. By integrating with PagedAttention's page-level memory abstraction, GrowPage preserves continuous batching and prefix caching. Experiments on reasoning benchmarks across multiple models show that GrowPage achieves a superior performance--throughput trade-off over existing approaches.

AI.tldr: GrowPage is an adaptive KV caching framework that dynamically adjusts memory allocation during LLM decoding based on real-time attention demand, improving performance-throughput tradeoffs for reasoning workloads.
AI.motivation: Current KV compression methods use fixed per-request budgets, which is inefficient because reasoning workloads have substantial demand variation: different requests need different KV capacities, and attention demands evolve during generation. The fixed approach leaves KV cache as a critical memory bottleneck.
AI.method: GrowPage maintains lightweight dual-timescale query summaries to capture recent and long-term attention behaviors. It uses their relative attention working sets to estimate demand evolution. At capacity boundaries, it either compresses KV states within current allocation or acquires additional physical pages when broader demand emerges. It integrates with PagedAttention's page-level memory abstraction.
AI.result: Experiments on reasoning benchmarks across multiple models show that GrowPage achieves a superior performance-throughput trade-off over existing approaches. It preserves continuous batching and prefix caching while dynamically managing KV capacity.
AI.conclusion: GrowPage successfully addresses the KV cache memory bottleneck by treating KV capacity as a runtime resource and making on-demand adjustments based on attention demand evolution, offering better efficiency for LLM serving on reasoning workloads.

title: LeanStream: A Speculate-and-Refine Streaming Framework for Efficient on-Device LLM Inference
comment: 6 pages, 13 figures. To appear in the Proceedings of the 32nd Annual International Conference on Mobile Computing and Networking (MobiCom '26)
summary: On-device LLM inference is attractive for privacy and responsiveness, but remains challenging on mobile and embedded devices because model weights far exceed available DRAM. Prior systems exploit activation sparsity and offload weights to SSD or flash storage, but face a fundamental systems trade-off: accurate sparse execution decisions require the latest context, whereas efficient computation-I/O overlap requires early prediction. As a result, existing designs either serialize execution or incur redundant weight fetches, extra computation, and large cache overheads. We present LeanStream, a streaming speculate-and-refine framework for efficient on-device LLM inference. LeanStream progressively refines computation, loading, and cache-retention priorities using partial GPU results, enabling fine-grained overlap between GPU execution and storage I/O. We implement LeanStream on both mobile and embedded platforms. Compared with prior on-device LLM inference systems, LeanStream reduces memory usage by 4.8$\times$ to 7.5$\times$ at the best throughput achieved by prior work, while further improving token generation throughput by 1.6$\times$ to 2.1$\times$.

AI.tldr: LeanStream is a streaming speculate-and-refine framework that enables efficient on-device LLM inference by progressively refining computation, loading, and cache priorities using partial GPU results, achieving better throughput and memory efficiency.
AI.motivation: On-device LLM inference is desirable for privacy and responsiveness, but faces challenges because model weights exceed available DRAM on mobile/embedded devices. Existing systems that exploit activation sparsity and offload weights to storage face a fundamental trade-off: accurate sparse execution decisions require the latest context, while efficient computation-I/O overlap requires early prediction, leading to serialized execution or redundant operations.
AI.method: LeanStream introduces a streaming speculate-and-refine framework that progressively refines computation, loading, and cache-retention priorities using partial GPU results. This enables fine-grained overlap between GPU execution and storage I/O by making speculative decisions early and refining them as more context becomes available.
AI.result: Implementation on both mobile and embedded platforms shows that compared to prior on-device LLM inference systems, LeanStream reduces memory usage by 4.8× to 7.5× at the best throughput achieved by prior work, while further improving token generation throughput by 1.6× to 2.1×.
AI.conclusion: LeanStream successfully addresses the fundamental trade-off in on-device LLM inference systems by enabling effective speculation and refinement, achieving significant improvements in both memory efficiency and throughput performance.

title: PPO-STGNN: A Proximal Policy Optimization Approach with Spatio-Temporal Graph Neural Networks for DAG Task Scheduling in Cloud-Edge-End Computing
summary: With the rapid development of the Internet of Things, computation intensive directed acyclic graph (DAG) tasks have become increasingly common in cloud-edge-end collaborative environments. However, cloud, edge, and end nodes are highly heterogeneous in computing capacity, network bandwidth, and energy consumption, which makes the efficient scheduling of tasks with complex dependencies an NP-hard problem. Traditional heuristic algorithms and conventional reinforcement-learning methods often fail to capture the spatio-temporal dynamics of system resources. This paper proposes PPO-STGNN, a DAG task-scheduling algorithm that integrates proximal policy optimization (PPO) with spatio-temporal graph neural networks (STGNNs). The method uses an STGNN to extract features from both the DAG task topology and the physical cloud-edge-end resource graph, and then optimizes the scheduling policy through PPO to minimize makespan and schedule length ratio (SLR) while improving CPU and memory load balancing. To accelerate convergence, a multi-teacher behavior-cloning mechanism is introduced for pretraining. Experimental results show that PPO-STGNN significantly improves load balancing while maintaining a low completion time, making it suitable for dynamic and heterogeneous cloud-edge- end DAG scheduling scenarios.

AI.tldr: PPO-STGNN is a novel DAG task-scheduling algorithm that combines proximal policy optimization with spatio-temporal graph neural networks to optimize scheduling in heterogeneous cloud-edge-end environments, achieving better load balancing and completion times than traditional methods.
AI.motivation: The increasing prevalence of computation-intensive DAG tasks in cloud-edge-end environments presents significant challenges due to system heterogeneity in computing capacity, network bandwidth, and energy consumption. Traditional heuristic algorithms and conventional reinforcement learning methods fail to effectively capture the spatio-temporal dynamics of system resources in these complex, dynamic environments.
AI.method: The proposed PPO-STGNN algorithm integrates proximal policy optimization (PPO) with spatio-temporal graph neural networks (STGNNs). It uses STGNN to extract features from both the DAG task topology and the physical cloud-edge-end resource graph. The scheduling policy is optimized through PPO to minimize makespan and schedule length ratio while improving CPU and memory load balancing. A multi-teacher behavior-cloning mechanism is introduced for pretraining to accelerate convergence.
AI.result: Experimental results demonstrate that PPO-STGNN significantly improves load balancing while maintaining low completion time. The algorithm shows superior performance in dynamic and heterogeneous cloud-edge-end DAG scheduling scenarios compared to traditional approaches.
AI.conclusion: PPO-STGNN represents an effective solution for DAG task scheduling in heterogeneous cloud-edge-end environments, successfully addressing the limitations of traditional methods by capturing spatio-temporal resource dynamics and optimizing for both performance metrics (makespan, SLR) and system efficiency (load balancing).

title: The Gradient Does Not See Rank: Rank-Indifference in Matrix-CODI on ProsQA
comment: Accepted at the ICML 2026 Mechanistic Interpretability Workshop, https://openreview.net/forum?id=Spof4PusVI. 9 pages. Corrects a data-entry error in the workshop version: the seed-1337 accuracy in the three-seed replication was reported as 80.47% (a control run); the archived value is 78.91%, so the three-seed mean is 81.0 +/- 2.0pp (was 81.5 +/- 1.2pp). All other results are unchanged
summary: Continuous chain-of-thought models compress reasoning into latent tokens. Matrix-valued variants, which route each latent token through a d x d matrix bottleneck, introduce rank as a single-sample structural observable on the latent matrix Z. If matrix latents carry parallel reasoning paths via superposition, rank should track them, and truncating Z to low rank should hurt accuracy on tasks whose solutions plausibly require multiple components. Across four training regimes of a matrix-CODI model (three on ProsQA, one on GSM8K-Aug below the learning threshold), the rank-k projection ablation curve is flat to within 0.6 percentage points. A three-seed replication yields 81.0 +/- 2.0 percentage points accuracy while the final effective rank of Z spans {4, 12, 13}; the loss does not reward any particular rank. To test whether rank-blindness arises from the flatten-then-project readout alone, we trained four readouts: a bilinear reparametrization, a bilinear-plus-GELU readout nonlinear in Z, an SVD-augmented readout feeding singular values through an MLP, and a quadratic readout in Z Z^T. All four rank-k curves remain flat (Spearman p-values 0.63, 0.14, 0.82, 0.46). The flat curves persist for readouts nonlinear in Z. A linear probe on Z underperforms a raw pretrained hidden state at target prediction (AUC 0.673 vs. 0.846). A negative control on vanilla GPT-2 SFT (no matrix bottleneck, no Z, three seeds, n=500) reproduces a flat rank-k curve under the same intervention paradigm with pooled-mean range 0.20pp, and a random-h sensitivity floor lands at the same accuracy: the rank-k ablation alone conflates rank-blindness with position-irrelevance.

AI.tldr: Matrix-valued chain-of-thought models show that rank ablation has minimal impact on accuracy, suggesting the models don't use rank to track parallel reasoning paths as expected.
AI.motivation: To test whether matrix-valued chain-of-thought models use rank as a structural observable to track parallel reasoning paths, as would be expected if latent matrices carry superimposed reasoning components.
AI.method: Conducted rank-k projection ablation studies across four training regimes of a matrix-CODI model (three on ProsQA, one on GSM8K-Aug). Tested with multiple readout architectures to check if rank-blindness is due to specific readout design. Used linear probes and negative controls with vanilla GPT-2 SFT.
AI.result: Rank-k projection ablation curves are consistently flat (within 0.6 percentage points) across all conditions. Different seeds produce similar accuracy (81.0 ± 2.0%) despite varying effective ranks (4, 12, 13). All tested readout architectures show flat rank-k curves. Linear probes on Z underperform raw pretrained hidden states. Negative controls show rank-blindness may conflate with position-irrelevance.
AI.conclusion: Matrix chain-of-thought models don't appear to use rank to track parallel reasoning paths as hypothesized. The flat rank-k ablation curves suggest rank-blindness, which persists across different readout architectures, indicating the models don't rely on the rank structure of latent matrices for reasoning.

title: What Matters for Aggressive Decoding-Time KV Eviction? Temporal Aggregation and Ranking Preservation
summary: Decoding-time KV cache compression research focuses heavily on designing better token scoring functions, while the temporal rule that aggregates scores across decode steps is often treated as an implementation detail. Under aggressive KV compression, we find that exponential-moving-average (EMA) aggregation makes approximately order-preserving scorer modifications largely indistinguishable at the eviction-set level. Value-norm and entropy variants remain highly correlated with attention and produce nearly unchanged retention sets, whereas KeyDiff, key norm, recency, and a learned scorer alter the ranking and degrade substantially. We associate this stability with the evaluated aggregation, which couples layer weighting and temporal retention. Building on this observation, we introduce InertiaKV, an EMA-based decoding-time eviction method, and InertiaKV-Lazy, its periodic-refresh variant, which yields 1.34-1.46x decode throughput relative to full refresh InertiaKV. We also study Score-Free decoding as a separate empirical operating point: it scores the full context once at the first decode step, freezes that ranking, and incurs an average quality change of +0.03 while removing all subsequent scoring. Across six open-weight backbones and the LongBench, LongBench-v2, and RULER benchmarks, the results identify temporal aggregation and ranking preservation as distinct, consequential design factors; they do not imply that scoring quality is irrelevant in general.

AI.tldr: KV cache compression research focuses heavily on token scoring, but temporal aggregation rules (how scores are combined across decoding steps) are just as important. The paper shows that with EMA aggregation, different scoring methods produce similar results, while with other aggregations they differ significantly.
AI.motivation: Current KV cache compression research overly focuses on designing better token scoring functions while treating the temporal aggregation rule (how scores are combined across decode steps) as an implementation detail. The paper aims to show that temporal aggregation is actually a critical design factor that significantly impacts compression performance.
AI.method: The authors analyze how different scoring functions perform under aggressive KV compression with different temporal aggregation methods, particularly focusing on EMA aggregation. They introduce InertiaKV (an EMA-based decoding-time eviction method) and InertiaKV-Lazy (its periodic-refresh variant). They also study "Score-Free decoding" which scores context once and freezes the ranking.
AI.result: EMA aggregation makes different scoring methods largely indistinguishable - value-norm and entropy variants remain highly correlated with attention and produce nearly unchanged retention sets. KeyDiff, key norm, recency, and learned scorers degrade substantially. InertiaKV-Lazy yields 1.34-1.46x decode throughput relative to full refresh InertiaKV. Score-Free decoding incurs only +0.03 average quality change while removing all subsequent scoring.
AI.conclusion: Temporal aggregation and ranking preservation are distinct, consequential design factors in KV cache compression - not just scoring quality. EMA-based methods provide stability, and freezing rankings after initial scoring can work surprisingly well. These findings don't imply scoring quality is irrelevant, but highlight the importance of aggregation rules.

title: Distilling deep optical flow stereo methods to retrieve dense three-dimensional wind fields
summary: Geostationary atmospheric motion vectors (AMVs) provide the dense horizontal wind vectors (u,v) and heights ingested into data assimilation systems. Traditional AMVs track features using window-based cross-correlation and estimate heights via infrared brightness temperatures paired with numerical weather prediction (NWP) background states, creating a circular dependency that yields inaccurate heights, high computational cost, and sparse retrievals. Stereo winds from GEO-GEO and GEO-LEO geometrically resolve heights from parallax shifts across different poses, eliminating NWP dependence and improving accuracy, but they remain computationally heavy with limited coverage. In this work, we replace window-based tracking in stereo matching with deep optical flow for efficient, improved retrieval. Fine-tuning balances a self-supervised geometric residual loss with supervised radiosonde reconstruction. To eliminate multi-satellite overlap requirements, we distill the stereo teacher into a single-satellite student model. Chi-square and height uncertainties from the teacher are emulated by the student for quality assurance. The student generates winds across full-disk GEO imagery globally. Validation compares stereo and student models against radiosondes, operational AMVs, ERA5 reanalysis, and EarthCARE cloud profiles. Results through triple collocation show that stereo winds improve performance beyond operational AMVs for water vapor bands (6.2, 6.9, and 7.3 μm), wit degradation in the long-wave infrared (11.2 μm) band.

AI.tldr: Deep learning approach replaces traditional window-based tracking for atmospheric motion vectors (AMVs) with optical flow and distills stereo winds into single-satellite student model for global coverage.
AI.motivation: Traditional AMV methods have circular dependencies on NWP background states leading to inaccurate heights, high computational costs, and sparse retrievals. Stereo winds improve accuracy by eliminating NWP dependence but remain computationally heavy with limited coverage.
AI.method: Replace window-based tracking with deep optical flow for efficient stereo matching. Fine-tune using self-supervised geometric residual loss and supervised radiosonde reconstruction. Distill stereo teacher into single-satellite student model to eliminate multi-satellite requirements, with quality assurance via chi-square and height uncertainty emulation.
AI.result: Stereo winds outperform operational AMVs for water vapor bands (6.2, 6.9, 7.3 μm) in triple collocation validation against radiosondes, operational AMVs, ERA5 reanalysis, and EarthCARE cloud profiles, though degrade in long-wave infrared (11.2 μm) band. Student model generates winds across full-disk GEO imagery globally.
AI.conclusion: Deep learning-based optical flow with teacher-student distillation enables more accurate, computationally efficient atmospheric motion vector retrieval with global coverage, overcoming limitations of traditional methods and stereo approaches while maintaining quality assurance.

title: CulturalMenuBench: Probing the Knowledge-Application Gap in Multimodal Culinary Reasoning
comment: Accepted to EMNLP 2026 Findings. Code and data: https://github.com/BobTsang-NLP/CulturalMenuBench
summary: Multimodal language models achieve near-ceiling scores on food recognition benchmarks, yet it remains unclear whether this success reflects genuine cultural understanding or mere visual matching. To probe this distinction, we introduce CulturalMenuBench, a benchmark of 4,870 items in 10 languages across 18 regions; its 10 tasks pair final-dish and step-by-step cooking images with ingredients, procedural text, and regional labels, spanning basic recognition to process-grounded cultural attribution. Evaluating 12 models exposes a substantial knowledge-application gap: models exceeding 94% on standard multiple-choice tasks drop to at most 56% when attributing dishes to Chinese regional cuisines, despite an identical four-way format. Diagnostic analyses explain why: error patterns are consistent with random guessing, accuracy tracks visual distinctiveness rather than cultural structure, and models classify cuisines more accurately from dish names alone than from images (+7-18 points). The knowledge is thus present but cannot be activated through visual input. An ablation confirms these tasks genuinely require procedural evidence: removing sequential cooking images selectively degrades process-grounded tasks while others remain stable. Overall, CulturalMenuBench shows that near-perfect recognition can conceal an inability to apply cultural knowledge, motivating training that explicitly connects perception, procedure, and cultural context. Code and data are publicly available.

AI.tldr: Multimodal models perform well on standard food recognition but fail at cultural understanding tasks, showing a knowledge-application gap where they can't activate cultural knowledge through visual inputs.
AI.motivation: Despite multimodal models achieving high scores on food recognition benchmarks, it's unclear whether this reflects genuine cultural understanding or just visual pattern matching. The researchers wanted to probe whether models truly understand cultural context or merely perform visual matching.
AI.method: Created CulturalMenuBench - a comprehensive benchmark with 4,870 items across 10 languages and 18 regions. It includes 10 tasks pairing final-dish and step-by-step cooking images with ingredients, procedural text, and regional labels. Tasks range from basic recognition to process-grounded cultural attribution. Evaluated 12 different models on this benchmark.
AI.result: Revealed a substantial knowledge-application gap: models scoring over 94% on standard multiple-choice tasks dropped to at most 56% on cultural attribution tasks. Error patterns showed random guessing, accuracy tracked visual distinctiveness rather than cultural structure, and models performed better classifying cuisines from dish names alone (+7-18 points) than from images. Procedural evidence is genuinely required for these tasks.
AI.conclusion: Near-perfect recognition performance can conceal an inability to apply cultural knowledge. The knowledge exists in models but can't be activated through visual input alone. This motivates the need for training approaches that explicitly connect perception, procedure, and cultural context.

title: Scaling Laws, Tabular Data and Actuarial Ratemaking Models
summary: Scaling laws in modern deep learning describe how held-out loss improves as model capacity, training data, and compute increase, often following power-law trends. We investigate whether analogous scaling regularities arise in actuarial ratemaking, where data are tabular, heterogeneous, and noisy, and where classical models such as GLMs remain strong baselines. Using a real-world motor insurance portfolio, we train models from different families across increasing fractions of the training data and multiple random seeds, evaluating out-of-sample Poisson deviance, a likelihood-based loss for Poisson count predictions in which lower values indicate better held-out fit. We find that all model families improve with additional data, but scaling exponents differ substantially: TabM exhibits markedly stronger data scaling than purely supervised tabular Transformers and standard MLP baselines. Transformer variants show weak parameter scaling unless augmented with additional inductive biases (TabM-style adaptation or self-supervision). These results provide quantitative guidance on model selection by data regime and suggest that effective scaling on actuarial tabular tasks depends on architecture and loss function objective design, with simple increases in Transformer size providing limited gains.

AI.tldr: Actuarial ratemaking models show scaling behavior with data size, but scaling exponents vary by architecture. TabM demonstrates stronger data scaling than Transformers, which need additional inductive biases to scale effectively.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether scaling laws observed in modern deep learning (where performance improves with more data/compute) also apply in actuarial ratemaking with tabular, heterogeneous, noisy data where classical GLMs are strong baselines.
AI.method: Using real-world motor insurance portfolio, train models from different families across increasing fractions of training data with multiple random seeds. Evaluate out-of-sample Poisson deviance (likelihood-based loss for Poisson count predictions).
AI.result: All models improve with more data, but scaling exponents differ substantially: TabM shows strongest data scaling, while supervised Transformers show weak scaling without additional inductive biases (TabM-style adaptation or self-supervision). Simple Transformer size increases provide limited gains.
AI.conclusion: Effective scaling in actuarial tabular tasks depends on architecture and loss function design, not just data/compute increases. TabM demonstrates superior data scaling properties, providing quantitative guidance for model selection based on data regime.

title: NeoRed: A Knowledge-Logic-Alignment Multimodal Large Language Model for Neonatal Respiratory Disease Diagnosis
summary: Neonatal respiratory diseases are a major cause of neonatal morbidity and mortality, posing substantial challenges in clinical practice. Despite recent advances, existing Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) face two key limitations in neonatal diagnosis: (1) domain gap arising from predominantly adult training data; (2) insufficient integration of multidimensional clinical context for accurate diagnosis. To address these challenges, we collect two real-world clinical datasets (NeoCXR and NeoCXR-EV) and propose NeoRed, to the best of our knowledge, the first MLLM tailored for neonatal respiratory disease, filling the gap in neonatal diagnostic reports generation. To enhance joint diagnosis from heterogeneous clinical context and chest X-rays, we design a novel Knowledge-Logic-Alignment (KLA) framework which constrains model behavior from three perspectives: 1) Knowledge Prior Injection (KPI) incorporates neonatologist-inspired diagnostic priors into multimodal representations, guiding disease-specific attention across modalities; 2) Diagnostic Logic Constraint (DLC) aligns the semantics of generated reports with multimodal diagnostic logic; and 3) Visual Semantic Alignment (VSA) establishes semantic correspondence between visual features and imaging conclusions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that NeoRed enables accurate neonatal diagnostic reports generation, achieving ROUGE-L of 53.29% and Clinical Efficacy F1 score of 65.19% on NeoCXR, outperforming existing MLLMs. NeoRed also preserves competitive report generation performance on adult benchmarks (MIMIC-CXR and IU-Xray). Datasets will be available upon application.

AI.tldr: NeoRed is the first multimodal large language model specifically designed for neonatal respiratory disease diagnosis, addressing domain gaps and clinical context integration through a novel Knowledge-Logic-Alignment framework.
AI.motivation: Neonatal respiratory diseases cause significant morbidity and mortality, but existing MLLMs have two key limitations: 1) domain gap from predominantly adult training data, and 2) insufficient integration of multidimensional clinical context for accurate diagnosis.
AI.method: Collected two real-world neonatal clinical datasets (NeoCXR and NeoCXR-EV) and proposed NeoRed with a Knowledge-Logic-Alignment (KLA) framework that includes: 1) Knowledge Prior Injection incorporating neonatologist diagnostic priors, 2) Diagnostic Logic Constraint aligning report semantics with diagnostic logic, and 3) Visual Semantic Alignment establishing correspondence between visual features and imaging conclusions.
AI.result: NeoRed achieves ROUGE-L of 53.29% and Clinical Efficacy F1 score of 65.19% on NeoCXR, outperforming existing MLLMs for neonatal diagnostic report generation. It also maintains competitive performance on adult benchmarks (MIMIC-CXR and IU-Xray).
AI.conclusion: NeoRed successfully fills the gap in neonatal diagnostic report generation by addressing domain-specific challenges through its novel KLA framework, demonstrating superior performance for neonatal respiratory disease diagnosis while maintaining generalizability to adult benchmarks.

title: Kernel Reboot: Breaking the Boundaries of Neural Tangent Kernels for Neural Fields
comment: Published in IEEE TPAMI, vol. 48, no. 9, pp. 10940-10957, Sep. 2026. Author version adds related-work references and biography updates; Figures 12 and 13 were regenerated from the same locked hyperparameter sweep. Tabulated results, reported best points, scientific claims, and conclusions are unchanged
summary: Neural fields (NFs) map continuous coordinates to signals such as color or density, but fast high-quality reconstruction from sparse observations remains difficult. Classical Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) regression gives closed-form fits, yet it is fundamentally linear and cannot accumulate reusable task priors. We develop three algorithms that address these gaps. NTK-KIP learns a distilled support set of coordinates (and optional labels) so that a finite NTK can inpaint large missing regions from little observed data, yielding a compact non-linear representation instead of a raw kernel solve. MetaQuill meta-learns a shared initialization for an INR so that new scenes can be adapted by updating only a small task-specific weight offset, which provides true feature learning and a reusable prior. Finally, MetaQuill-KIP fuses both ideas: it seeds the task with a KIP-style non-linear warm start, then refines only that small offset around the meta-learned initialization. MetaQuill-KIP achieves high-PSNR reconstructions and semantically plausible inpainting under very sparse observations, while requiring only lightweight per-instance adaptation, whereas diffusion-style baselines typically depend on large pretrained generative priors and costly per-image tuning. This shows that NTK-driven neural fields can be made both non-linear and meta-learnable, narrowing the gap between analytic kernels and practical few-shot reconstruction.

AI.tldr: NTK-driven neural fields become non-linear and meta-learnable through three new algorithms (NTK-KIP, MetaQuill, MetaQuill-KIP) for high-quality reconstruction from sparse observations with lightweight adaptation.
AI.motivation: Neural fields struggle with fast high-quality reconstruction from sparse observations. Classical NTK regression is linear and cannot accumulate reusable task priors, creating a gap between analytic kernels and practical few-shot reconstruction.
AI.method: Three algorithms: 1) NTK-KIP learns distilled support sets for non-linear representation via finite NTK inpainting, 2) MetaQuill meta-learns shared INR initialization for feature learning with small task-specific offsets, 3) MetaQuill-KIP fuses both approaches with KIP-style warm start plus refinement around meta-learned initialization.
AI.result: MetaQuill-KIP achieves high-PSNR reconstructions and semantically plausible inpainting under very sparse observations with lightweight per-instance adaptation, outperforming diffusion-style baselines that require large pretrained priors and costly tuning.
AI.conclusion: NTK-driven neural fields can be made both non-linear and meta-learnable, narrowing the gap between analytic kernels and practical few-shot reconstruction for neural fields.

title: Feature Reconfiguration With Visual Prior for Medical Lesion Segmentation
summary: Lesion segmentation in medical images plays a critical role in clinical diagnosis and treatment planning. Despite significant advances, lesion segmentation remains challenging due to two major factors: (1) complex background interference; (2) diverse lesion morphology. Existing encoder-decoder based methods mainly focus on enhancing feature extraction or redesigning decoding strategies. However, they lack early prior guidance and feature reconfiguration during the encoding stage, limiting their effectiveness in handling these challenges. To address these limitations, we propose FreNet, a feature reconfiguration framework with visual priors, which performs pixel-level reconfiguration before encoding and feature-level reconfiguration during encoding for precise medical lesion segmentation. To suppress background responses, we propose an Implicit Prior Neural Network (IPNN), which models a continuous spatial field and leverages visual prior from SAM to reconfigure input image before encoding stage. To better handle diverse lesion morphology, we design a Dual-domain Feature Reconfiguration (DFR) module to progressively reconfigure backbone features during encoding stage. Within DFR, the Frequency Decoupling Module (FDM) decouples backbone features in frequency domain to enhance foreground-background discriminability, while the Spatial Localization Module (SLM) spatially relocates and improving spatial stability after frequency decoupling. Extensive experiments on 9 medical image segmentation benchmarks across three imaging modalities demonstrate that FreNet significantly outperforms state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods. On the challenging ETIS dataset, our method achieves Dice improvements of 5.0% over SOTA method and 7.2% over SAM.

AI.tldr: FreNet: A feature reconfiguration framework with visual priors that improves lesion segmentation through pixel-level reconfiguration before encoding and feature-level reconfiguration during encoding, outperforming SOTA methods on 9 medical benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Lesion segmentation in medical images remains challenging due to complex background interference and diverse lesion morphology. Existing encoder-decoder methods lack early prior guidance and feature reconfiguration during encoding, limiting effectiveness.
AI.method: Proposes FreNet with two key components: (1) Implicit Prior Neural Network (IPNN) that models continuous spatial field and uses SAM visual priors to reconfigure input images before encoding; (2) Dual-domain Feature Reconfiguration (DFR) module with Frequency Decoupling Module for frequency-domain feature enhancement and Spatial Localization Module for spatial stabilization during encoding.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on 9 medical image segmentation benchmarks across three imaging modalities show significant SOTA improvements. On ETIS dataset, achieves Dice improvements of 5.0% over SOTA and 7.2% over SAM.
AI.conclusion: FreNet effectively addresses background interference and diverse lesion morphology through systematic feature reconfiguration with visual priors, demonstrating superior performance and robustness across multiple medical imaging modalities and datasets.

title: Routing Is Not Enough: Diagnosing Intra-Adapter Subspace Contention in MoE+LoRA Fine-Tuning
comment: 13 pages, 1 figure, 16 tables. Accepted to Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026
summary: Multi-domain fine-tuning often combines MoE routing with LoRA, assuming that token-level routing separates domain-specific updates. We test this assumption in MoE+LoRA using Python code paired with biomedical text and mathematical reasoning. Although these domains show near-disjoint expert routing, adding biomedical data substantially increases code perplexity, indicating that routing separation alone may not prevent negative transfer. To localize the failure, we introduce Jaccard routing overlap and adapter-gradient cosine similarity, which measure expert sharing and update compatibility, respectively. These diagnostics indicate that interference arises mostly from nearly orthogonal domain gradients competing within the same low-rank adapter subspace. We address this issue with SpawnLoRA, which dynamically adds gated sub-adapters inside MoE experts when adapter-level contention is detected, while keeping the router fixed. We evaluate SpawnLoRA on Phi-tiny-MoE-instruct and OLMoE-1B-7B across multiple mixture settings and find that it effectively reduces negative transfer compared with standard and rank-adaptive LoRA. These results demonstrate that structural separation inside experts provides benefits beyond routing or rank expansion alone.

AI.tldr: MoE+LoRA routing doesn't prevent negative transfer between domains; SpawnLoRA adds dynamic sub-adapters to handle gradient competition within experts.
AI.motivation: The paper challenges the assumption that MoE routing combined with LoRA can effectively separate domain-specific updates and prevent negative transfer between domains during fine-tuning.
AI.method: Researchers test MoE+LoRA on Python code with biomedical text and math, introduce Jaccard routing overlap and adapter-gradient cosine similarity diagnostics, and propose SpawnLoRA which dynamically adds gated sub-adapters inside MoE experts when contention is detected.
AI.result: Despite near-disjoint expert routing, adding biomedical data substantially increases code perplexity. SpawnLoRA effectively reduces negative transfer compared to standard and rank-adaptive LoRA across multiple mixture settings on Phi-tiny-MoE-instruct and OLMoE-1B-7B.
AI.conclusion: Routing separation alone isn't sufficient to prevent negative transfer; structural separation inside experts (via SpawnLoRA) provides benefits beyond routing or rank expansion, addressing interference from orthogonal domain gradients competing within the same adapter subspace.

title: Dalek: A Constructive Agent Machine
summary:
We present Dalek, a closed machine designed for agents that realizes self-maintenance, self-evolution, self-reproduction, and self-organization on any substrate satisfying a general host contract. The machine is built from three primitives---actors, messages, and channels. Four obligations---a host boundary, a construction language, admissible transitions, and rule heredity---give its boundary, identity, and closure a structural basis.
  Von Neumann's 1948 self-reproducing automaton supplies a hereditary constructional core: a self-description together with a constructor, a copier, and a controller. Dalek combines this core with the four obligations and rederives its medium for a text-and-message agent substrate, adding explicit structures for boundary, identity, history, and growth. A large language model and a compiler occupy the payload position and form a general capability producer. New capabilities are authored, compiled, installed into the description, and inherited by descendants. The same path produces the machine's own organs and even its runtime, closing heredity and evolution within the machine.

AI.tldr: Dalek is a closed machine architecture for agents that enables self-maintenance, evolution, reproduction, and organization across substrates via actors, messages, and channels with hereditary capabilities.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to create a machine architecture that can achieve complete self-sufficiency - self-maintenance, self-evolution, self-reproduction, and self-organization - on any substrate that satisfies a general host contract, addressing the challenge of creating truly autonomous, evolvable systems.
AI.method: Combines Von Neumann's 1948 self-reproducing automaton (with self-description, constructor, copier, controller) with four architectural obligations (host boundary, construction language, admissible transitions, rule heredity). Implements using three primitives: actors, messages, and channels. Uses a large language model and compiler as a capability producer for creating new capabilities that can be authored, compiled, installed into descriptions, and inherited.
AI.result: The Dalek machine achieves hereditary constructional closure by adding explicit structures for boundary, identity, history, and growth to Von Neumann's core. It can produce its own organs and runtime through the same capability creation path, enabling heredity and evolution to be fully contained within the machine architecture.
AI.conclusion: Dalek demonstrates a practical realization of a closed, self-sufficient machine architecture that can maintain, evolve, reproduce, and organize itself on any suitable substrate, achieving full heredity and evolutionary closure by combining Von Neumann's self-reproduction principles with modern architectural constructs and AI-based capability production.

title: Frontier LLMs are effective batch optimizers: Assessing reasoning models in continuous and discrete settings
summary: Frontier large language models (LLMs) have become attractive priors for optimization due to their large-scale pretraining that enables them to navigate a variety of optimization settings. However, the effectiveness of modern reasoning LLMs in batch optimization settings remains underexplored. Here we investigate the performance of the current generation of frontier LLMs as batch optimizers in both continuous and discrete settings. We find that while LLMs are competitive zero-shot batch optimizers for numerical test functions, their performance is brittle compared to classical non-LLM optimization approaches. However, LLM priors are significantly better in semantically rich settings, indicating that their batch optimization behavior is highly effective when navigating and reasoning over the discrete spaces most similar in structure to their pretraining data.

AI.tldr: LLMs show potential as batch optimizers but perform best in discrete, semantically rich spaces similar to their pretraining data, while being brittle compared to classical methods for numerical optimization.
AI.motivation: To investigate the effectiveness of frontier LLMs as batch optimizers in continuous and discrete settings, given that their large-scale pretraining makes them attractive priors for optimization but their performance in batch optimization remains underexplored.
AI.method: Evaluating current generation frontier LLMs as batch optimizers across both continuous and discrete optimization settings, comparing their performance against classical non-LLM optimization approaches.
AI.result: LLMs are competitive zero-shot batch optimizers for numerical test functions but show brittleness compared to classical methods. However, LLM priors significantly outperform in semantically rich settings where discrete spaces resemble their pretraining data structure.
AI.conclusion: LLMs' batch optimization effectiveness is domain-dependent - they excel in discrete, semantically meaningful spaces similar to their training data, suggesting their optimization capabilities are strongest when leveraging semantic understanding rather than pure numerical optimization.

title: GPS-Bench: A Governance Policy Benchmark for Automating Policy Analysis
summary: Policy analysis requires more than predicting whether a proposal will pass: it requires identifying who will be affected, how those actors respond, and what follows. LLM-based policy simulations model these processes at scale, but their validity is hard to establish when plausible behaviour is never compared with observed outcomes. We introduce GPS-Bench, an evidence-grounded benchmark for governance policy simulation that links policies to relevant actors, actor actions and downstream impacts using legislative records, lobbying disclosures, regulatory documents, corporate filings, economic data and other public evidence. Actors are reconstructed from the dated record rather than prompted as archetypes, so a persona is an evidence object with provenance; a human-annotated pool forms the Gold evaluation set, while cases labelled by a separate LLM from retrieved evidence are treated as Silver supervision and never as test labels. Because every inference mode reads the same grounded state and emits the same schema, GPS-Bench turns "does multi-agent simulation help?" into a controlled comparison: we contrast joint reasoning, independent and communicating actor agents, graph-based methods and weight-level fine-tuning over one policy state. Fine-tuning on the grounded record gives the strongest actor-level impact prediction, and decomposition does not beat it; what decomposition adds is mechanism. Agents hold private, non-identical evidence, each seeing its own exposure clause, and address named partners with concrete joint proposals, what they offer, what they need in return, and why acting together beats acting alone, so the coalitions that form can be checked against the commitments the record holds. GPS-Bench therefore gives a common empirical setting for studying when evidence, actor modelling and multi-agent interaction improve the prediction and interpretation of policy outcomes.

AI.tldr: GPS-Bench is an evidence-grounded benchmark for governance policy simulation that uses real legislative records and other public evidence to evaluate different multi-agent simulation approaches for predicting policy outcomes.
AI.motivation: Current LLM-based policy simulations lack validation because they don't compare simulated behaviors with actual observed outcomes. Policy analysis requires understanding who is affected, how actors respond, and downstream impacts, which current methods don't sufficiently address with empirical grounding.
AI.method: Create GPS-Bench using legislative records, lobbying disclosures, regulatory documents, corporate filings, and economic data to reconstruct real actors as evidence objects. Use human-annotated Gold evaluation set and LLM-labeled Silver supervision set from retrieved evidence. Compare multiple simulation methods: joint reasoning, independent/communicating actor agents, graph-based methods, and weight-level fine-tuning on the same policy state.
AI.result: Fine-tuning on grounded evidence provides the strongest actor-level impact prediction, outperforming decomposition methods. What decomposition adds is mechanism explanation - showing how coalitions form through private evidence sharing and concrete joint proposals. The benchmark enables controlled comparison of how evidence, actor modeling, and multi-agent interaction improve policy outcome prediction.
AI.conclusion: GPS-Bench provides an empirical framework for studying when evidence grounding, actor modeling, and multi-agent interactions actually improve policy outcome prediction and interpretation, moving beyond mere passage prediction to understanding real-world policy impacts and coalition formation dynamics.

title: Portable Causal Fairness Across Synthetic Data Generator Families
summary: When a statistical agency or regulator releases synthetic data in place of sensitive records, it chooses the generator that produces the table, and can shape that generator so unfair pathways are absent. DECAF made this concrete on one non-private GAN: three fairness definitions become three sets of edge cuts on the generator's causal graph. Whether the mechanism belongs to DECAF, or to causal factorisation itself, was untested. We port all three definitions to nine generators from three unrelated families (marginals-based, GAN, and diffusion, each with differentially private variants), across three levels of formal privacy guarantee, over 2,520 matched-pair runs on Adult and COMPAS datasets. The mechanism transfers everywhere, and our new causal diffusion backbone yields the fairest release of any family we tested, at fidelity close to the marginals tier. Applying the cut barely moves fidelity, only costs a downstream classifier about $0.07$ to $0.15$ AUC on average, and adding privacy guarantees don't make the data less fair.
