AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates that fairness interventions (three causal fairness definitions applied as edge cuts in DECAF) transfer effectively across nine different data generators from three families (marginals, GAN, diffusion) with differential privacy variants, showing causal fairness mechanisms work broadly and diffusion models produce fairest results.
AI.motivation: When statistical agencies release synthetic data instead of sensitive records, they need to ensure fairness in the generated data by removing unfair pathways. DECAF proposed fairness interventions on generators, but it was unclear whether this fairness mechanism was specific to DECAF or general to causal factorization approaches.
AI.method: Port three causal fairness definitions (from DECAF) to nine different generators from three unrelated families: marginals-based, GAN, and diffusion models, each with differentially private variants. Test across three privacy guarantee levels with 2,520 matched-pair runs on Adult and COMPAS datasets.
AI.result: The fairness mechanism transfers successfully across all generator families. Causal diffusion backbones produce the fairest releases among tested families, with fidelity close to marginals-based approaches. Applying fairness cuts has minimal impact on fidelity and only slightly reduces downstream classifier performance (0.07-0.15 AUC on average). Privacy guarantees don't compromise fairness.
AI.conclusion: Causal fairness mechanisms are generalizable across different generator types and privacy settings, with diffusion models emerging as particularly effective for producing fair synthetic data while maintaining reasonable fidelity and classifier performance.

title: HalluPeer: A Taxonomy-driven Benchmark for Detecting Hallucinations in Scientific Peer Reviews
summary: The growing scale of academic peer review has motivated the use of Large Language Models (LLMs) as review assistants, yet LLMs can generate fluent but unsupported claims that undermine review reliability. Existing hallucination benchmarks are not designed for peer review, where verification requires grounding claims in long, technical papers. We introduce HalluPeer, a benchmark for detecting hallucinations in scientific peer reviews, providing aligned triples of paper content, human-written reviews, and hallucination-injected reviews, annotated for detection, classification, and localization. Our pipeline induces a peer-review-specific hallucination taxonomy, identifies review contexts, and injects hallucinations with automated filtering. Experiments on 12K papers and 38K reviews show that existing detectors struggle to separate hallucinations from legitimate critique, while evaluation on authentic reviews demonstrates that HalluPeer-defined hallucination patterns occur in real peer reviews, highlighting the critical need for source-aware verification. Our project page can be found in https://github.com/Lin-TzuLing/HalluPeer.git

AI.tldr: HalluPeer is a benchmark for detecting hallucinations in scientific peer reviews, featuring paper-review triples with hallucination annotations, showing existing detectors struggle with peer-review-specific hallucination detection.
AI.motivation: As LLMs are increasingly used as peer review assistants, they can generate fluent but unsupported claims that undermine review reliability. Existing hallucination benchmarks are not designed for peer review, where verification requires grounding claims in long, technical papers.
AI.method: Developed a benchmark with aligned triples of paper content, human-written reviews, and hallucination-injected reviews. Created a peer-review-specific hallucination taxonomy, identified review contexts, and injected hallucinations with automated filtering. Evaluated on 12K papers and 38K reviews.
AI.result: Experiments show existing detectors struggle to separate hallucinations from legitimate critique. Evaluation on authentic reviews demonstrates that HalluPeer-defined hallucination patterns occur in real peer reviews, highlighting the need for source-aware verification.
AI.conclusion: HalluPeer addresses the critical need for source-aware verification in peer review, providing a specialized benchmark to improve hallucination detection in scientific peer reviews where existing methods fall short.

title: Language-encoded network topology enables large language models to reason about complex networks
summary: Networks describe systems in biology and beyond, from protein interactions and social relationships to power grids and citation records. Reasoning about such systems requires understanding their structure: which elements are central, which connections bridge separate communities, and how it changes when elements are removed. Although large language models (LLMs) excel at natural language, they struggle with such questions when networks are given as edge lists, sentences or measurement tables, because their structural meaning must be inferred. Here we introduce BioGlyph, which compiles network topology into an interpretable and transferable language of structural roles. BioGlyph combines graph partitioning and structural measurements to identify roles such as hubs, community cores and cross-community connectors, and fixed rules to translate them into a universal vocabulary. The representation describes each element through its structural role, supporting evidence and semantic consequences, leaving both the network and the LLM unchanged. Across twenty networks spanning five domains, BioGlyph substantially improves open LLMs' ability to answer structural reasoning questions, outperforming edge-based, numerical and learned representations by up to 26 percentage points in system accuracy. Ablations show that the gain comes from explicitly encoding structural roles in semantically interpretable terms. The gain is more prominent in dense, community-structured networks and diminishes in sparse networks whose topology is more readily inferred from text. In a budding-yeast protein-interaction network, BioGlyph exposes biological organization: cross-community connectors are enriched for essential genes, whereas peripheral proteins are depleted. BioGlyph thus provides an interpretable representation for both language models and scientists to reason about network structure.

AI.tldr: BioGlyph is a method that translates network topology into interpretable structural roles (hubs, community cores, connectors) using a universal vocabulary, significantly improving LLMs' ability to answer structural reasoning questions about networks.
AI.motivation: LLMs struggle with understanding network structure when presented as edge lists, sentences, or measurement tables, because the structural meaning of connections must be inferred. Networks are fundamental to understanding biological and other complex systems, but current representations don't capture structural roles effectively for language models.
AI.method: BioGlyph combines graph partitioning and structural measurements to identify structural roles like hubs, community cores, and cross-community connectors. It uses fixed rules to translate these roles into a universal vocabulary, creating an interpretable representation that describes each element through its structural role, supporting evidence, and semantic consequences while leaving both the network and LLM unchanged.
AI.result: Across 20 networks spanning 5 domains, BioGlyph substantially improves open LLMs' ability to answer structural reasoning questions, outperforming edge-based, numerical, and learned representations by up to 26 percentage points in system accuracy. The gain comes from explicitly encoding structural roles in semantically interpretable terms. In a budding-yeast protein-interaction network, BioGlyph reveals biological organization: cross-community connectors are enriched for essential genes, whereas peripheral proteins are depleted.
AI.conclusion: BioGlyph provides an interpretable representation that enables both language models and scientists to reason about network structure effectively, bridging the gap between network topology and natural language understanding.

title: The Attention Triangle in Audio-Video Models
summary: Audio-video diffusion models rely on cross-modal attention to coordinate text, sound, and visual content, yet this same mechanism can introduce subtle and systematic semantic leakage. We study these models by probing and analyzing the ``attention triangle,'' comprising the three cross-attention edges connecting the text, audio, and video streams, and examine how semantic information is routed across modalities during generation. Our analysis reveals that routing along the audio-video edge is bidirectional: audio can influence video generation, while video can influence audio generation. This edge is shaped by biases encoded in the model's parameters and emerges as a major contributor to leakage: when prompts are in tension with learned priors, cross-modal interactions may override the intended conditioning and reroute semantics toward visually canonical but incorrect outcomes. These effects suggest that semantic artifacts arise not merely from attention spreading beyond its intended target, but from structured, bias-driven interactions along specific pathways. Building on this perspective, we extract attention-derived signals that expose how semantics are distributed and grounded across modalities, and use them as a diagnostic tool to both analyze and deliberately incur leakage under controlled conditions. This enables us to probe the internal dynamics of cross-modal routing and isolate the role of individual interactions. We further leverage these signals to guide inference-time interventions that encourage more consistent cross-modal alignment. Extensive experiments support our analysis and demonstrate improved semantic grounding while preserving generation quality.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes semantic leakage in audio-video diffusion models through cross-modal attention pathways, identifying biased routing patterns and developing interventions for better alignment.
AI.motivation: Audio-video diffusion models using cross-modal attention suffer from semantic leakage where conditioning information gets overridden by learned biases, leading to incorrect generation outcomes that contradict intended prompts.
AI.method: Analyzes the "attention triangle" - three cross-attention edges connecting text, audio, and video streams. Extracts attention-derived signals to diagnose leakage, probes internal dynamics of cross-modal routing, and develops inference-time interventions to improve alignment.
AI.result: Reveals that audio-video routing is bidirectional and major contributor to leakage, identifies structured bias-driven interactions along specific pathways, demonstrates diagnostic tools to analyze leakage, and shows interventions that improve semantic grounding while preserving generation quality.
AI.conclusion: Semantic artifacts in audio-video diffusion arise from structured, bias-driven cross-modal interactions rather than just attention overspreading; attention-derived signals enable both analysis and controlled intervention for better cross-modal alignment.

title: The 2026 PNPL Competition: Word Classification and Efficient Cross-Subject Generalisation in LibriBrain100
summary:
The ambition of the 2025 PNPL competition (Landau et al., 2025) was to launch a multi-year curriculum for non-invasive speech decoding. Designed to progress from foundational tasks toward the linguistic complexity required for a practical brain-computer interface (BCI), it set the stage with speech detection and phoneme classification tasks. Winning submissions reached F1-macro scores of 95.6% and 73.6% on the respective tasks (Elvers et al., 2026), highly significant advances. This success was built on the LibriBrain dataset (Özdogan et al., 2025), the largest within-subject MEG dataset recorded at the time with ${\sim}50$ hours of data for one subject. However, while within-subject scale drives strong decoding performance, a practical BCI must generalise to new users from minutes of data, not hours.
  The 2026 PNPL competition responds to this challenge with LibriBrain100 (Mantegna et al., 2026), an extended LibriBrain dataset with 32 additional subjects (${\sim}40$ minutes each) plus even more within-subject data (${\sim}80$ hours). Advancing the curriculum of tasks to focus on word classification, two complementary tracks are presented in this competition: the Deep track targets within-subject word classification at scale, aiming at the best possible performance; the Broad track targets cross-subject generalisation, progressively reducing the amount of subject-specific fine-tuning data from ${\sim}40$ to ${\sim}20$ to ${\sim}10$ minutes, a duration that falls within a clinically feasible range and brings us a step closer to a non-invasive BCI capable of restoring communication to people living with profound paralysis.

AI.tldr: The 2026 PNPL competition introduces LibriBrain100 dataset with cross-subject word classification tasks, advancing non-invasive speech BCI development from within-subject to clinically feasible cross-subject generalization.
AI.motivation: The 2025 PNPL competition achieved strong within-subject speech decoding performance, but practical BCIs must generalize to new users with minimal data (minutes rather than hours). There's a need to bridge the gap between research performance and clinically feasible deployment for paralyzed patients.
AI.method: 1) Created LibriBrain100 dataset with 32 additional subjects (~40 minutes each) plus more within-subject data (~80 hours). 2) Introduced two competition tracks: Deep track for within-subject word classification at scale, and Broad track for cross-subject generalization with progressive reduction of fine-tuning data from ~40 to ~20 to ~10 minutes.
AI.result: The 2025 competition achieved F1-macro scores of 95.6% for speech detection and 73.6% for phoneme classification using LibriBrain dataset. The 2026 competition builds on this by advancing to word classification tasks with cross-subject generalization objectives.
AI.conclusion: The 2026 PNPL competition represents a significant step toward clinically feasible non-invasive speech BCIs by shifting focus from within-subject to cross-subject generalization with minimal fine-tuning data, bringing the field closer to practical applications for paralyzed patients.

title: KC-Bench: A Dynamic Interactive Benchmark for Evaluating Knowledge Conflicts in LLM Agents
summary: As LLMs increasingly act through tools, they must reconcile user instructions, parametric knowledge, and dynamic environmental observations before taking actions. We introduce KC-Bench, a controlled multi-turn benchmark for measuring this capability across world-knowledge conflicts, input inconsistencies, and multi-source temporal conflicts. Its 238 tasks are manually screened from more than 1,000 generated candidates and combine a user simulator, stateful tools, deterministic environment assertions, an open-source natural-language evaluator, and human trajectory verification. Evaluation of nine models, including DeepSeek-V4-Flash, GLM-5.2, and MiniMax-M3, shows substantial cross-domain variation: no model handles factual correction, identity consistency checking, and temporal conflict resolution reliably across all settings. In the simulated environments, missed conflicts can propagate to tool calls or synthetic protected-data flows. KC-Bench isolates this model-level behavior rather than ranking complete agent frameworks, and provides a reproducible diagnostic for developing conflict-aware reasoning and execution safeguards.

AI.tldr: KC-Bench is a controlled multi-turn benchmark for evaluating how LLMs handle conflicts between user instructions, parametric knowledge, and environmental observations, with tests across world-knowledge conflicts, input inconsistencies, and multi-source temporal conflicts.
AI.motivation: As LLMs increasingly use tools to act in dynamic environments, they need to properly reconcile potentially conflicting information from user instructions, their parametric knowledge, and real-time environmental observations. Current models struggle with handling these conflicts reliably, which can lead to problematic tool calls or data flows.
AI.method: Created KC-Bench with 238 manually screened tasks from over 1,000 generated candidates. The benchmark combines: a user simulator, stateful tools, deterministic environment assertions, an open-source natural-language evaluator, and human trajectory verification. Evaluated nine models including DeepSeek-V4-Flash, GLM-5.2, and MiniMax-M3.
AI.result: Substantial cross-domain variation observed: no model reliably handled factual correction, identity consistency checking, and temporal conflict resolution across all settings. In simulated environments, missed conflicts can propagate to tool calls or synthetic protected-data flows.
AI.conclusion: KC-Bench provides a reproducible diagnostic for developing conflict-aware reasoning and execution safeguards in LLMs. It isolates model-level behavior rather than ranking complete agent frameworks, offering targeted insights into how models handle conflicting information sources.

title: B2B Customer Conversion Prediction: A Document Representation, Graph Theory, and CatBoost Driven Methodology
comment: 10 pages, 6 figures. Presented at the 2nd Workshop on End-End Customer Journey Optimization at KDD 2023
summary: In the one-time selling B2B context, the buying cycle may last months or even years. During the long process, targeting customers that have a high potential to make purchases and recommending personalized campaigns accordingly are important for effective marketing. For this goal, we study the following problems, B2B customer data aggregation, customer feature generation, and prediction of whether a B2B customer would show interest in making a purchase (i.e., prediction of conversion into sales funnel). We propose an algorithm to aggregate individual contacts to the B2B customer level based on multiple keys. For non-standardized keys such as company names, we propose a novel architecture to cluster them in a domain encompassing irregularities such as spelling mistakes and spelling variants. We then define and generate a set of features and apply the CatBoost model for customer conversion prediction. Our framework achieves 91\% prediction accuracy. Based on the prediction results and analysis of the model, we then discuss personalized campaign recommendations to foster conversion.

AI.tldr: Framework for B2B customer prediction: aggregates contact data, cleans company names via clustering, generates features, uses CatBoost for conversion prediction with 91% accuracy, enables personalized campaigns.
AI.motivation: B2B sales cycles are long (months/years), making it crucial to identify high-potential customers early and recommend personalized campaigns for effective marketing. Need to handle messy B2B data with irregularities.
AI.method: 1) Multi-key algorithm to aggregate individual contacts to B2B customer level; 2) Novel clustering architecture for non-standardized company names (handles spelling mistakes/variants); 3) Feature generation; 4) CatBoost model for conversion prediction.
AI.result: Framework achieves 91% prediction accuracy for B2B customer conversion. Model analysis provides insights for personalized campaign recommendations to foster conversion.
AI.conclusion: Proposed end-to-end framework effectively handles B2B data challenges, predicts customer conversion with high accuracy, and enables data-driven personalized marketing campaigns in long B2B sales cycles.

title: A computable representation of the physical laboratory enables verifiable workflows
summary: Making science computable requires representations of both scientific knowledge and the physical world in which scientific claims are tested. A computable representation of the physical laboratory is established through typed research objects, capability-bound operations and a compositional workflow algebra. It provides the physical-world counterpart to machine-readable knowledge, expressing workflows as programs over evolving laboratory states with explicit dependencies, decisions, iteration and concurrency. The representation was implemented in a modular agentic robotic laboratory by binding formal operations to executable Function Skills. For diverse scientific intents, capability-relative workflows were generated, while stateful simulation propagated object transformations and verified operation preconditions and laboratory constraints before dispatch. The proposed representation and its engineering framework jointly establish a general computational interface between agent reasoning and capability-bound physical transformations, providing a foundation for end-to-end autonomous scientific discovery.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a computable representation of physical laboratories using typed research objects, capability-bound operations, and workflow algebra to connect machine-readable knowledge with physical-world experimentation.
AI.motivation: Making science computable requires representations that bridge scientific knowledge and the physical world where scientific claims are tested. There's a need to establish a computational interface between agent reasoning and physical laboratory transformations.
AI.method: Developed a computable representation using typed research objects, capability-bound operations, and a compositional workflow algebra. Implemented this in a modular agentic robotic laboratory by binding formal operations to executable Function Skills. Used stateful simulation to propagate object transformations and verify operation preconditions before dispatch.
AI.result: Successfully generated capability-relative workflows for diverse scientific intents. The representation enabled expressing workflows as programs over evolving laboratory states with explicit dependencies, decisions, iteration, and concurrency. The framework verifies operation preconditions and laboratory constraints before dispatch.
AI.conclusion: The proposed representation and engineering framework establish a general computational interface between agent reasoning and capability-bound physical transformations, providing a foundation for end-to-end autonomous scientific discovery.

title: FlowBalance: Verifier-Grounded Self-Improvement from On-Policy Reasoning Experience
comment: 28 pages, 7 figures, 10 tables. Code and blog available
summary: A reasoning model can improve from its own on-policy experience, but this inner loop is fragile: terminal verifiers provide reliable yet sparse supervision, while dense same-model guidance can reinforce false confidence or overconcentrate learning on a narrow solution mode. We introduce FlowBalance, a verifier-grounded self-improvement method that learns a normalized distribution over complete responses. For each on-policy trajectory, a frozen training-time view of the same policy uses privileged context to produce token-level log-probability gains, which are aggregated into a trajectory-level self-guidance score. FlowBalance calibrates this score with the verifier-derived group advantage: guidance is retained on positive-advantage trajectories, reversed on negative-advantage trajectories, and disabled when the rollout group provides no outcome preference. The resulting energy exponentially reweights a reference policy, and profiled trajectory balance fits the normalized target with one log-partition estimate per rollout group. This realizes outcome-calibrated self-guidance via trajectory balance, without a separate token-level imitation loss. Our analysis establishes within-group contrast preservation, a minimum-change reverse-KL characterization, monotonic verifier control of target reward, and an exact correction against false-positive self-guidance on rejected responses. On mathematical reasoning, FlowBalance improves average performance over FlowRL on both Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B, while also improving training speed and stability, avoiding direct OPSD's response-length collapse, and exhibiting higher correct-strategy diversity in a controlled AIME24 diagnostic.

AI.tldr: FlowBalance is a verifier-grounded self-improvement method that learns normalized distributions over complete responses, using outcome-calibrated self-guidance via trajectory balance to improve reasoning models without separate token-level imitation loss.
AI.motivation: Current reasoning model self-improvement approaches have limitations: terminal verifiers provide sparse but reliable supervision, while dense same-model guidance can reinforce false confidence or concentrate learning on narrow solution modes, creating a fragile inner loop.
AI.method: FlowBalance uses a frozen training-time policy view with privileged context to produce token-level log-probability gains, aggregates these into trajectory-level self-guidance scores, then calibrates them with verifier-derived group advantage. It retains guidance on positive-advantage trajectories, reverses it on negative ones, and disables it when no outcome preference exists. The method realizes outcome-calibrated self-guidance via trajectory balance with one log-partition estimate per rollout group.
AI.result: On mathematical reasoning tasks, FlowBalance improves average performance over FlowRL on both Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B models, while also improving training speed/stability, avoiding response-length collapse seen in direct OPSD, and exhibiting higher correct-strategy diversity in AIME24 diagnostics.
AI.conclusion: FlowBalance provides an effective verifier-grounded self-improvement framework that addresses limitations of existing methods through outcome-calibrated self-guidance and trajectory balance, offering improved performance, stability, and solution diversity while maintaining theoretical guarantees like contrast preservation and false-positive correction.

title: Analysis of Prompt Engineering for Drug Toxicity Prediction
summary: Clinical trials in the UK can cost up to £1.3 million, with approximately 90% drug failure rate. Toxicity is a major contributing factor in drug failure. Testing is time and cost intensive. In recent years, the use of artificial intelligence has been increasingly explored to aid in the prediction of drug toxicity, with extensive use of large language models (LLMs). However, LLMs can show considerable variation when minor changes are made to prompts, which raises concerns about their sensitivity to prompt engineering. Prompt engineering is used to optimise a prompt given to an LLM to generate the desired output. This paper proposes a method to analyse prompt engineering for drug toxicity prediction. The aim of the paper is to investigate the importance of prompt phrasing for drug toxicity prediction. LLMs were prompted to identify chemical properties of significance when predicting drug toxicity. Prompts were constructed to investigate; job role, prompt structuring, and rule interpretation. LLMs were then used to generate datasets, using the identified features from initial prompting, which were then passed to machine learning algorithms. The experiments show that the natural variance which occurs in LLMs outweighs any fine-tuning of prompts. There were, however, substantial improvements in model performance when using chemoinformatic code to extract features instead of using LLM-generated values. The proposed analysis methodology is applicable to a wide range of prompt types across different areas of bioinformatics.

AI.tldr: LLMs show significant variability in drug toxicity prediction that outweighs prompt engineering effects, but chemoinformatic feature extraction substantially improves model performance.
AI.motivation: Clinical trials are extremely expensive with high failure rates (up to £1.3M, 90% failure), with toxicity being a major factor. AI/LLMs are increasingly used for toxicity prediction but show concerning sensitivity to prompt variations, raising questions about prompt engineering reliability.
AI.method: Developed a method to analyze prompt engineering for drug toxicity prediction by prompting LLMs to identify significant chemical properties. Investigated prompt phrasing variations across job roles, prompt structuring, and rule interpretation. Used LLM-generated features to create datasets, then fed these to machine learning algorithms. Compared results with chemoinformatic code-based feature extraction.
AI.result: The natural variance in LLMs outweighed any fine-tuning effects from prompt engineering. However, substantial performance improvements were achieved when using chemoinformatic code to extract features instead of relying on LLM-generated values.
AI.conclusion: While LLMs show promise for drug toxicity prediction, their inherent variability limits prompt engineering benefits. The proposed analysis methodology is broadly applicable across bioinformatics domains and highlights the advantage of using traditional chemoinformatic methods over LLM-generated features.

title: Selective Hypergraph Refinement for Frozen Graph Clustering
summary: Existing graph-clustering methods typically improve clustering performance by optimizing model parameters and node representations. Effective means of further improving the clustering results of an already trained and frozen model, however, remain limited. We study post-processing for frozen graph clustering. After checkpoint fixation, the procedure uses no labels and updates neither model parameters, node representations, nor the original graph structure. Instead, it exploits an attribute hypergraph to supplement higher-order relations that ordinary graphs cannot readily express, thereby refining existing cluster assignments. Because global hypergraph refinement can yield both performance gains and erroneous updates, we propose Selective Hypergraph Refinement (SHR). The method generates candidate residual directions from the hypergraph and evaluates their reliability using graph structure, node attributes, and matched-null evidence. It updates only nodes with sufficient support and otherwise retains their original assignments. Further analysis shows that whether a node changes cluster is jointly governed by its native assignment gap and the directional strength of the refinement. In a controlled common-suite evaluation, 13 of 15 backbone-dataset cells had a positive mean macro gain, one produced exact no-action, and one was negative. The cell-equal macro gain was 0.066 pp (95% bootstrap CI, [0.030, 0.107] pp), while only 0.209% of hard assignments changed on average. A broader 15-combination native-interface evaluation yielded a macro gain of 0.137 pp at a mean change ratio of 0.375%. These results indicate that frozen clustering outputs retain a limited but measurable refinement space after training. The effect is heterogeneous across backbone-dataset pairs, and broader coverage also increases exposure to negative transfer.

AI.tldr: SHR is a post-processing method that selectively refines frozen graph clustering outputs using attribute hypergraphs without updating model parameters or representations.
AI.motivation: Existing methods lack effective ways to improve clustering results of already trained and frozen models. There's limited post-processing capability for frozen graph clustering after model checkpoint fixation.
AI.method: Selective Hypergraph Refinement (SHR) uses an attribute hypergraph to supplement higher-order relations that ordinary graphs cannot express. It generates candidate residual directions from the hypergraph and evaluates reliability using graph structure, node attributes, and matched-null evidence. It only updates nodes with sufficient support, otherwise retaining original assignments.
AI.result: In controlled evaluation: 13/15 backbone-dataset cells had positive mean macro gain, 1 produced no-action, 1 negative. Cell-equal macro gain was 0.066 pp (95% CI [0.030, 0.107] pp). Only 0.209% of hard assignments changed on average. Broader evaluation: macro gain of 0.137 pp at mean change ratio of 0.375%.
AI.conclusion: Frozen clustering outputs retain a limited but measurable refinement space after training. The effect is heterogeneous across backbone-dataset pairs, and broader coverage increases exposure to negative transfer.

title: Synthetic Semantic Supervision for Contrastive Code Representation Learning in Small Transformers: An Empirical Study
summary: General-purpose code embeddings power tools for code search, classification, and retrieval. Compact transformer encoders for code typically rely on either human-written docstrings (labor-intensive and inconsistent) or mined structural signals such as execution traces (setting-specific and costly to collect). We empirically study an alternative: contrastive pretraining of small encoders with synthetically generated natural-language descriptions emphasizing code functionality and intent, paired with code in a dual-encoder framework at training and discarded at inference. We benchmark this approach against pretraining-based baselines, generalist LLMs, and embedding-specific models on eight retrieval, classification, and generation tasks across C, C++, and Java. Synthetic semantic supervision yields statistically significant gains over pretraining baselines of the same inference-time size on five of eight tasks, with parity on two more; once fine-tuned, it matches or exceeds zero-shot models two orders of magnitude larger on classification, and it stays on par with execution-aware supervision at matched pretraining data, suggesting a scalable, effective alternative to existing code-representation paradigms.

AI.tldr: Synthetic natural-language descriptions paired with code during contrastive pretraining produce effective code embeddings that compete with much larger models and execution-based methods.
AI.motivation: Existing code embedding methods rely on either labor-intensive human-written docstrings (inconsistent) or costly execution traces (setting-specific and expensive to collect). There's a need for scalable, effective alternatives for code representation.
AI.method: Contrastive pretraining of small encoders using synthetically generated natural-language descriptions that emphasize code functionality and intent. These descriptions are paired with code in a dual-encoder framework during training but discarded at inference time.
AI.result: The approach achieves statistically significant gains over pretraining baselines of the same inference-time size on 5 out of 8 tasks, with parity on 2 more. When fine-tuned, it matches or exceeds zero-shot models two orders of magnitude larger on classification, and performs similarly to execution-aware supervision with matched pretraining data.
AI.conclusion: Synthetic semantic supervision provides a scalable and effective alternative to existing code representation paradigms, offering competitive performance without the costs and limitations of human annotations or execution traces.

title: Latent Energy Action Planning with World Models
summary: Latent world models support efficient model predictive control from high-dimensional observations, yet optimizing a single learned latent objective can favor action sequences whose decoder-predicted terminal descriptor does not match the goal descriptor. We introduce Latent Energy Action Planning (LEAP), which treats the complete action horizon as a differentiable variable and optimizes it through a frozen LeWorldModel (LeWM). LEAP couples terminal latent goal matching with a terminal-window state energy. Low energy requires the predicted terminal latent to agree with the goal latent and the decoder-predicted terminal descriptor to agree with the goal descriptor. A frozen goal-conditioned proposal initializes the search, a quasi-Newton solver refines actions through the autoregressive rollout, and post-optimization projection enforces the admissible action range. Across four control domains using the officially released LeWM checkpoints, the complete LEAP planning system raises mean success from 77.5% for LeWM planned with the cross-entropy method (LeWM+CEM) to 94.8% under a matched protocol, a 17.3-percentage-point improvement, while retaining the frozen LeWM representation and predictor.

AI.tldr: LEAP introduces differentiable action horizon optimization through frozen world models, coupling latent goal matching with terminal-window state energy for improved planning success.
AI.motivation: Latent world models can favor action sequences where predicted terminal descriptors don't match actual goal descriptors when optimizing a single learned latent objective.
AI.method: Treats complete action horizon as differentiable variable optimized through frozen LeWorldModel, couples terminal latent goal matching with terminal-window state energy, uses frozen goal-conditioned proposal initialization, quasi-Newton solver refinement, and post-optimization projection.
AI.result: Raises mean success from 77.5% (LeWM+CEM) to 94.8% across four control domains using official LeWM checkpoints, a 17.3-percentage-point improvement while retaining frozen representation and predictor.
AI.conclusion: LEAP demonstrates effective planning by optimizing action sequences through frozen world models with combined latent matching and energy-based objectives, significantly improving success rates.

title: Counterfactual Routing Using Integer Programming with Constraint Generation
summary: We present our submission to the IJCAI 2025 'Counterfactual Routing Competition' (CRC 25). The goal of the competition is to find counterfactual explanations for the shortest path problem. This requires deciding what the minimal changes to a road network would make a route chosen by the user the optimal route. This enables explanations such as "Your suggested route would indeed have been optimal, if road X were not a bicycle path." Our solution models the problem as an integer program, iteratively incorporating constraints until an exact solution is found. In the final evaluation on held-out test instances, our method ranked fourth in solution quality and obtained its solution fastest on every instance, with an average runtime of 9.0 seconds compared to 118.8 seconds for the next-fastest submission.

AI.tldr: A submission to IJCAI 2025 Counterfactual Routing Competition that uses integer programming to find minimal network changes making user routes optimal, achieving 4th in quality and fastest runtime.
AI.motivation: The competition aims to provide counterfactual explanations for shortest path routing decisions, enabling human-understandable explanations like "Your route would have been optimal if road X were not a bicycle path." This helps users understand why certain routes weren't selected and what conditions would make their preferred routes optimal.
AI.method: Models the counterfactual routing problem as an integer program and solves it using an iterative constraint incorporation approach. The method systematically adds constraints until an exact solution is found, ensuring minimal changes to the road network that would make the user's route optimal.
AI.result: Ranked fourth in solution quality in the final evaluation on held-out test instances. Notably achieved the fastest runtime on every instance with an average of 9.0 seconds, significantly faster than the next-fastest submission at 118.8 seconds (over 13x faster).
AI.conclusion: The integer programming approach with iterative constraint incorporation provides an effective method for counterfactual routing explanations, balancing solution quality with exceptional computational efficiency, making it practical for real-world routing applications.

title: Geometry-Aware Graph Construction via Adaptive Spectral Bandwidth Control
comment: Accepted at IEEE MLSP 2026. 6 pages, 4 figures
summary: Kernelized graph methods - spectral clustering, diffusion maps, and sparse kernel -regression graphs - that use Gaussian kernels depend on the choice of Gaussian bandwidth sigma, which governs the spectral character of the local kernel operator. When sigma is too small, the kernel overestimates local complexity and treats each sample as an independent direction; when sigma is too large, the kernel collapses multiple directions together, the condition number diverges, and all geometric discrimination is lost. We propose a choice of scale to make the spectral complexity of the kernel consistent with the intrinsic complexity of the underlying manifold. We propose a per-node bandwidth criterion that operationalizes this principle by jointly matching the kernel's effective rank to the local intrinsic dimension estimated via minimum spanning tree, anchoring the search in the manifold-consistent log-log scaling regime. We evaluate SSL embeddings from six encoders on CIFAR-100, showing that adaptive bandwidth consistently improves leave-one-out (LOO) classification and label propagation (LP) accuracy over fixed-bandwidth methods and competing adaptive methods.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a local bandwidth selection method for Gaussian kernel graph algorithms that matches kernel effective rank to local intrinsic dimension via minimum spanning tree estimation, improving semi-supervised learning performance over fixed-bandwidth approaches.
AI.motivation: Current kernelized graph methods using Gaussian kernels suffer from sensitivity to bandwidth parameter σ: too small σ overestimates local complexity treating each sample as independent, while too large σ collapses directions, causes condition number divergence, and loses geometric discrimination. Existing fixed-bandwidth approaches are suboptimal for varying local manifold structures.
AI.method: Proposes a per-node bandwidth selection criterion that matches the kernel's effective rank to the local intrinsic dimension. Uses minimum spanning tree to estimate local intrinsic dimension, anchoring the search in the manifold-consistent log-log scaling regime. This creates adaptive bandwidths tailored to local manifold complexity.
AI.result: Evaluated on CIFAR-100 with six different encoders for SSL embeddings, showing that adaptive bandwidth consistently improves leave-one-out classification and label propagation accuracy over fixed-bandwidth methods and competing adaptive methods.
AI.conclusion: The proposed adaptive bandwidth selection method provides a principled way to make kernel spectral complexity consistent with underlying manifold complexity, leading to improved performance in semi-supervised learning tasks compared to existing approaches.

title: Artificial Intelligence for Energy Optimization in Data Centers
summary: Data centers are increasingly optimized by artificial intelligence and, at the same time, increasingly loaded by it. The literature treats these as two unrelated problems: control studies model workload as an exogenous arrival process, while sustainability studies model infrastructure as a fixed multiplier. We screen roughly 194 papers retrieved through a documented protocol, code 63 of them, and report what the coding shows. Of 28 primary control-oriented studies, 18 are validated in simulation alone and 5 reach physical hardware or a production facility; none account for water withdrawal, and none account for embodied carbon. Reported savings intervals across four technique families overlap almost completely, which means the field cannot presently rank its own methods. Ten recurring gaps are scored for consequence and tractability, and we set out CLEAR-DC, a framework coupling a control-policy branch to a workload-demand branch through an explicit elasticity term, reads out net rather than direct benefit, and emits a schema-conformant record covering energy, carbon, water, embodied share and validation venue. The framework is an architectural and methodological proposal, not a trained system; the contribution we defend empirically is the corpus analysis and the reporting schema derived from it. Coding sheet, derived statistics and all result artifacts: https://github.com/Kimalice/AI-for-Energy-Optimization-in-Data-Centers-Closing-the-Optimizer-Load-Loop

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes 194 papers on AI-driven data center optimization, finding critical gaps in existing research (lack of validation, omission of water/embodied carbon, inability to rank methods) and proposes CLEAR-DC, a comprehensive framework that couples control policies with workload demand while accounting for energy, carbon, water, and embodied impacts.
AI.motivation: Current research on AI-optimized data centers treats control optimization and sustainability as separate problems: control studies ignore environmental impacts, while sustainability studies treat infrastructure as fixed. This creates a disconnect where AI both optimizes and increases data center energy consumption, leading to incomplete understanding of net benefits.
AI.method: 1) Systematic screening of ~194 papers using documented protocol; 2) Detailed coding of 63 papers; 3) Analysis of validation methods and measurement gaps; 4) Development of CLEAR-DC framework with explicit coupling between control policies and workload demand through elasticity terms; 5) Proposal of standardized reporting schema covering energy, carbon, water, embodied impacts, and validation venue.
AI.result: 1) Of 28 primary control-oriented studies: 18 validated only in simulation, 5 reached physical hardware/production; 2) No studies accounted for water withdrawal or embodied carbon; 3) Reported savings intervals across technique families overlapped completely, preventing method ranking; 4) Identified 10 recurring research gaps with scored consequence and tractability; 5) Created comprehensive coding sheet and statistics for reproducibility.
AI.conclusion: The AI-for-energy-optimization field lacks proper validation, omits critical environmental factors (water, embodied carbon), and cannot rank its own methods. CLEAR-DC provides a needed architectural framework for holistic assessment that couples optimization with actual demand, tracks net rather than direct benefits, and enables standardized, comparable reporting of environmental impacts across studies.

title: Proactive Service Agents: A Unified Decision Framework, Methods, and Evaluation
summary: Large language model agents can plan, invoke tools, and modify external states, yet most systems still take an explicit user instruction as a fixed starting point. Proactive service moves the decision upstream: an agent must infer service opportunities from incomplete environmental and user signals, choose among remaining silent, asking, assisting, and acting, and account for interruption, misunderstanding, overreach, and privacy costs. This survey gives an operational definition centered on initiative and formulates the problem as a partially observable sequential decision process constrained by authorization and risk. The formulation represents timing, content, and delivery within one structured action, while making explicit the option value of waiting, the decision value of questions, and feedback-induced state changes. On this basis, we organize existing methods along one decision pipeline (state and need estimation, intervention gating, action construction, and feedback adaptation) and describe prescribed, predictive, model based, and return optimizing mechanisms as nonexclusive policy-construction components. We further normalize decision units and three-axis evidence descriptors across streaming dialogue, screen, video, software-engineering, and human-agent collaboration resources, and formalize metrics for triggering, timing, calibration, user burden, safety, and policy value. The synthesis shows why offline classification performance alone does not predict deployment benefit and why long-term memory is not a defining condition of proactivity. Reliable proactive service instead requires calibrated incremental intervention value, verifiable authorization, recoverable execution, and counterfactual evidence.

AI.tldr: A survey on proactive AI agents that initiate actions based on incomplete signals rather than waiting for explicit user instructions, framing the problem as a sequential decision process with authorization constraints and organizing methods along a decision pipeline.
AI.motivation: Current AI agents typically require explicit user instructions, but real-world service often requires proactively identifying opportunities from incomplete environmental and user signals, balancing benefits against interruption, misunderstanding, overreach, and privacy risks.
AI.method: Formalizes proactive service as a partially observable sequential decision process constrained by authorization and risk. Organizes methods along a decision pipeline: state/need estimation, intervention gating, action construction, and feedback adaptation. Classifies policy mechanisms as prescribed, predictive, model-based, and return-optimizing.
AI.result: Provides a unified framework that represents timing, content, and delivery within structured actions, making explicit option value of waiting, decision value of questions, and feedback-induced state changes. Normalizes decision units and evidence descriptors across diverse domains (dialogue, screen, video, software-engineering, human-agent collaboration).
AI.conclusion: Proactive service success requires calibrated incremental intervention value, verifiable authorization, recoverable execution, and counterfactual evidence rather than offline classification performance or long-term memory. The framework explains why current evaluation metrics fail to predict deployment benefits and guides development of reliable proactive agents.

title: DE-Venus: A Data-Efficient RLVR Framework for Large Language Models
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) improves large language model reasoning, but its practical scaling is constrained by expensive on-policy rollouts and the cost of obtaining reliable targets at scale. Existing methods address sample selection, incomplete supervision, or noisy labels separately, often entangling supervision logic with distributed training and hindering controlled comparison and reuse. We present DE-Venus, a unified framework for data-efficient RLVR that treats supervision as evolving state across data preparation and policy optimization. It organizes this lifecycle into three modules: Active Data Selection allocates training and annotation budgets; Weak Supervision Construction derives learning signals from unlabeled examples; and Training-Time Supervision Refinement filters or corrects unreliable supervision. DE-Venus supports seven representative methods and a data-selection pipeline by expressing method-specific decisions as offline dataset transitions or online transformations of targets, rewards, batches, and advantages while preserving verl's distributed execution contracts. Across public benchmarks and three business scenarios, separate configurations preserve or improve model quality with only 10% of labels or as little as 13% of relevant data; selected business configurations also reduce observed convergence steps by 63%--75%. DE-Venus thus reduces annotation and training costs without sacrificing scalable RL execution.

AI.tldr: DE-Venus is a unified framework that reduces annotation and training costs for reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) by treating supervision as evolving state and organizing it into three modules for data selection, weak supervision construction, and supervision refinement.
AI.motivation: RLVR improves LLM reasoning but faces practical scaling constraints due to expensive on-policy rollouts and high costs of obtaining reliable targets at scale. Existing methods address sample selection, incomplete supervision, or noisy labels separately, often entangling supervision logic with distributed training and hindering comparison and reuse.
AI.method: DE-Venus organizes the RLVR lifecycle into three modules: 1) Active Data Selection for budget allocation, 2) Weak Supervision Construction for deriving signals from unlabeled examples, and 3) Training-Time Supervision Refinement for filtering/correcting unreliable supervision. The framework supports seven representative methods and expresses method-specific decisions as offline dataset transitions or online transformations while preserving distributed execution contracts.
AI.result: Across public benchmarks and three business scenarios, configurations preserve or improve model quality with only 10% of labels or as little as 13% of relevant data. Selected business configurations reduce observed convergence steps by 63%-75%, reducing annotation and training costs without sacrificing scalable RL execution.
AI.conclusion: DE-Venus successfully reduces the practical scaling constraints of RLVR by providing a unified framework that treats supervision as evolving state, enabling data-efficient reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards while maintaining or improving model quality.

title: A Large Open Multi-Energy Corpus of Soil Compaction Tests, with Machine-Learning Baselines
summary: Every engineered fill is specified by a maximum dry density and an optimum moisture content. Each determination needs a full Proctor test. Published correlations rest on one to four hundred specimens, usually from one laboratory at one compactive energy, and are seldom released. This paper releases a corpus without those limits. It holds 2,854 laboratory compaction tests from six public sources, across 162 provenance groups and four Proctor energy levels, with fines from 1.5 to 100%. Every record is audited to the Proctor method its source names, and no energy is inferred. Screening on the zero-air-voids condition removed 11.8% of harmonised records, and 5.7% of those with a measured specific gravity. A material share of published compaction data is physically impossible. The optimum degree of saturation over the corpus is 0.815 at a coefficient of variation of 11%. That is a baseline, not a constant. Both parameters are then estimated from one classification suite and the compaction standard. A tabular foundation model reaches R2 0.824 for density and 0.784 for water content under random folds. It reaches 0.727 and 0.696 with folds drawn around provenance, and 0.520 and 0.614 with a whole source held out. Compactive energy is negligible marginally yet decisive conditionally. Density on the 66 modified-Proctor records is predicted at R2 0.740 with it and -0.651 without. Symbolic regression yields closed forms coupled through a phase relation. No predicted pair can then exceed the zero-air-voids line. The predictions are for screening, not acceptance.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a large corpus of 2,854 compaction tests across multiple sources and energies, showing that published compaction correlations are often unreliable and based on physically impossible data. It develops predictive models for maximum dry density and optimum moisture content using classification data.
AI.motivation: Traditional Proctor test correlations are limited by small datasets, single laboratory sources, restricted energy levels, and lack of transparency. There's a need for more comprehensive, validated compaction data and reliable predictive models that can work across different conditions.
AI.method: Compiled 2,854 laboratory compaction tests from six public sources across 162 provenance groups and four Proctor energy levels. Applied data auditing to match Proctor methods, removed physically impossible data (11.8% failed zero-air-voids check), and developed predictive models using classification data and compaction standards. Used both tabular foundation models and symbolic regression with phase relation constraints.
AI.result: Found that optimum degree of saturation averages 0.815 with 11% variation. Tabular model achieved R² 0.824 for density and 0.784 for water content with random folds. Performance degraded with provenance folds (R² 0.727/0.696) and source holdout (R² 0.520/0.614). Compactive energy proved conditionally important - critical for modified-Proctor records (R² 0.740 with energy vs -0.651 without). Symbolic regression produced physically-constrained closed-form predictions.
AI.conclusion: Published compaction data contains physically impossible measurements. Reliable predictions can be made from classification data for screening purposes, but compactive energy must be considered when conditions differ from standard Proctor tests. The developed models provide practical tools for preliminary assessment of fill materials.

title: Rethinking World Models for Safety-Critical Embodied Systems
summary: World models have progressed from compact latent dynamics to generative, controllable, and interactive simulators of embodied environments. However, high predictive likelihood and visual fidelity do not necessarily ensure that a model preserves the evidence required for safe decision-making. This perspective identifies three structural mismatches in current world modeling: likelihood versus risk, prediction versus intervention, and finite-horizon prediction versus accumulated consequences. We propose the Risk-Informed World Model (RIWM) as a decision-centric research direction for safety-critical embodied systems. RIWM organizes world modeling around consequences, intervention, epistemic uncertainty, and recoverability, and integrates four interdependent capabilities: decision-relevant representation, counterfactual reasoning, safety-critical episodic memory, and runtime safety assurance. It distinguishes physical, social, and operational consequences while using epistemic uncertainty to qualify the evidence supporting action. We further discuss open challenges in identifying consequential futures, validating counterfactual reasoning, maintaining revisable safety memories, translating learned consequences into executable constraints, and determining when evidence is sufficient to act. This perspective argues that future world models should move beyond predicting likely futures toward identifying which futures matter, revising judgments through experience, and recognizing when to act, revise, sense, defer, or abstain.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that current world models focus too much on prediction and visual fidelity, while ignoring safety-critical decision-making requirements. It proposes Risk-Informed World Models (RIWM) as a new approach that prioritizes consequences, uncertainty, and recoverability over mere likelihood.
AI.motivation: Current world models excel at prediction and visual fidelity but fail to support safe decision-making in safety-critical embodied systems. There's a structural mismatch between predictive accuracy and risk assessment, with models not preserving evidence needed for safety decisions.
AI.method: The paper proposes RIWM as a decision-centric research direction that organizes world modeling around consequences, intervention, epistemic uncertainty, and recoverability. It integrates four capabilities: decision-relevant representation, counterfactual reasoning, safety-critical episodic memory, and runtime safety assurance.
AI.result: The paper establishes a conceptual framework for RIWM that distinguishes physical, social, and operational consequences while using epistemic uncertainty to qualify evidence supporting action. It identifies open challenges but doesn't present empirical results.
AI.conclusion: World models should evolve beyond predicting likely futures to focus on identifying consequential futures, revising judgments through experience, and recognizing when to act, revise, sense, defer, or abstain. This decision-centric approach is essential for safety-critical applications.

title: Gradients Know What Outcomes Don't: Unlocking Reinforcement Learning for LLM Reasoning with Gradient-Aligned Rewards
summary: Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) drives chain-of-thought reasoning in large language models, yet its binary outcome reward cannot distinguish among correct trajectories. Existing dense reward alternatives, from surface heuristics to process reward models, either ignore the expert solutions already present in training corpora or require expensive offline annotation. We propose Gradient-Aligned Reward (GAR), which operates in the policy's own gradient space: truncated backpropagation through the output projection layer extracts a compact gradient vector for each rollout, and cosine similarity with an expert-anchor gradient yields a dense, reasoning-aware reward with less than 9% wall-clock overhead. We prove that this cosine admits a multiplicative decomposition into prediction-error and activation-pattern factors, providing a concrete characterization of what the alignment signal measures. On Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B, GAR consistently improves over GRPO and other baselines on competition-level math benchmarks and transfers to GPQA Diamond and MMLU-Pro without domain-specific data. Code and data are available at https://github.com/LQgdwind/GAR.

AI.tldr: Gradient-Aligned Reward (GAR) is a new RLVR method that provides dense rewards by measuring gradient space alignment between model rollouts and expert solutions, offering reasoning-aware supervision with minimal computational overhead.
AI.motivation: Current RLVR methods have limitations: binary outcome rewards don't distinguish among correct trajectories, while existing dense reward alternatives either ignore expert solutions in training data or require expensive offline annotation.
AI.method: GAR operates in the policy's own gradient space, using truncated backpropagation through the output projection layer to extract compact gradient vectors for each rollout. Cosine similarity with an expert-anchor gradient yields dense, reasoning-aware rewards with <9% wall-clock overhead.
AI.result: GAR consistently outperforms GRPO and other baselines on competition-level math benchmarks using Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B models, and shows strong transfer performance to GPQA Diamond and MMLU-Pro without domain-specific data.
AI.conclusion: GAR provides an effective, efficient method for dense reward generation in RLVR by leveraging gradient space alignment, offering theoretical guarantees about what the alignment signal measures and practical performance improvements across multiple reasoning benchmarks.

title: DNative-Twin: Decision Graphs and Digital Twins for Reconstructable Agentic Decisions
summary: AI agents increasingly gather evidence, invoke tools, apply constraints, and produce decisions that people or software may commit to action. A final output alone cannot show which evidence, tool state, rule, authorization, or action path produced it. We present DNative-Twin, a graph-native digital twin that records a committed agentic decision as a typed trajectory and re-executes its decision mechanism under declared conditions. The graph links the state observed by the agent, the path it followed, and the authority behind the resulting action. The twin synchronizes this information, replays the mechanism in isolation, and compares it under controlled changes. We instantiate the framework in enterprise decision processes using three public process logs and controlled replay suites. The experiments identify a specific failure: graph structure localizes represented changes but cannot determine the consequence of an unobserved tool state. In a three-condition controlled experiment with 300 injected instances, unresolved-divergence recall increased from 0 to 0.667 when replay-contract state was added and to 1.0 when verification results were also available; the held-out set contained no critical-class instance. Across 500--5,000 BPI 2020 cases, median end-to-end time increased from 0.794 to 8.889 seconds on the reported platform. These results separate the roles of graph structure, replay context, and verification evidence in reviewing a decision mechanism.

AI.tldr: DNative-Twin is a graph-native digital twin system that records and re-executes AI agent decision mechanisms for auditing and analysis, enabling controlled replay and comparison to understand how decisions were made.
AI.motivation: Current AI agent decisions lack transparency - final outputs don't show which evidence, tool states, rules, authorizations, or action paths produced them, making it impossible to audit or understand decision mechanisms.
AI.method: The system records committed agent decisions as typed trajectories in a graph-native digital twin, then re-executes the decision mechanism under declared conditions. The graph links observed state, decision paths, and authority behind actions, enabling synchronization, isolated replay, and comparison under controlled changes.
AI.result: Experiments on enterprise processes showed: 1) Graph structure localizes changes but can't determine consequences of unobserved tool states; 2) In 300 injected instances, unresolved-divergence recall improved from 0 to 0.667 with replay-contract state, and to 1.0 with verification evidence; 3) Across 500-5,000 BPI 2020 cases, median end-to-end time increased from 0.794 to 8.889 seconds.
AI.conclusion: DNative-Twin successfully separates the roles of graph structure, replay context, and verification evidence in decision review, providing a framework for auditing AI agent decisions while identifying that graph structure alone is insufficient for handling unobserved tool states.

title: From Zero to Hero: An Open LLM Ecosystem for Armenian
comment: 18 pages, 4 figures, 13 tables. Data and model: https://huggingface.co/collections/COPA-AI/armenian-llm-ecosystem. Code: https://github.com/COPATeam/armenian_llm_ecosystem
summary: Pretraining data for Armenian, a morphologically rich and low-resource language, is scarce, and no open Armenian LLM has been released with the data and recipe needed to reproduce it. To address this gap, we curate and release two datasets. ArmWeb is an extensively validated corpus of 4.37M Armenian news documents. ArmSTEM is a parallel English-Armenian collection of 373K math and science problems with step-by-step solutions, translated into Armenian and verified through both answer-preserving LLM judgment and human evaluation. Continued pretraining of Gemma-4-E4B on these datasets yields arm-gemma-e4b, which outperforms every existing open Armenian model as well as its unadapted base, and is the first open Armenian LLM with complete training data and recipe. Our ablations show that news-only continued pretraining improves fluency while eroding knowledge, a pattern we also observe in existing Armenian models, and that a small share of verified translated STEM data reverses the loss. We further find that the largest public Armenian corpora overlap web-derived evaluation panels heavily, including a train/test self-overlap inside FineWeb-2. We openly release all data, models, and code.

AI.tldr: Armenian language lacks high-quality pretraining data and reproducible LLMs; authors curate and release validated Armenian news (ArmWeb) and STEM translation (ArmSTEM) datasets, train arm-gemma-e4b which outperforms existing models, showing news-only training hurts knowledge but STEM data reverses this.
AI.motivation: Armenian is a morphologically rich, low-resource language with scarce pretraining data. No open Armenian LLM exists with reproducible data and training recipe, creating a gap for high-quality Armenian language models.
AI.method: 1) Created ArmWeb: 4.37M Armenian news documents with extensive validation. 2) Created ArmSTEM: 373K parallel English-Armenian math/science problems with step-by-step solutions, translated and verified via LLM judgment and human evaluation. 3) Continued pretraining of Gemma-4-E4B on these datasets to create arm-gemma-e4b.
AI.result: arm-gemma-e4b outperforms all existing open Armenian models and its unadapted base. News-only pretraining improves fluency but erodes knowledge (pattern observed in existing Armenian models), while verified STEM data reverses the knowledge loss. Also found heavy train/test overlap in public Armenian corpora and FineWeb-2.
AI.conclusion: High-quality, validated datasets (ArmWeb for news, ArmSTEM for technical content) enable creation of superior Armenian LLMs. Balanced data mix (news + STEM) is crucial for maintaining both fluency and knowledge. All data, models, and code are openly released to advance Armenian NLP.

title: Transfiver: Human-AI Co-Inference through a Shared Editable State
summary:
Long-term human-AI interaction is difficult because the information that guides inference is updated implicitly by the model and is not directly inspectable or controllable by the user. We introduce the TRANSparent Framework for Interactive, Verifiable, Editable Representation (Transfiver), an architecture for human-AI co-inference through a shared editable state. Its central idea is that interaction-specific information is maintained in a single persistent state $(S_t)$ that both the model and the human update.
  Transfiver distinguishes two modes of state evolution. In an implicit stream update, the model interprets ongoing interaction and decides whether new information revises an existing state item or creates a new one. In an explicit directed edit, a human inspects and modifies an addressed item. Both act on the same underlying state, so a human correction changes the state that subsequent computation reads, rather than adding another instruction or separate record.
  The architecture separates shared parameters $(θ)$, learned before ordinary use, from the persistent state $(S_t)$, which evolves during deployment without parameter retraining. Extending Transfiver to rich natural-language, relational, and large-scale shared states remains open.

AI.tldr: Transfiver introduces a transparent framework for human-AI co-inference through a shared editable state that both humans and AI can update and inspect, enabling verifiable and controllable long-term interaction.
AI.motivation: Long-term human-AI interaction is challenging because AI models update inference information implicitly, making it not directly inspectable or controllable by users, creating opacity and lack of user agency in the interaction process.
AI.method: Proposes Transfiver architecture with a persistent shared editable state (S_t) that both model and human update. Features two state evolution modes: implicit stream updates (model interprets interaction and updates state) and explicit directed edits (human inspects and modifies state items), both acting on the same underlying state.
AI.result: Introduces an architecture that separates shared learned parameters (θ) from evolving persistent state (S_t), enabling human corrections to directly change the state that subsequent computation reads rather than adding separate instructions. Framework allows state evolution during deployment without parameter retraining.
AI.conclusion: Transfiver provides a foundation for transparent, interactive, verifiable, and editable human-AI co-inference, though extending it to rich natural-language, relational, and large-scale shared states remains an open challenge for future work.

title: Time Without Timesteps: Simulating Coupled Dynamical Systems via Self-Consistency
summary: Numerical simulation of dynamical systems is usually organized as a causal march through time: each state is computed from the previous one. We explore a different formulation for coupled systems. For each subsystem type we train a neural surrogate mapping a full driving trajectory and initial condition directly to a full output trajectory; following classical waveform relaxation, coupled systems are assembled by enforcing self-consistency among these trajectories: simulation becomes a fixed-point problem over complete trajectories rather than a stepwise rollout. On coupled van der Pol oscillators and Hodgkin-Huxley neuron networks, sequential depth becomes the number of solver iterations: 4-10 Newton iterations where the reference integrator takes 1500 steps. The gradient likewise loses its time recursion: it becomes a linear system solved by GMRES at memory independent of solver depth. A single scalar measured from the learned operator, the spectral radius of its Jacobian, predicts in advance where the coupled solve will converge; past that boundary, unrolled backpropagation diverges and a Neumann adjoint fails, while the implicit gradient remains correct to 0.04%. We report where the approach succeeds and where surrogate error degrades it.

AI.tldr: A neural waveform relaxation method that replaces stepwise simulation with fixed-point solving over full trajectories, reducing computational depth and enabling stable gradients for coupled dynamical systems.
AI.motivation: Traditional numerical simulation of dynamical systems requires causal marching through time with many steps. The authors seek to reduce computational depth and improve gradient stability for coupled systems by reformulating the simulation as a fixed-point problem.
AI.method: For each subsystem type, train neural surrogates mapping driving trajectories and initial conditions directly to full output trajectories. Assemble coupled systems by enforcing self-consistency among trajectories using waveform relaxation (fixed-point solving). Use Newton iterations (4-10) instead of stepwise integration (1500 steps). Compute gradients as linear systems solved by GMRES with memory independent of solver depth.
AI.result: Achieved 4-10 Newton iterations vs 1500 integration steps, with the spectral radius of the learned operator's Jacobian predicting convergence boundaries. Implicit gradient remains accurate (0.04%) where unrolled backpropagation diverges and Neumann adjoint fails.
AI.conclusion: Waveform relaxation with neural surrogates transforms simulation into efficient fixed-point solving, significantly reducing sequential depth while maintaining gradient accuracy, though success depends on surrogate quality and identified convergence boundaries.

title: Govern the Model, Not Only the Data: Storage, Circulation, and Learning in Creative AI
summary: Federated learning is increasingly presented as a privacy-preserving advance: personal data remain on the device, and only model updates are shared. It borrows the vocabulary of the federated social web, yet inverts its logic, distributing computation while the resulting model stays with whoever convened the training. We argue that federation is not in itself a remedy for extractive AI, because outcomes depend on who governs the data and the model and who has agency over the practices that shape them. We describe three layers at which a creative community can hold its work: storage, circulation, and learning. Examining artist-governed trusts, cooperatives, and consent infrastructures, we show that creator governance is established at storage and circulation but stops at learning: contributors can consent to training, yet have little say over the resulting model or its federation. We map the research space this opens, pairing technical open problems with the human questions from which they unfold. We propose four design principles for a creative data commons that governs models and their federation, not only datasets: govern the model, not only the corpus; make the terms legible at the moment of contribution; design for refusal as a first-class state; and decide stewardship in the open and account for it.

AI.tldr: Federated learning is not inherently privacy-preserving or anti-extractive - true protection depends on governance over data, models, and practices, not just technical distribution. The paper argues for extending creator governance from storage/circulation to learning, proposing principles for model governance in creative data commons.
AI.motivation: The paper is motivated by the critique that federated learning, while marketed as privacy-preserving, actually maintains extractive relationships where model ownership remains centralized. There's a need to shift from technical decentralization to actual governance over AI models and their training processes.
AI.method: The paper examines three governance layers (storage, circulation, learning) through analysis of artist-governed systems like trusts, cooperatives, and consent infrastructures. It maps research problems by pairing technical challenges with human governance questions and proposes design principles.
AI.result: The analysis shows current creator governance stops at storage and circulation but fails at learning - contributors can consent to training but have little say over resulting models or federation. The paper identifies this gap and proposes four principles for creative data commons.
AI.conclusion: True anti-extractive AI requires governing models and their federation, not just datasets. The paper proposes moving beyond technical federation to establish creative data commons with governance principles that ensure contributors have agency over models throughout their lifecycle.

title: SimpleDesign: A Joint Model for Protein Sequence and Structure Codesign
comment: Published in Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR), 2026. https://openreview.net/forum?id=wPfw7GkMns
summary: Proteins are fundamental to biological processes, with their function determined by the complex interplay between the amino acid sequence and the three-dimensional structure. Developing generative models capable of understanding this intrinsically multi-modal relationship is crucial for fields like drug discovery and protein engineering. Existing models often rely on a multi-stage training process where autoencoders that tokenize data into latent representations are trained in a first stage. Secondly, a generative model is trained on the latent representation of the autoencoder(s), i.e., generative modeling in a latent space. We hypothesize that this multi-stage training is not necessary to obtain performant co-design models and thus present SimpleDesign, an effective multi-modal protein design model trained directly in the data space. SimpleDesign leverages a single-stage end-to-end objective that combines discrete cross-entropy for sequences and a regression objective for structures. In order to effectively model the difference in sequence and structure modalities, we develop a Mixture-of-Transformer architecture that allows modality-specific processing while keeping global self-attention over both modalities. We train SimpleDesign on over 2M sequence-structure pairs achieving strong performance across co-design and unconditional sequence/structure generation benchmarks.

AI.tldr: SimpleDesign is an end-to-end multi-modal protein design model that directly co-designs sequences and structures without multi-stage training, achieving strong performance on protein design benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing protein generative models use multi-stage training with separate autoencoders for tokenization and latent space modeling, which may be unnecessary for effective co-design of sequences and structures.
AI.method: SimpleDesign uses single-stage end-to-end training with discrete cross-entropy for sequences and regression for structures, plus a Mixture-of-Transformer architecture for modality-specific processing with global self-attention.
AI.result: Trained on over 2M sequence-structure pairs, SimpleDesign achieves strong performance across co-design and unconditional sequence/structure generation benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Multi-stage training is unnecessary for performant protein co-design models; SimpleDesign demonstrates effective direct data-space training with modality-specific processing can achieve strong results.
