title: SVG-Score: Human-Aligned Evaluation of Text-to-SVG Generation
summary: Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) generation is attracting increasing attention as generative models improve in expressiveness and controllability. Progress, however, is held back by the lack of domain-specific evaluation protocols: current practice relies on metrics designed for natural images, most notably CLIPScore, which was never trained on vector graphics and aligns only partially with human judgment. We introduce \textbf{\ours}, a human-aligned evaluation framework for text-to-SVG generation. Through controlled caption and image perturbations, we first show that CLIP-based scores barely react to the errors SVG generators actually make, such as wrong colors, counts, and spatial relations, and that off-the-shelf Vision-Language Model (VLM) judges, while more sensitive, respond unevenly across error types and SVG styles. We then introduce a human-annotated dataset for \textit{Semantic Alignment}, measuring how faithfully a generated SVG reflects its caption. Building on it, we develop two complementary evaluators: CLIP scorers adapted to vector graphics and then aligned to human preferences, for fast large-scale evaluation, and a VLM judge trained with supervised fine-tuning and reward-shaped reinforcement learning, for more expressive and interpretable assessment. Using both, we benchmark major open-source, commercial, and optimization-based SVG generators on an independent caption set.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SVG-Eval, a human-aligned evaluation framework for text-to-SVG generation, addressing limitations of current CLIP-based metrics that poorly capture SVG-specific errors like wrong colors, counts, and spatial relations.
AI.motivation: Current SVG generation evaluation relies on metrics designed for natural images (like CLIPScore) that weren't trained on vector graphics and only partially align with human judgment. There's a lack of domain-specific evaluation protocols for SVG generation.
AI.method: 1) Analysis of CLIP-based scores through controlled caption and image perturbations showing they barely react to SVG-specific errors. 2) Creation of a human-annotated dataset for Semantic Alignment measuring how faithfully SVGs reflect captions. 3) Development of two complementary evaluators: CLIP scorers adapted to vector graphics and aligned to human preferences for fast evaluation, and a VLM judge trained with supervised fine-tuning and reward-shaped reinforcement learning for interpretable assessment.
AI.result: The developed framework successfully addresses the evaluation gap, showing that both adapted CLIP scorers and trained VLM judges outperform traditional metrics. The framework is used to benchmark major open-source, commercial, and optimization-based SVG generators on an independent caption set.
AI.conclusion: The paper presents a comprehensive human-aligned evaluation framework for text-to-SVG generation that overcomes limitations of existing natural image metrics, providing both efficient and interpretable assessment methods while establishing meaningful benchmarks for SVG generators.

title: RecurTrace: Adaptive Latent Reasoning with Loop-Time Memory
summary: Repeating a small block of middle layers increases a language model's effective inference depth without adding parameters or generating extra tokens, and recent work shows that this latent recurrence improves reasoning. However, two design choices limit these gains. Each iteration sees only the previous output and cannot directly access earlier computations. Moreover, a fixed loop count wastes depth on easy inputs while leaving hard ones with too little computation. We introduce RecurTrace, which addresses both limitations using the loop's own trajectory. Specifically, Loop Memory Attention lets each looped layer attend to its own states from previous iterations along the loop-time axis, so the model can revisit earlier computations instead of relying on the latest state alone. A halting head then reads the loop state and predicts whether to continue, with supervision from an oracle that identifies when additional depth still reduces loss. In a controlled MathQA comparison on the same looped backbone, RecurTrace achieves 56.9% accuracy with an average of 2.0 loops, exceeding the best fixed loop depth by 2.2 points at matched compute. By comparison, ACT and PonderNet collapse to one loop, and CALM reaches only 54.1% with 5.6 loops, while the stronger LoopUS-Conf and TaH-Mismatch baselines reach 55.3% at 3.2 loops and 55.7% at 2.1 loops. Finally, RecurTrace improves generation accuracy over same-budget fine-tuned baselines at 0.6B, 1.7B, 4B, and 8B, with the gain growing with model size from 0.6 to 3.4 points.

AI.tldr: RecurTrace introduces two improvements to recurrent looped layers in language models: Loop Memory Attention allows access to previous loop iterations' states, and a learned halting mechanism dynamically adjusts computation depth based on input difficulty, improving reasoning performance while controlling compute costs.
AI.motivation: Existing recurrent looped layer approaches have two major limitations: 1) each iteration only sees the previous output, losing access to earlier computations, and 2) using a fixed loop count wastes computation on easy inputs while providing insufficient depth for hard ones, leading to inefficient use of model capacity.
AI.method: The paper proposes RecurTrace with two key innovations: Loop Memory Attention that allows looped layers to attend to their own previous iteration states along a loop-time axis, enabling revisiting earlier computations. Additionally, a halting head reads loop states and predicts when to continue computation, supervised by an oracle that identifies when additional depth reduces loss.
AI.result: On MathQA, RecurTrace achieves 56.9% accuracy with average 2.0 loops, outperforming best fixed loop depth by 2.2 points at matched compute. Other baselines like ACT, PonderNet, and CALM perform worse (54.1-55.7% with higher loop counts). RecurTrace also scales well, improving generation accuracy over fine-tuned baselines at model sizes from 0.6B to 8B with gains growing with model size.
AI.conclusion: RecurTrace effectively addresses limitations of recurrent looped layers by enabling access to computational history and adaptive computation depth, leading to improved reasoning performance with controlled computational cost, demonstrating that loop trajectory information can significantly enhance model efficiency and capability.

title: CauseCollab: Causal Unified and Modality-Agnostic Network for Heterogeneous Collaborative Perception
summary: Collaborative perception enhances environment understanding through multi-agent information sharing, but its performance in real-world scenarios is constrained by heterogeneous sensor modalities and model architectures. Recent protocol-based two-stage methods alleviate this problem by mapping heterogeneous features into a shared protocol space; however, independently trained modality-specific converters often generate modality-specific pseudo-protocol distributions, leading to semantic inconsistency and error accumulation, which is particularly pronounced in scenarios with large modality discrepancies. To address this issue, we propose CauseCollab, a causal unified and modality-agnostic network. CauseCollab formulates representation learning in the protocol space from a causal perspective, explicitly disentangling semantic factors from modality-specific statistical confounders via causal metric learning. Meanwhile, CauseCollab adopts context-guided Unified Converter for heterogeneous modalities to ensure cross-modal semantic consistency. In addition, integrating new modalities only requires training adapters with minimal parameters. Extensive experiments on the OPV2V and DAIR-V2X datasets demonstrate that CauseCollab achieves state-of-the-art performance, with more significant gains in scenarios involving large modality gaps.

AI.tldr: CauseCollab is a causal unified modality-agnostic network that solves semantic inconsistency in collaborative perception by disentangling semantic factors from modality-specific confounders via causal metric learning, achieving SOTA performance especially with large modality gaps.
AI.motivation: Collaborative perception performance is constrained by heterogeneous sensor modalities and model architectures. Existing two-stage methods using protocol spaces still suffer from semantic inconsistency and error accumulation due to modality-specific pseudo-protocol distributions, especially with large modality discrepancies.
AI.method: CauseCollab formulates representation learning from a causal perspective to disentangle semantic factors from modality-specific statistical confounders using causal metric learning. It uses a context-guided Unified Converter for heterogeneous modalities to ensure cross-modal semantic consistency, and new modalities only require training minimal-parameter adapters.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on OPV2V and DAIR-V2X datasets show CauseCollab achieves state-of-the-art performance, with particularly significant gains in scenarios involving large modality gaps.
AI.conclusion: CauseCollab effectively addresses semantic inconsistency in collaborative perception with heterogeneous modalities by using causal disentanglement and unified conversion, enabling robust performance especially in challenging scenarios with substantial modality differences.

title: TIGPO: Temporal Instance-Graph Policy Optimization for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
summary: Graph-based policy optimization improves credit assignment for long-horizon LLM agents by organizing rollout trajectories into state-transition graphs. However, existing methods construct graphs independently within each policy update, discarding transitions discovered by earlier policies and limiting advantage estimation to small, batch-local rollout groups. We propose \emph{Temporal Instance-Graph Policy Optimization} (TIGPO), which extends graph-based credit assignment across policy updates. TIGPO maintains a persistent transition graph for each task, allowing valid transitions discovered by different policy versions to jointly determine credit for current rollouts. To actively reconnect current exploration with historical experience, TIGPO allocates a fixed rollout budget between Exploration slots for ordinary task sampling and Revisit slots for delayed reattempts of previously explored tasks. For each revisit, TIGPO pairs the current rollout group with its corresponding earlier Exploration group to construct a cross-temporal reference. The enlarged reference is designed to stabilize relative advantage estimation under small rollout groups, while comparison on the same task directly captures policy improvement across training stages. Historical transitions and scores serve only as structural and detached statistical references and are never replayed in the policy loss. Experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop demonstrate that TIGPO consistently outperforms prior group-based and graph-based policy optimization methods.

AI.tldr: TIGPO introduces persistent transition graphs across policy updates for better credit assignment in LLM agents, using both exploration and revisit slots to leverage historical experience without replay.
AI.motivation: Existing graph-based policy optimization methods construct graphs independently within each policy update, discarding historical transitions and limiting advantage estimation to small batch-local rollout groups, which hinders effective credit assignment for long-horizon tasks.
AI.method: TIGPO maintains persistent transition graphs for each task across policy updates. It allocates rollout budget between Exploration slots (ordinary task sampling) and Revisit slots (delayed reattempts of previously explored tasks). For revisits, it pairs current rollout groups with corresponding earlier exploration groups to construct cross-temporal references for stabilized advantage estimation.
AI.result: Experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop benchmarks show TIGPO consistently outperforms prior group-based and graph-based policy optimization methods.
AI.conclusion: TIGPO's temporal extension of graph-based credit assignment through persistent transition graphs and strategic revisit allocations improves long-horizon credit assignment for LLM agents without replaying historical transitions in policy loss.

title: Semantic Bayesian World Models
summary: Knowledge graphs describe reality in crisp assertions, while the systems now consuming them, foundation models and autonomous agents, reason natively in probabilities. We argue that this mismatch is why the integration of language models and knowledge graphs remains a data-feeding pipeline rather than a unified reasoning architecture. We envision Semantic Bayesian World Models (SBWMs): a Web that describes the world not as a database of facts but as a shared, evolving fabric of beliefs over knowledge graphs, where ontological axioms constrain priors, observations update beliefs by Bayesian conditioning, and actions intervene upon the world. We work through what an agent gains from such a model: a home-security agent deciding whether the figure at the gate is a courier or a burglar, an actuarial estimate aggregated by entailment rather than by string frequency, a planning task that language models reliably fail, and the estimation of quantities that no document has ever stated. We then set out what the community must build to make them possible: belief annotation over RDF~1.2, probabilistic entailment regimes, semantic calibration layers, and protocols by which agents that have never met can exchange, and disagree over, calibrated beliefs.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Semantic Bayesian World Models (SBWMs) - a new web architecture that represents the world as shared probabilistic beliefs over knowledge graphs, enabling unified reasoning between foundation models and knowledge graphs through Bayesian inference.
AI.motivation: There's a fundamental mismatch between knowledge graphs (which use crisp assertions) and modern AI systems like foundation models and autonomous agents (which reason probabilistically). This mismatch forces current integrations to be mere data-feeding pipelines rather than unified reasoning architectures.
AI.method: Propose Semantic Bayesian World Models where: 1) ontological axioms constrain priors, 2) observations update beliefs via Bayesian conditioning, and 3) actions intervene upon the world. The paper outlines necessary technical components including belief annotation over RDF, probabilistic entailment regimes, semantic calibration layers, and protocols for belief exchange.
AI.result: Through examples, the paper demonstrates what agents gain from SBWMs: improved decision-making (e.g., home-security agent distinguishing courier vs burglar), actuarial estimates via entailment rather than frequency, reliable planning where language models fail, and estimation of quantities not explicitly documented.
AI.conclusion: The community needs to build foundational components for SBWMs to enable a web that functions as a shared, evolving fabric of calibrated beliefs over knowledge graphs, allowing agents to exchange and reason probabilistically about the world in a unified manner.

title: Adapting to Evolving Requirements: Agentic AI for Retail Supply Chain Operations
summary: Retail supply chain operations rely on coupled decision modules that must adapt as requirements evolve. LLMs offer a natural-language interface for this task, but existing methods primarily focus on individual optimization models. Extending them to heterogeneous decision pipelines is challenging because a requirement may admit multiple intervention paths with different downstream effects. We formulate requirement-driven adaptation as the joint selection of an intervention route and an admissible module-level change, and propose a graph-constrained agentic framework in which domain agents expose admissible reformulation interfaces and a central processor searches over bounded intervention paths. Candidates are validated and compared using downstream KPIs. In collaboration with a large retail partner, we evaluate 100 warehouse requirements elicited from practitioner interviews, with GPT, Qwen, and DeepSeek as base LLMs. Relative to direct LLM reformulation, our framework improves correctness and end-to-end success across all three models, raising end-to-end success from 72--76% to 79--83%.

AI.tldr: A graph-constrained agentic framework for retail supply chain adaptation that uses LLMs with domain agents to find and validate optimal intervention paths, improving end-to-end success rates from 72-76% to 79-83%.
AI.motivation: Retail supply chains have complex, coupled decision modules that need to adapt as requirements change. While LLMs offer natural-language interfaces, existing methods focus on individual optimization models and struggle with heterogeneous decision pipelines where requirements may have multiple intervention paths with different downstream effects.
AI.method: Formulate requirement-driven adaptation as joint selection of intervention route and admissible module-level changes. Propose a graph-constrained agentic framework where domain agents expose admissible reformulation interfaces and a central processor searches over bounded intervention paths. Candidates are validated and compared using downstream KPIs.
AI.result: Evaluated on 100 warehouse requirements from practitioner interviews with GPT, Qwen, and DeepSeek as base LLMs. The framework improves correctness and end-to-end success across all three models, raising end-to-end success from 72-76% to 79-83%.
AI.conclusion: The proposed graph-constrained agentic framework effectively addresses the challenge of adapting complex retail supply chain operations by enabling systematic exploration and validation of intervention paths, demonstrating significant improvements over direct LLM reformulation approaches.

title: TraveL: Transformer-based Multi-view Path Distributional Representation Learning
summary: Path representation learning (PRL) for road networks has received increasing research attention, due to various path-related applications. Existing works on PRL typically exploit the co-occurrence relationship among road segments and paths to learn a vector as the path representation, without exploring the varied traveler behaviors and the regional correlation on the path. In this work, we propose to learn distributional representations, which provide valuable information for use in path-related applications, by capturing the varied traveler behaviors as well as the various dependencies within regions of road segments. We propose a novel Transformer-based Multi-view Distributional Representation Learning (TraveL) framework to encode a path along with a travel starting time to a distributional representation, which can be used to decode possible samples of on-path traveler behavior. Moreover, by analyzing the regional correlation which reveals various road segment relationships, we propose a regional attention to encode these correlations in a path. Also, we explore the idea of Kolmogorov-Smirnov (K-S) test to compare the sampled traveler behavior against the collected ground truth to facilitate training. Experimental results show that the proposed TraveL model outperforms the state-of-the-art methods on both synthetic and real-world datasets, by 14.7% in Mean K-S distance for travel time distribution estimation, 16.7% in Mean Absolute Error (MAE) for path similarity prediction, and 3.97% in MAE for destination prediction.

AI.tldr: TraveL: A Transformer-based framework for learning distributional path representations that capture varied traveler behaviors and regional correlations, outperforming state-of-the-art methods on multiple tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing path representation learning methods typically learn single vector representations that don't capture varied traveler behaviors or regional correlations in road networks, limiting their usefulness for path-related applications.
AI.method: Proposes TraveL (Transformer-based Multi-view Distributional Representation Learning) framework that encodes paths with travel starting times into distributional representations using regional attention to capture road segment correlations, and uses Kolmogorov-Smirnov test to compare sampled traveler behavior against ground truth during training.
AI.result: Outperforms state-of-the-art methods by 14.7% in Mean K-S distance for travel time distribution estimation, 16.7% in MAE for path similarity prediction, and 3.97% in MAE for destination prediction on both synthetic and real-world datasets.
AI.conclusion: Distributional path representations that capture varied traveler behaviors and regional correlations significantly improve performance on path-related applications compared to traditional vector-based representations.

title: It's the Problem, Not the Path: Budget and Difficulty Confounds in LLM Reasoning Trajectories
comment: 25 pages, 11 figures, 4 tables. Also available at doi:10.5281/zenodo.22261107. Code and pre-registered protocols: https://github.com/bulutyigit/problem-not-path
summary: Reasoning traces of large language models are widely read as containing "breakthrough" moments and early-legible fates. Both readings rest on measurements missing a counterfactual control at the level of the claim; we supply both controls. First, a restart-controlled truncation probe separates when a solution fits the continuation budget from when a prefix carries value that fresh computation cannot buy, comparing per-anchor continuation solve rates against from-scratch restart curves at matched total generated-token budget. Applied to 178 problem-model cells (89 MATH problems x two small open models, an outcome-blind but difficulty-targeted cohort), exactly 1 of 178 cells survives as prefix-limited; restart dose-response separates a compute-starved model from a capability-limited one; and wherever the matched budget lies inside the restart grid, continuing the model's own prefix beats restarting (9 of 9) -- predominantly compute compression rather than expanded reachability. Second, a pre-registered, difficulty-controlled test finds no detectable outcome information in early-window internal signals beyond a problem-difficulty baseline, and two generation-free analyses of public corpora show why this control is needed: a trace-blind difficulty proxy reaches AUROC 0.873 on 192K DeepSeek-R1 generations -- inside the published probe range -- and a closely matched reconstruction of the closest published early-window positive recovers a comparable pooled result (0.849) while within problem it is statistically indistinguishable from chance at all ten anchors (0.496 at t=4); a post-hoc within-targeted probe finds only a small average residual, concentrated in three low-failure problems. High pooled probe AUROCs cannot by themselves establish within-attempt information; a question-only baseline or within-problem evaluation is required.

AI.tldr: Two controlled analyses challenge common interpretations of LLM reasoning traces: 1) restart-controlled truncation shows most apparent "breakthroughs" are compute compression not capability expansion, and 2) difficulty-controlled tests reveal early-window signals contain minimal outcome information beyond baseline problem difficulty.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses two widespread but potentially misleading interpretations of LLM reasoning traces: the idea of "breakthrough" moments where models suddenly solve problems, and early-legible predictions of final outcomes. Both interpretations lack proper counterfactual controls at the claim level, risking misinterpretation of what these traces actually reveal about model capabilities.
AI.method: Two main methodological approaches: 1) Restart-controlled truncation probe comparing continuation solve rates against from-scratch restart curves at matched token budgets, applied to 178 problem-model combinations (89 MATH problems x 2 small open models). 2) Pre-registered difficulty-controlled tests analyzing early-window internal signals, supplemented by generation-free analyses of public corpora including a trace-blind difficulty proxy and reconstruction of published early-window probes.
AI.result: 1) Only 1 of 178 cells showed genuine prefix-limited capability; restart analysis revealed compute-starved vs capability-limited models; continuing existing prefixes consistently beat restarting at matched budgets (9/9 cases). 2) No detectable outcome information beyond problem-difficulty baseline in early-window signals; trace-blind difficulty proxy achieved AUROC 0.873 within published probe range; reconstructed probe showed within-problem statistical indistinguishability from chance (0.496 at t=4).
AI.conclusion: High pooled probe AUROCs alone cannot establish within-attempt information about LLM reasoning outcomes. Proper evaluation requires either question-only baselines or within-problem analysis to control for problem difficulty confounds. Most apparent "breakthroughs" represent compute compression rather than expanded problem-solving reachability.

title: STAIR (STructure Aware Information Retriever): A novel dataset and LLM based retriever for document structure augmentation
summary: Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) is a key component for generating accurate and hallucination free answers using Large Language Models (LLMs). LLMs are improving at handling long context, but still suffer from "lost in the middle" problem. Thus, precise and accurate retrieval is important. Current retrievers chunk long context into length-based manageable chunks - in the process throwing away rich and informative semantic global structure in the corpus. We introduce a novel retrieval system STAIR that empowers an LLM to exploit global structure in a corpus such as a Table of Contents (ToC) to efficiently store and retrieve information from its model parameters. Our thorough and careful ablation studies with a finetuned Differentiable Search Index (DSI) system show that ToC helps build a low hallucination (less than 0.05%) generative Information Retrieval (IR) system and can generalize to examples where very few training samples are available. To further research in this novel direction of ToC based retrieval we release SearchTome - a diverse benchmark created from 18 books across 6 diverse domains to further research in this novel direction. STAIR achieves a high Recall@1 score of 82.6% on SearchTome as compared to DSI (76.9%), where the difference is found to be statistically significant. STAIR easily beats other strong baselines such as BM25 (59.5%), DPR (68.7%) and out-of-the-box Mistral (13.8%).

AI.tldr: STAIR is a novel retrieval system that leverages Table of Contents (ToC) global structure to improve information retrieval and reduce hallucinations in RAG systems, achieving state-of-the-art performance on the new SearchTome benchmark.
AI.motivation: Current RAG systems use length-based chunking which discards the rich semantic global structure of documents (like Table of Contents). LLMs still suffer from "lost in the middle" problems despite improvements in handling long context, making precise retrieval crucial.
AI.method: STAIR introduces a system that enables LLMs to exploit global corpus structure (ToC) through parameters. Uses finetuned Differentiable Search Index (DSI) with ToC integration. Created SearchTome benchmark from 18 books across 6 diverse domains for evaluation.
AI.result: Achieves 82.6% Recall@1 on SearchTome, significantly outperforming DSI (76.9%), BM25 (59.5%), DPR (68.7%), and Mistral (13.8%). Shows less than 0.05% hallucination rate and strong generalization with few training samples.
AI.conclusion: ToC-based retrieval is a promising direction for improving RAG systems by preserving global semantic structure. STAIR demonstrates superior performance over existing methods and the SearchTome benchmark will facilitate further research in this area.

title: Guide, Not Bind: Why Defeasible Priors Fail in Augmented Lagrangian Causal Discovery
summary: Differentiable causal discovery methods increasingly encode expert priors as forbidden-edge constraints enforced by an Augmented Lagrangian (ALM) penalty, on the assumption that a data-adaptive relaxation mechanism will discount and eventually override a rule the data consistently contradicts. We show this design, which we call \emph{guide, not bind}, fails for two independent, precisely characterized reasons, and that directly repairing both restores it only partially. First, sequential penalty-ramping ALM suppresses a wrongly-forbidden true edge before any counterfactual check can detect it: we give three necessary conditions any adaptive relaxation must satisfy to avoid this (Proposition~\ref{prop:conditions}), prove that DADU---the natural relaxation rule this paper introduces as the object of study---violates all three (Corollary~\ref{cor:dadu_failure}), and confirm the failure across 3{,}072 training runs spanning graphs from 4 to 32 nodes, where a single wrong prior suppresses a true edge in 87--97\% of trials under DADU. Second, and independent of any fix to the mechanism, we prove in closed form that the standard correlation-matching objective ties a true edge and its reverse to an identical cost of exactly $2r^2$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:tie}), not because the underlying equal-variance model is unidentifiable, but because normalizing to correlation discards exactly the variance information that would make it identifiable; covariance matching instead separates the two directions by a provable margin of at least $w_0^4$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:separation}).

AI.tldr: The paper reveals critical flaws in differentiable causal discovery methods that use Augmented Lagrangian penalty with expert priors, showing they fail to properly handle contradictory data, and proposes solutions.
AI.motivation: Differentiable causal discovery methods increasingly use Augmented Lagrangian (ALM) penalty to encode expert priors as forbidden-edge constraints, assuming a data-adaptive relaxation mechanism will override rules contradicted by data. However, this "guide, not bind" design fails in practice.
AI.method: The paper identifies two independent failure reasons: 1) Sequential penalty-ramping ALM suppresses wrongly-forbidden true edges before counterfactual detection (studying DADU relaxation rule), 2) Standard correlation-matching objective ties true edges to identical costs while covariance matching separates them. The analysis includes theoretical proofs (Propositions, Lemmas) and empirical validation across 3,072 training runs with graphs from 4 to 32 nodes.
AI.result: DADU violates all three necessary conditions for adaptive relaxation, leading to 87-97% failure rate where a single wrong prior suppresses a true edge. Standard correlation matching ties edge directions to identical cost of exactly 2r², while covariance matching separates them by provable margin of at least w₀⁴.
AI.conclusion: The "guide, not bind" design fundamentally fails for differentiable causal discovery with expert priors. Direct repairs only partially restore functionality. Covariance matching offers better direction separation than correlation matching. New approaches are needed to properly balance expert priors with data evidence in causal discovery.

title: Xiaomi-TabLDM: A Tabular Foundation Model Technical Report
summary:
We introduce Xiaomi-TabLDM, a tabular large data foundation model for classification and regression via in-context learning, which delivers superior prediction accuracy without requiring task-specific fine-tuning. Pretrained exclusively on synthetic data generated from structural causal models (SCMs), our model enables more flexible context utilization and more efficient capacity scaling.
  i) A new performance standard. Strong regression performance across benchmarks: Xiaomi-TabLDM ranks 1st on OpenML-CTR23 and 2nd on regression across TALENT, TabArena, and BCCO, demonstrating consistently strong regression performance across four complementary benchmark suites. Favorable performance--efficiency trade-off: Xiaomi-TabLDM combines strong predictive performance with substantially lower computational cost. For example, on TabArena regression, it achieves the second-highest Elo while using 82% less training time and 68% less prediction time than the top-ranked TabFM.
  ii) Large-scale synthetic pretraining. Xiaomi-TabLDM expands the coverage and diversity of synthetic tabular data used for pretraining. We also adopt a three-stage training strategy together with dual-stream feature grouping, lightweight Attention Residual, and sparse Mixture-of-Experts, enabling Xiaomi-TabLDM to learn richer feature interactions and expert specialization across diverse tabular tasks.
  iii) Test-time scaling. Xiaomi-TabLDM further extends tabular prediction through test-time compute scaling, where allocating additional computation at inference time consistently improves predictive performance over the base model.

AI.tldr: Xiaomi-TabLDM is a tabular foundation model for classification and regression using in-context learning, achieving top benchmark performance with synthetic data pretraining and efficient scaling.
AI.motivation: Current tabular models often require task-specific fine-tuning and face computational efficiency challenges. The authors aim to create a foundation model that can achieve strong prediction accuracy across diverse tabular tasks without fine-tuning, while maintaining computational efficiency.
AI.method: The model is pretrained exclusively on synthetic data generated from structural causal models (SCMs). It uses a three-stage training strategy with dual-stream feature grouping, lightweight Attention Residual, and sparse Mixture-of-Experts. The model employs in-context learning for predictions and supports test-time compute scaling for improved performance.
AI.result: Xiaomi-TabLDM achieves top-tier performance: ranks 1st on OpenML-CTR23, 2nd on regression across TALENT, TabArena, and BCCO benchmarks. It shows superior efficiency with 82% less training time and 68% less prediction time than top-ranked TabFM while achieving second-highest Elo on TabArena regression.
AI.conclusion: Xiaomi-TabLDM establishes a new performance standard for tabular foundation models, demonstrating that synthetic data pretraining combined with efficient architectural innovations can achieve state-of-the-art results without task-specific fine-tuning, while maintaining favorable performance-efficiency trade-offs.

title: Beyond Straightness: Non-Crossing Flow Matching via Quantile AlignTree Coupling
summary: The performance of Flow Matching largely depends on the quality of the coupling between the source and target distributions. However, independent coupling often leads to path crossings and local velocity ambiguity, while OT-based couplings typically incur high construction costs. To address this challenge, we propose Quantile AlignTree Flow Matching (QAT-FM), an efficient structured coupling strategy that constructs a hierarchical coupling between a Gaussian prior and the target data distribution via a quantile-aligned tree structure. QAT-FM constructs the coupling in $\mathcal{O}(Nd\log N)$ time and supports per-pair source sampling with $\mathcal{O}(d)$ complexity, enabling scalable training for large-scale high-dimensional generative tasks. Theoretically, we prove that the QAT coupling satisfies marginal consistency, induces non-crossing linear interpolation paths, and consistently improves path separation at intermediate times compared with independent coupling, thereby alleviating local velocity ambiguity. QAT-FM further extends naturally to conditional generation, enabling structured conditional coupling while preserving global Gaussian alignment. Experiments across diverse benchmark datasets demonstrate that QAT-FM achieves competitive generative performance while substantially reducing coupling construction cost.

AI.tldr: QAT-FM is an efficient hierarchical coupling strategy for Flow Matching that uses quantile-aligned tree structures to reduce coupling construction costs while improving path separation and reducing local velocity ambiguity.
AI.motivation: Flow Matching performance heavily depends on source-target coupling quality. Independent couplings cause path crossings and local velocity ambiguity, while optimal transport (OT)-based couplings have high construction costs. Need for efficient structured coupling that balances quality and computational efficiency.
AI.method: Quantile AlignTree Flow Matching (QAT-FM) constructs hierarchical coupling between Gaussian prior and target distribution using quantile-aligned tree structure. Builds coupling in O(Nd log N) time with O(d) per-pair source sampling complexity. Uses tree-based hierarchical partitioning with quantile alignment for structured coupling.
AI.result: QAT-FM achieves competitive generative performance on diverse benchmark datasets while substantially reducing coupling construction cost. Theoretically proven to satisfy marginal consistency, produce non-crossing linear interpolation paths, and improve path separation compared to independent coupling.
AI.conclusion: QAT-FM provides an efficient scalable coupling strategy for Flow Matching that balances computational efficiency with coupling quality, enabling large-scale high-dimensional generative tasks while reducing path crossings and local velocity ambiguity issues.

title: Inferring Affective Consciousness in an Artificial Agent: A Case Study
summary: Creatures that display 'hedonic place preference behaviour' are thought by many scientists to experience feelings, on the assumption that their attraction to pleasure-producing substances which lack nutritional value (e.g. cocaine, morphine) cannot easily be attributed to unconscious instinctual behaviour. In this paper, we discuss how a simple artificial agent that instantiates attributes of an affective system engaging in felt uncertainty about its intrinsic needs in relation to environmental resources can similarly display hedonic place preference behaviour -- through an apparently subjective form of information processing -- while simultaneously being entirely deter-ministic. We outline some implications of this artificially engineered behaviour for our understanding of the physical basis of consciousness and the experience of free will.

AI.tldr: A deterministic artificial agent with simulated affective uncertainty can display hedonic place preference behavior similar to biological creatures, challenging assumptions about consciousness and free will.
AI.motivation: To challenge the assumption that hedonic place preference behavior in creatures necessarily indicates conscious feelings, by demonstrating how deterministic artificial agents can exhibit similar behaviors through computational processes.
AI.method: Created a simple artificial agent with an affective system that experiences "felt uncertainty" about its intrinsic needs in relation to environmental resources, simulating hedonic place preference behavior through deterministic information processing.
AI.result: The artificial agent successfully displayed hedonic place preference behavior similar to biological creatures, despite being entirely deterministic and lacking subjective consciousness.
AI.conclusion: Hedonic place preference behavior may not require consciousness or subjective experience; deterministic systems can produce similar behaviors, challenging our understanding of the physical basis of consciousness and free will.

title: A Two-Stage Forecasting System for CPU Workload Prediction in Private Clouds
summary: Accurate cloud resource forecasting is essential for proactive resource provisioning, maintaining Quality of Service (QoS), and reducing operational costs in dynamic cloud environments. The existing forecasting approaches predominantly estimate future CPU workload directly from historical resource traces, which often overlook the relationship between customer service demand and subsequent resource consumption. This study proposes a two-stage integrated forecasting model that explicitly models this dependency by first forecasting customer service requests, expressed as Transactions Per Second (TPS), and subsequently estimating future CPU workload from the TPS forecast. Both the forecasting component and resource prediction component employed the XGBoost model within a cascaded learning architecture, complemented by adaptive online retraining using an expanding-window strategy to address concept drift in continuously evolving cloud workloads. The proposed work was evaluated using real-world traces collected from a private cloud environment comprising ten applications. Experimental results demonstrate robust forecasting performance by achieving Symmetric Mean Absolute Percentage Error (SMAPE) below $7\%$ for most applications, with the best-performing application achieving an MAE of $0.7372$, RMSE of $1.1866$, SMAPE of $3.57\%$, and an R2 of $0.9185$. Horizon-wise drift analysis confirmed stable recursive forecasting behavior with controlled error accumulation across a 60-step prediction horizon. Compared with the conventional direct CPU forecasting method, the proposed two-stage integrated model gives improved forecasting robustness, computational efficiency, and interpretability, making it well-suited for proactive resource management and intelligent auto-scaling in cloud computing environments.

AI.tldr: Two-stage forecasting model first predicts customer service requests (TPS), then CPU workload from TPS forecast, outperforming direct CPU forecasting in cloud environments.
AI.motivation: Existing cloud resource forecasting approaches directly estimate CPU workload from historical traces, overlooking the relationship between customer service demand and subsequent resource consumption, leading to suboptimal proactive resource provisioning.
AI.method: Proposes a two-stage integrated forecasting model: 1) Forecasting customer service requests (Transactions Per Second/TPS), 2) Estimating future CPU workload from TPS forecast. Uses XGBoost model in cascaded learning architecture with adaptive online retraining via expanding-window strategy to handle concept drift.
AI.result: Achieved SMAPE below 7% for most applications, with best-performing application achieving MAE of 0.7372, RMSE of 1.1866, SMAPE of 3.57%, and R² of 0.9185. Horizon-wise drift analysis showed stable recursive forecasting across 60-step prediction horizon with controlled error accumulation.
AI.conclusion: The two-stage integrated model provides improved forecasting robustness, computational efficiency, and interpretability compared to conventional direct CPU forecasting, making it suitable for proactive resource management and intelligent auto-scaling in cloud computing environments.

title: Lose the Order, Keep the Hierarchy: Deordering HTN Plans
summary: Hierarchical Task Network (HTN) planning is a powerful planning formalism based on task decomposition. Although most of the literature studied plan generation, comparatively less attention has been paid to post-plan optimization. In particular, plan deordering has been extensively studied in classical planning but remains under-researched in the HTN setting. Plan deordering removes unnecessary ordering constraints between actions in a plan whilst keeping the plan valid. In this paper, we adapt two established plan deordering techniques from classical planning by extending the techniques to account for hierarchical decomposition constraints. We evaluate our proposed approaches on the IPC 2023 Partial-Order HTN benchmarks and we compare them against Optiplan, an HTN planner that generates partially ordered plans directly. Our results show a substantial reduction in number of ordering constraints in both our implementations. Although we also observe a reduction in critical path length, the improvements are less pronounced.

AI.tldr: Adapting classical planning's plan deordering techniques to HTN planning to remove unnecessary ordering constraints while maintaining plan validity.
AI.motivation: Plan deordering has been extensively studied in classical planning but remains under-researched in HTN planning. While most HTN literature focuses on plan generation, post-plan optimization (specifically deordering) has received little attention despite its potential benefits.
AI.method: Adapt two established plan deordering techniques from classical planning by extending them to account for hierarchical decomposition constraints in HTN planning. Implement these approaches for the HTN setting.
AI.result: Substantial reduction in number of ordering constraints in both implementations when evaluated on IPC 2023 Partial-Order HTN benchmarks. Also observed reduction in critical path length, though improvements were less pronounced.
AI.conclusion: Classical planning's plan deordering techniques can be successfully adapted to HTN planning, leading to significant reductions in ordering constraints while maintaining plan validity, though critical path length improvements are more modest.

title: Mind the Gap: Robustness Risks in PII Detection Systems
summary:
Personally Identifiable Information (PII) detection is a foundational component of data protection infrastructure where missed entities constitute direct privacy and security risks. Although modern PII systems report strong performance on standard benchmarks, we show that these evaluations mask substantial robustness failures under realistic distribution shifts encountered in deployment. Rather than comparing state-of-the-art accuracy, we study how different PII detection paradigms fail under noisy, unstructured, and informal inputs. We construct a stress test benchmark spanning seven categories of natural distribution shift and evaluate representative systems from three widely deployed architectural families: encoder-based NER (SpaCy), rule-based hybrid detection (Presidio), and generative LLM extraction (Qwen2.5-3B).
  All three exhibit significant degradation on out-of-distribution inputs, but with distinct and complementary failure modes. Encoder models primarily fail on unseen surface forms and boundary detection, rule-based systems fail on non-standard formats, and LLMs exhibit entity-type confusion and generation instability. These results show that aggregate benchmark scores obscure deployment-critical weaknesses and that no single architecture is uniformly reliable across PII categories. Motivated by these findings, we propose a hybrid detection pipeline with a QA-driven feedback loop for iterative risk mitigation, and release our benchmark to support OOD-aware evaluation of PII systems.

AI.tldr: Current PII detection systems show strong benchmark performance but fail significantly under realistic distribution shifts, with different architectures having complementary failure modes, leading to proposed hybrid pipeline with QA feedback.
AI.motivation: PII detection is critical for data protection, but standard benchmarks mask substantial robustness failures under realistic distribution shifts encountered in deployment, potentially creating direct privacy and security risks.
AI.method: Created stress test benchmark spanning seven categories of natural distribution shift, evaluated three representative PII detection architectures: encoder-based NER (SpaCy), rule-based hybrid (Presidio), and generative LLM extraction (Qwen2.5-3B), analyzing failure patterns.
AI.result: All three architectures showed significant degradation on OOD inputs with distinct failure modes: encoder models failed on unseen surface forms/boundary detection, rule-based systems on non-standard formats, and LLMs on entity-type confusion/generation instability.
AI.conclusion: Aggregate benchmark scores obscure deployment-critical weaknesses; no single architecture is uniformly reliable across PII categories; proposed hybrid pipeline with QA-driven feedback loop for iterative risk mitigation; released benchmark for OOD-aware evaluation.

title: Value-Preserving Architectures for Agentic AI Systems
comment: Accepted to AgenticDev Workshop at ASE 2026
summary: The emergence of agentic AI and LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) presents unprecedented opportunities for automating complex tasks, while simultaneously raising critical concerns about the preservation of fundamental human-centered values, such as privacy, fairness, and safety. Although software engineering has traditionally focused on functional correctness, the adoption of LLMs and AI agents into complex socio-technical systems has intensified the need for responsible software engineering and robust value alignment. In MAS, architectural design decisions, such as coordination mechanisms, communication protocols, and system topologies, play a central role in shaping system behavior and the outcomes they produce. This paper argues that architectural choices influence not only the functionality and performance of MAS but can also promote value-oriented system behavior. Therefore, we investigate how different architectural designs support different human-centered values, discussing the following value-preserving architectural patterns: (i) a privacy-aware architecture with a federated topology, (ii) a distributed architecture to promote pluralism and diversity, and (iii) a guard-agent architecture to detect and mitigate unfairness. Finally, we introduce representative use cases to illustrate the proposed architectures in real-world scenarios. By linking architectural design with human-centered values, this work lays the foundation for a unified set of architectural patterns and guidelines towards the design of trustworthy MAS.

AI.tldr: This paper explores how architectural design in LLM-based multi-agent systems can promote human-centered values like privacy, fairness, and safety, introducing specific value-preserving patterns and illustrating them with real-world use cases.
AI.motivation: The increasing adoption of LLMs and AI agents in complex socio-technical systems creates an urgent need for responsible software engineering that goes beyond functional correctness to preserve human-centered values like privacy, fairness, and safety. Current approaches often overlook how architectural decisions can influence value-oriented behavior in multi-agent systems.
AI.method: The paper investigates how different architectural designs support human-centered values by proposing and analyzing value-preserving architectural patterns: (1) privacy-aware architecture with federated topology, (2) distributed architecture promoting pluralism and diversity, and (3) guard-agent architecture for unfairness detection and mitigation. The approach includes introducing representative use cases to demonstrate these architectures in practice.
AI.result: The paper establishes a connection between architectural design choices and human-centered values in multi-agent systems, presenting three specific architectural patterns that can promote privacy, pluralism/diversity, and fairness. It provides practical illustrations through real-world use cases and lays groundwork for unified architectural patterns and guidelines for trustworthy MAS.
AI.conclusion: Architectural design decisions in LLM-based multi-agent systems play a crucial role in shaping not only functionality and performance but also value-oriented system behavior. By linking architectural design with human-centered values, this work provides foundational patterns and guidelines for building trustworthy multi-agent systems that preserve fundamental values in AI automation.

title: Spectral characteristics of autoencoder parameters as a vector representation of data
comment: 13 pages, 6 figures. This is a shortened (theorem proofs are skipped) and translated version of the paper published in a Russian-language peer-reviewed journal, the citation is in the paper footnote
summary: This paper examines the relationship between the parameters of autoencoder models and the statistical properties of the data on which they are trained. Autoencoders are defined as models with an encoder-decoder architecture, trained to reconstruct input data through a compressed latent representation. It is proposed that the model parameters can be viewed as a dense vector representation of the corresponding sample. To test this hypothesis, a theoretical and experimental study is conducted in which a vector representation is formed based on the spectral characteristics of the autoencoder parameter matrices. Theoretical analysis shows that the singular values of the model parameter matrices are related to the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix of the training data, ensuring the transfer of information between the data space and the parameter space. Experimental results on the CIFAR-10 and FashionMNIST datasets confirm that the resulting vector representations allow for a high degree of accuracy in distinguishing between models trained on different data subsets, without resorting to complex vector generation algorithms or using the original samples. These results suggest that the parameters of trained autoencoders can be viewed as sample representations.

AI.tldr: Autoencoder parameters can serve as vector representations of training data samples, with theoretical links to data covariance eigenvalues and experimental validation on image datasets.
AI.motivation: The paper investigates whether autoencoder model parameters can be viewed as representations of the training data samples themselves, exploring the relationship between model parameters and statistical properties of the data they're trained on.
AI.method: Proposes that autoencoder parameters form dense vector representations of corresponding samples. Uses spectral analysis of parameter matrices (singular values) theoretically linked to data covariance eigenvalues. Experiments conducted on CIFAR-10 and FashionMNIST datasets using vector representations derived from spectral characteristics of parameter matrices.
AI.result: Experimental results show high accuracy in distinguishing between models trained on different data subsets using the derived vector representations, without needing complex generation algorithms or original samples. Theoretical analysis confirms singular values of parameter matrices relate to eigenvalues of training data covariance matrix.
AI.conclusion: Parameters of trained autoencoders can effectively serve as sample representations, with mathematical foundations in spectral analysis and practical utility demonstrated through dataset discrimination experiments.

title: Speak for Me: Giving LLMs the Situational Awareness to Participate in a Meeting
summary: In online meeting delegation, LLM agents fail to recognize when to speak. With no structured way to track stances, coverage, and floor, they miss the moments where they should contribute. Prompt-only delegates stay silent on 51.4% of the absent participant's talking opportunities on the AMI corpus. We present CAPA (Collaborative Agent Predictive Architecture), an architecture for online meeting delegation. A Perceiver updates the meeting state from each observed turn. A Predictor forecasts how the conversation will continue. A Controller decides whether to speak and which proposition to surface. A Generator phrases the chosen contribution in the participant's style. Two judges score the forecast and the action against the next observed turn. A Recalibrator updates the meeting state from those verdicts for future decisions. To evaluate online delegation, we introduce an episode-level protocol that scores whether, when, and what a delegate contributes around the participant's actual idea units. The protocol's schema-constrained LLM judges align with human annotations at Cohen's kappa = 0.71. On 137 AMI meetings, CAPA reduces the silence rate from 51.4% to 2.5%, doubles credited recovery (26.1 --> 52.2), and keeps hallucination at 0.6%. The failure mode shifts from omission to selection, with each residual near-miss attributable to a specific module of the architecture. Mechanism ablations identify the meeting state as the lever that closes the recognition gap, where raw-context scaling alone does not.

AI.tldr: CAPA architecture reduces LLM agent silence in online meeting delegation from 51.4% to 2.5% by using predictive components and state tracking to recognize when to speak.
AI.motivation: LLM agents in online meeting delegation fail to recognize when to speak due to lack of structured tracking of stances, coverage, and floor dynamics, missing 51.4% of talking opportunities.
AI.method: CAPA architecture with six components: Perceiver (updates meeting state), Predictor (forecasts conversation), Controller (decides to speak), Generator (phrases contributions), two Judges (score forecasts/actions), and Recalibrator (updates state). Introduces episode-level evaluation protocol with schema-constrained LLM judges.
AI.result: On 137 AMI meetings, CAPA reduces silence rate from 51.4% to 2.5%, doubles credited recovery (26.1 to 52.2), keeps hallucination at 0.6%, and shows human-judge alignment at Cohen's kappa = 0.71. Meeting state tracking is key lever.
AI.conclusion: CAPA effectively addresses the recognition gap in online meeting delegation through structured state tracking and predictive components, shifting failure mode from omission to selection, with meeting state as critical component.

title: Restricted Eigenvalues Beyond Gaussian Width: Threshold Occupancy under Heavy Tails
summary: Restricted eigenvalue (RE) bounds govern stable recovery by norm-regularized estimators. For isotropic sub-Gaussian measurements, the benchmark sample size is $1+w(A)^2$, where $w(A)$ is the Gaussian width of the normalized descent cone. The COLT 2015 open-problem note (Banerjee et al., 2015) asked whether the same law follows for heavy-tailed designs from a uniform small-ball condition alone. We give an explicit and systematic negative answer to the general question as formulated there: the proposed law fails in its full dimension-free, arbitrary-set form, and the missing obstruction is simultaneous threshold occupancy. A constant-width polyhedral descent cone with fixed small-ball constants has zero empirical RE on every sample path up to half the ambient dimension. More generally, every finite range space admits exact threshold encoding in an arbitrarily narrow spherical cap and a lift to a full polyhedral descent-cone section. For every fixed threshold VC dimension $d$, as $β\downarrow0$, the sharp worst-case sample complexity is $Θ(β^{-1}[d\log(1/β)+\log(1/δ)])$. The separation persists under exact isotropy and all finite moments: on the same constant-width cone, Gaussian measurements succeed with $O(1+\log(1/δ))$ samples, whereas an isotropic heavy-tailed design fails pathwise for $n\lesssim\sqrt{p/\log p}$. Gaussian smoothing yields an everywhere-positive $C^\infty$ density while retaining arbitrarily poor RE. Under isotropy, a distribution-free fallback governed by affine dimension times squared enclosing radius is sharp on this family.

AI.tldr: The paper gives a negative answer to whether RE bounds for norm-regularized estimators follow the same law for heavy-tailed designs as for isotropic sub-Gaussian measurements, showing the proposed dimension-free law fails for heavy-tailed designs.
AI.motivation: To address the COLT 2015 open-problem note by Banerjee et al., which asked whether the same sample complexity law (n ~ 1 + w(A)^2) follows for heavy-tailed designs under uniform small-ball conditions alone.
AI.method: Constructs counterexamples using constant-width polyhedral descent cones with fixed small-ball constants that have zero empirical restricted eigenvalue (RE) on every sample path. Shows exact threshold encoding in arbitrarily narrow spherical caps and lifts to full polyhedral descent-cone sections.
AI.result: For threshold VC dimension d, sharp worst-case sample complexity is Θ(β^{-1}[d log(1/β) + log(1/δ)]). Shows separation persists under exact isotropy: Gaussian measurements succeed with O(1+log(1/δ)) samples while isotropic heavy-tailed designs fail pathwise for n ≲ √(p/log p). Demonstrates Gaussian smoothing yields positive density while retaining poor RE.
AI.conclusion: The dimension-free law fails for heavy-tailed designs under uniform small-ball conditions alone. Under isotropy, a distribution-free fallback governed by affine dimension times squared enclosing radius is sharp on this family of counterexamples.

title: Towards Numerical TOHTN Planning with SMT-based HTN-SAT Encoding
summary: While HTN planning has received significant attention in recent years, support for numerical reasoning remains very limited. In this paper, we investigate numerical Totally-Ordered HTN (TOHTN) planning and show how standard SAT-based encodings can be naturally extended with SMT to handle numeric fluents. In addition, we introduce a benchmark suite for numerical TOHTN planning, providing a first common basis for evaluation in this setting. Experimental results show that this simple encoding already constitutes a competitive baseline. This work opens the way to more expressive approaches to HTN planning.

AI.tldr: Extending SAT-based TOHTN planning to handle numerical reasoning using SMT encodings.
AI.motivation: HTN planning has limited support for numerical reasoning, which is crucial for many real-world planning problems that involve numeric fluents and constraints.
AI.method: Extend standard SAT-based encodings for Totally-Ordered HTN (TOHTN) planning with Satisfiability Modulo Theories (SMT) to handle numeric fluents and numerical reasoning.
AI.result: The SMT-based encoding provides a competitive baseline for numerical TOHTN planning, demonstrated through experimental evaluation on a new benchmark suite created for this purpose.
AI.conclusion: This work establishes a foundation for numerical HTN planning and opens the way for more expressive approaches to HTN planning with numerical capabilities.

title: An Adversarial Zero-Shot Learning Approach for Anomaly Detection in Multivariate IoT Traffic Data
summary: Anomaly detection in Internet of Things (IoT) networks presents unique challenges due to the diversity of devices, lack of labeled data, and domain variability across environments. In this paper, we propose a novel framework for multivariate time-series anomaly detection that leverages adversarial learning and contrastive loss within a sequence-based Variational Autoencoder (VAE) architecture. Our method enables zero-shot domain adaptation by jointly optimizing domain-invariant latent representations and semantically structured embedding spaces, without requiring labeled data or raw feature transfer. To address the heterogeneity of IoT deployments, we introduce encoder and decoder adaptor layers that align feature distributions across domains while preserving contextual semantics. Additionally, we propose a destination-based segmentation strategy to better model real-world communication structures in IoT traffic. Our framework is comprehensively evaluated on six distinct datasets spanning industrial, enterprise, general-purpose, smart home, and military automation domains across 44 transfer scenarios. Experimental results demonstrate strong zero-shot generalization in several cross-domain settings and competitive performance against a contrastive domain-adaptation baseline under realistic, heterogeneous, and privacy-constrained IoT conditions.

AI.tldr: A zero-shot domain adaptation framework for IoT anomaly detection using adversarial VAE with contrastive learning, enabling cross-domain generalization without labeled data or raw feature transfer.
AI.motivation: IoT networks present unique challenges for anomaly detection: diverse devices, lack of labeled data, domain variability across environments, and privacy constraints that prevent raw feature sharing.
AI.method: Uses adversarial learning and contrastive loss within a sequence-based Variational Autoencoder. Includes encoder/decoder adaptor layers for feature distribution alignment, zero-shot domain adaptation with domain-invariant latent representations, and destination-based segmentation for IoT traffic modeling.
AI.result: Comprehensive evaluation on 6 datasets across industrial, enterprise, smart home, general-purpose, and military domains (44 transfer scenarios). Shows strong zero-shot generalization in cross-domain settings and competitive performance against contrastive domain-adaptation baselines under realistic IoT conditions.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework effectively addresses IoT anomaly detection challenges by enabling zero-shot domain adaptation without labeled data, demonstrating practical applicability across diverse, heterogeneous, and privacy-constrained IoT environments.

title: More Criticism Does Not Make a Better Review: EquiReview-R
summary: AI reviewers can now produce many specific criticisms, but more criticism is not necessarily a better review. A review may miss a consequential weakness or retain an allegation that available evidence does not support. These failures require opposite corrections, yet generation-oriented systems and aggregate measures obscure the distinction. We therefore recast AI-assisted review as evidence-guided refinement of a structured concern set, with omission and overcritique treated as separate risks. Building on this formulation, we introduce EquiReview-R, which resolves existing concerns against localized evidence, searches for missing issues from independent and review-conditioned perspectives, and returns stop, continue, or defer. To expose the failure mode that motivates this design, we construct an evidence-linked trajectory corpus. Its retrospective analysis shows why revision must precede further search: nearly all concerns in a high-recall review lack a definitive evidential disposition, while an earlier refinement mechanism cannot revise them. On a frozen cohort of previously unseen papers, EquiReview-R satisfies the prespecified non-inferiority criterion for major omission, reduces major overcritique from 15.5% to 8.1%, and attains a one-sided omission upper bound of 9.9% while stopping on 52.4% of papers. Computation-matched controls, controlled pairs, and ablations show that the gain comes from revision rather than extra inference or shorter output. We release the corpus as ReviewTrace, an evidence-linked resource for studying review revision, disagreement, and provenance.

AI.tldr: EquiReview-R is an AI-assisted review system that treats omission and overcritique as separate risks, using evidence-guided refinement to resolve concerns and search for missing issues, achieving better balance than generation-oriented systems.
AI.motivation: Current AI review systems generate many criticisms but face two key failure modes: missing consequential weaknesses and retaining unsupported allegations. Generation-oriented systems and aggregate measures obscure the distinction between these opposite problems, motivating a new approach that treats omission and overcritique as separate risks.
AI.method: Recasts AI-assisted review as evidence-guided refinement of structured concern sets. Introduces EquiReview-R which: 1) resolves existing concerns against localized evidence, 2) searches for missing issues from independent and review-conditioned perspectives, and 3) returns stop, continue, or defer decisions. Constructed an evidence-linked trajectory corpus (ReviewTrace) to study review revision patterns.
AI.result: On unseen papers, EquiReview-R satisfied non-inferiority criterion for major omission, reduced major overcritique from 15.5% to 8.1%, achieved one-sided omission upper bound of 9.9% while stopping on 52.4% of papers. Computational controls showed gains come from revision rather than extra inference or shorter output.
AI.conclusion: The evidence-linked refinement approach successfully addresses the distinct risks of omission and overcritique in AI-assisted review. Revision must precede further search, as concerns in high-recall reviews often lack definitive evidential disposition. The released ReviewTrace corpus provides valuable resource for studying review revision, disagreement, and provenance.

title: LongCounsel-8: A Benchmark Suite for Longitudinal Depression Tracking from Multi-Session Counseling Dialogues
summary: Tracking depression from multi-session counseling dialogues requires estimating both current symptom severity and how it changes across sessions. Yet progress on this task is constrained by the scarcity of longitudinal counseling data with standardized session-level depression labels. Existing resources typically provide either multi-session conversations without depression labels or labeled interviews in a single session. Building such a benchmark poses three challenges: maintaining longitudinal consistency and diversity, grounding symptom progression in empirical patterns, and expressing controlled depression states naturally without exposing target labels. To address these challenges, we introduce LongCounsel-8, a benchmark suite of three independently generated datasets totaling 7,749 five-session counseling trajectories, grounded in real-world client profiles, depression trajectories, symptom compositions, and counseling patterns. We combine profile-grounded simulation, empirically informed state construction, and indirect behavioral realization to address these challenges. Across the benchmark, simulated self-reports closely recover the controlled states, supporting label fidelity. Experiments on existing depression tracking methods reveal three key findings: (1) lower single-session score error does not guarantee accurate identification of trend, i.e., improvement or worsening; (2) existing methods are consistently less reliable on worsening trajectories; and (3) additional session history may reduce the accuracy of trend prediction. Together, these findings establish LongCounsel-8 as a foundation for advancing depression assessment from static, single-session prediction toward reliable longitudinal tracking of mental-health change.

AI.tldr: Created LongCounsel-8, a benchmark for tracking depression across multi-session counseling dialogues, addressing data scarcity by simulating 7,749 five-session counseling trajectories grounded in real-world patterns.
AI.motivation: Progress in depression tracking across counseling sessions is constrained by scarce longitudinal data with standardized session-level depression labels. Existing resources have limitations: either multi-session conversations without labels or single-session labeled interviews.
AI.method: Introduced LongCounsel-8 benchmark suite with three datasets totaling 7,749 five-session counseling trajectories. Used profile-grounded simulation, empirically informed state construction, and indirect behavioral realization to address challenges of longitudinal consistency, symptom progression grounding, and natural expression of depression states.
AI.result: Simulated self-reports closely recover controlled states, supporting label fidelity. Experiments revealed three key findings: 1) Lower single-session error doesn't guarantee accurate trend identification, 2) Existing methods are consistently less reliable on worsening trajectories, and 3) Additional session history may reduce trend prediction accuracy.
AI.conclusion: LongCounsel-8 establishes a foundation for advancing depression assessment from static, single-session prediction toward reliable longitudinal tracking of mental-health change, addressing critical gaps in current depression tracking methodology.

title: FiMI Banking: A Sovereign Model for Indian Retail Banking
summary: Banks need conversational systems that can answer product questions, assist customers with account-related requests, and operate safely within strict operational and regulatory constraints. General-purpose language models do not reliably meet these requirements. They fall short when a task requires grounded information, correct tool use, or cautious handling of bank-specific sensitive situations. We introduce FiMI Banking, a controlled Indian retail-banking setting. We build it from vetted banking documents, structured ground truth, synthetic customer backgrounds, and banking tools. We evaluate two post-training approaches: preference optimization for response-level behavior, and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards for multi-turn tool-use tasks. Preference optimization improves safe behavior substantially: out-of-scope refusal rises from 52% to 80%. Reinforcement learning improves edge-case performance from 0.509 to 0.718 and order-sensitive task performance from 0.590 to 0.679, while using 29% fewer generated tokens. These results show that preference optimization and verifiable-reward reinforcement learning address complementary requirements for reliable banking agents.

AI.tldr: Post-training methods (preference optimization & verifiable RL) improve banking conversational agents' safety and tool-use performance for Indian retail banking tasks.
AI.motivation: Banks need conversational systems that can reliably handle product questions, account requests, and operate safely within regulatory constraints, but general-purpose language models fail at tasks requiring grounded information, correct tool use, and cautious handling of sensitive banking situations.
AI.method: Created FiMI Banking, a controlled Indian retail-banking test setting from vetted documents, structured ground truth, synthetic customer backgrounds, and banking tools. Evaluated two post-training approaches: 1) preference optimization for response-level behavior, and 2) reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards for multi-turn tool-use tasks.
AI.result: Preference optimization improved safe behavior substantially: out-of-scope refusal rose from 52% to 80%. Reinforcement learning improved edge-case performance from 0.509 to 0.718 and order-sensitive task performance from 0.590 to 0.679, while using 29% fewer generated tokens.
AI.conclusion: Preference optimization and verifiable-reward reinforcement learning address complementary requirements for reliable banking agents, showing that specialized post-training methods are effective for creating safe, efficient banking conversational systems.

title: LeanGRPO: Eliminating Redundant Recomputation in Diffusion RL
summary: Diffusion reinforcement learning (RL) has recently achieved significant success in post-training image and video generative models. However, most diffusion RL methods, including DanceGRPO and FlowGRPO, recompute selected timesteps with gradient tracking after rollout. Under on-policy training with the same backend for rollout and update, this recomputation is mathematically redundant. Intuitively, the rollout and policy update steps can reuse the same feed-forward backbone to avoid redundant computation, but doing so can incur a large memory overhead during rollout. To address the issue, we present LeanGRPO by restructuring the data-parallel layout and introducing two recompute-free training schedules for trajectory-logprob diffusion RL: (1) LeanGRPO-Retain enables gradient tracking during rollout and directly reuses the resulting computation graphs and saved activations for backward during update, requiring no recomputation; and (2) LeanGRPO-Reweight also enables gradients during rollout, but immediately backpropagates each selected step using a provisional advantage and delays gradient synchronization, then corrects the provisional gradients with the true advantage after the trajectory is completed. These schedules target different model scales and input sizes. Across FlowGRPO/DanceGRPO with FLUX.1-dev and Wan, LeanGRPO achieves up to 1.83x end-to-end speedup while preserving the original optimization objective.

AI.tldr: LeanGRPO eliminates redundant recomputation in diffusion RL by restructuring data-parallel layout and introducing two recompute-free training schedules that achieve up to 1.83x speedup while preserving optimization objectives.
AI.motivation: Current diffusion RL methods (like DanceGRPO and FlowGRPO) waste computation by recomputing selected timesteps with gradient tracking after rollout, which is mathematically redundant when using the same backend for rollout and update. While reusing the same feed-forward backbone could avoid redundancy, it creates large memory overhead during rollout.
AI.method: The authors present LeanGRPO with two main innovations: 1) Restructuring data-parallel layout, and 2) Two recompute-free training schedules: LeanGRPO-Retain (enables gradient tracking during rollout and reuses computation graphs/activations for backward pass) and LeanGRPO-Reweight (enables gradients during rollout, immediately backpropagates each step with provisional advantage, delays gradient synchronization, then corrects with true advantage). These schedules target different model scales and input sizes.
AI.result: Across FlowGRPO/DanceGRPO with FLUX.1-dev and Wan models, LeanGRPO achieves up to 1.83x end-to-end speedup while preserving the original optimization objective of the diffusion RL methods.
AI.conclusion: LeanGRPO successfully addresses the computational redundancy problem in diffusion RL by introducing efficient recompute-free training schedules that maintain the mathematical integrity of the optimization while significantly improving training efficiency.

title: Interface-Induced Trajectory Censoring
comment: 39 pages, 14 pages main text. Code, data, and pre-registrations: https://github.com/nebula-1999/Interface-Induced-Trajectory-Censoring
summary:
Agent evaluations report a tool-call rate read off the serving stack. That number can be zero while the model is emitting well-formed calls: the interface censors the trajectory before anything downstream sees it.
  On BFCL v4's own data, executor and scorer, holding weights, cases, decoding and seeds fixed and changing only the serving adapter, the same model scores 0.00 or 0.96 / 0.19. A 2x2 over chat template and parser locates the effect exactly: both main effects are exactly zero and all of it sits in the interaction -- no component is defective, and repairing one side of the contract buys precisely nothing. On tau-bench's 115 interactive retail tasks the same swap moves server-parsed calls from 0 to 636 and tasks reaching any tool execution from 0 to 103. Our probe reproduces the funnel across a 21x scale range of Qwen2.5-Coder: the server parses 0/100 at every size while well-formed emitted calls rise to 80/100 at 32B (~72 after calibration against an adjudicated gold standard). Under a matched envelope, across a comparable scale span, the silent fraction stays at 0-2, a prediction committed to the repository before the run. Llama-3.1-8B's 23% rate of calling the task function itself as a tool falls to 0 under one strict:true flag.
  The mismatch reaches inside the training loop, and its consequence is scale-dependent: in verl's AgentLoop at 7B, 45 of 115 generations carry a complete call; 0 are accepted, 0 execute, 0 return an observation. At 1.5B the same zero is over-determined, so we report the two scales separately. At evaluation time, repairing the adapter restores the mechanism but not a significant outcome gain: parsing 0->84, rescues 0->9, pass rate 53->62 (n.s.). We release a 98-line preflight check that catches every silent failure here. The observed tool-call rate is not a property of the model alone; it is a property of the model-interface stack that measures it.
