AI.tldr: The paper reveals that reported tool-call rates in agent evaluations can be misleading due to interface censorship, where models emit correct tool calls that get silently filtered by the serving stack, creating a fundamental model-interface mismatch that persists across different model scales and training regimes.
AI.motivation: There's a critical mismatch between what language models actually generate and what gets recorded in agent evaluations. The reported tool-call rate can be zero even when models are emitting well-formed calls, because the interface silently filters them before downstream systems see them. This creates misleading performance metrics that don't reflect the model's actual capabilities.
AI.method: The authors conduct systematic experiments across multiple benchmarks (BFCL v4, tau-bench, Qwen2.5-Coder at 21x scale range, Llama-3.1-8B, verl's AgentLoop) while holding everything constant except the serving adapter. They use controlled 2x2 designs over chat templates and parsers to isolate effects, and implement a probe to reproduce the issue across different model sizes. They also develop a 98-line preflight check to detect silent failures.
AI.result: The mismatch is systematic: with BFCL v4, the same model scores 0.00 or 0.96/0.19 just by changing the adapter. On tau-bench, switching adapters moves server-parsed calls from 0 to 636 and executed tasks from 0 to 103. Qwen2.5-Coder shows server parsing 0/100 at all sizes while actual emitted calls rise to 80/100 at 32B. The problem reaches inside training loops and has scale-dependent consequences, with AgentLoop showing 45 complete calls generated at 7B but 0 accepted/executed.
AI.conclusion: The observed tool-call rate is not an intrinsic property of the model but rather a property of the entire model-interface stack. Interface issues can completely mask model capabilities, and the mismatch persists across training regimes and scales. The authors provide a practical detection tool to catch these silent failures in evaluation pipelines.

title: Coupled Scaling: A Representational Accessibility Framework for Neural Scaling Laws
comment: 35 pages, 2 figures. Code and reproducibility artifacts: https://github.com/quintonvina/coupled-scaling/tree/v1.0-reanalysis
summary: Existing theories derive neural scaling from data geometry or a specified data-model spectrum, but systems trained on the same data can scale differently when architecture or optimization changes the representations they can efficiently reach. We introduce Coupled Scaling, a task-conditioned framework in which finite-budget scaling depends on the relation between task structure and the geometry accessible to an architecture-optimization system. In a solvable mode-truncation model, loss separates into target energy outside architectural support and an unresolved supported tail. For an arbitrary priority order, the residual lies between the best-N supported tail and the tail beyond the largest completed high-value prefix. If the cumulative-tail and coverage log-rates are $γ_{A,T}$ and $ρ_{A,O,T}$, the residual exponent lies in $[ρ_{A,O,T}γ_{A,T},γ_{A,T}]$. Under bounded off-prefix gain, the completed prefix is rate-determining and $α_{A,O,T}=ρ_{A,O,T}γ_{A,T}$; for $a_{A,T,j}\asymp j^{-b_{A,T}}$, this gives $α_{A,O,T}=ρ_{A,O,T}(b_{A,T}-1)$. A fixed-kernel specialization derives the training-time exponent from the near-zero tail of a task-weighted spectral measure defined independently of the loss fit. The framework separates architectural support from finite-budget acquisition and motivates two tests: static task-relevant geometry should track loss at a common budget, while multiscale geometry should track coupling-specific exponent ordering, including reversal across contrasting tasks. An audit of released emergence trajectories identifies the controls needed for a direct factorial test that measures geometry separately from the scaling fit.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Coupled Scaling, a framework where neural scaling depends on the relationship between task structure and the geometry accessible to a particular architecture-optimization system, rather than just data geometry.
AI.motivation: Existing theories derive neural scaling solely from data geometry or data-model spectrum, but systems trained on the same data can scale differently due to architecture and optimization affecting what representations they can efficiently reach.
AI.method: Proposes a task-conditioned framework called Coupled Scaling that models finite-budget scaling using a solvable mode-truncation model where loss separates into target energy outside architectural support and unresolved supported tail.
AI.result: For arbitrary priority order, residual loss lies between best-N supported tail and tail beyond largest completed high-value prefix. Derives residual exponent bounds and specific formulas for power-law decays. Framework separates architectural support from finite-budget acquisition and provides tests for static and multiscale geometry.
AI.conclusion: Coupled Scaling framework explains architecture-specific scaling phenomena and provides methods to test predictions about task-relevant geometry and scaling exponents. Audit shows need for controlled factorial tests to measure geometry separately from scaling fit.

title: Common-Witness Certificates and Sharp Feature Bounds for Counterfactual Image Auditing
summary: An image editor may satisfy every regional plausibility constraint separately even when no single latent explanation fits the complete output. We formalize this local-to-global failure using a common witness grade and witness nerve. The framework separates auditing from causal identification: shared exogeneity alone allows every coupling of the regime marginals, whereas an externally justified witness relation yields sharp partial-identification bounds for prespecified image features. Helly-type arguments provide short incompatibility certificates for quasiconvex losses, heterogeneous action strata, and finite witness atlases; a blocker-hypergraph formula gives exact repair counts. Simultaneous confidence regions for the regime marginals give finite-sample outer coverage of the complete identified interval. Controlled MNIST, Morpho-MNIST, and smallNORB studies demonstrate the predicted local-global separation, while synthetic experiments test sharp bounds, certificate recovery, and structured computation. The method audits a declared feature relation and does not identify unrestricted pixel-level counterfactuals.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a formal framework using witness nerve theory to detect when multiple locally plausible image edits collectively violate global coherence, providing methods to audit feature relations and compute partial identification bounds.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to address a critical problem in image editing where individual regions can be plausibly modified according to local constraints, but the complete edited image lacks a single coherent latent explanation. This local-to-global failure occurs when edited regions are individually reasonable but collectively incompatible.
AI.method: The method uses a witness nerve framework to separate auditing from causal identification. It employs Helly-type arguments to provide short incompatibility certificates for quasiconvex losses, heterogeneous action strata, and finite witness atlases. The approach uses a blocker-hypergraph formula for exact repair counts and constructs simultaneous confidence regions for regime marginals to achieve finite-sample outer coverage of identified intervals.
AI.result: Results demonstrate the predicted local-global separation in controlled studies using MNIST, Morpho-MNIST, and smallNORB datasets. Synthetic experiments validate sharp bounds, certificate recovery, and structured computation. The framework successfully audits declared feature relations while showing it cannot identify unrestricted pixel-level counterfactuals.
AI.conclusion: The witness nerve framework provides a principled way to detect when locally plausible image edits are globally incompatible. It offers practical tools for auditing feature relationships with partial identification bounds and finite-sample guarantees, while recognizing its limitations in identifying unrestricted pixel-level counterfactuals.

title: WeatherNext 3: Increasing resolution and performance of global weather models with raw observations
summary: State-of-the-art AI weather models have shown impressive medium-range forecast skill and computational efficiency, but suffer two key shortcomings: their forecasts have lower spatial and temporal resolution than the best physics-based models and they are exclusively initialized with and trained on analysis data. As a result, they cannot directly make use of observations, and any biases in the analysis are inherited by the forecast. WeatherNext 3 addresses these shortcomings and establishes a new state-of-the-art for probabilistic medium-range forecasting skill. First, WeatherNext 3 generates new forecasts every hour (rather than every 6 hours like traditional global models) by ingesting low-latency geostationary satellite data. Second, WeatherNext 3's temporal and spatial resolution are on par with physics-based global models, with hourly time steps and 0.1 degree resolution for single-level variables, including solar radiation and cloud cover. Third, WeatherNext 3 moves beyond traditional analysis variables by learning to predict satellite-derived precipitation estimates, as well as tropical cyclone and station observations. Modelling sparse station data allows WeatherNext 3 to make 2m temperature and dewpoint predictions at any location and time, conditioned on local geographical features, with substantially lower error than competing global models, even when evaluated against unseen stations. Together, WeatherNext 3's capabilities move operational AI-based weather forecasting beyond emulating the traditionally distinct stages of data assimilation, forecasting and post-processing, which helps to further push the frontier of performance and granularity for global weather prediction.

AI.tldr: WeatherNext 3 is an advanced AI weather model that generates hourly probabilistic forecasts with 0.1° resolution, directly ingests satellite data, and predicts beyond traditional analysis variables including precipitation, tropical cyclones, and station observations, achieving state-of-the-art skill.
AI.motivation: Current AI weather models have two key shortcomings: (1) lower spatial/temporal resolution compared to physics-based models, and (2) exclusive initialization/training on analysis data, preventing direct use of observations and perpetuating analysis biases.
AI.method: WeatherNext 3 addresses these by: 1) Generating hourly forecasts using low-latency geostationary satellite data, 2) Achieving 0.1° resolution and hourly time steps matching physics-based models, 3) Learning to predict satellite-derived precipitation, tropical cyclones, and station observations, enabling 2m temperature and dewpoint predictions at any location.
AI.result: The model establishes new state-of-the-art for probabilistic medium-range forecasting skill, with substantially lower error than competing global models when evaluated against unseen stations, and enables predictions at any location/time conditioned on local geography.
AI.conclusion: WeatherNext 3 moves operational AI weather forecasting beyond emulating traditional stages of data assimilation, forecasting, and post-processing, pushing the frontier of performance and granularity for global weather prediction through integrated, observation-driven modeling.

title: The Dually Flat Geometry of Planning as Inference
summary: We present an alternative characterization of the occupancy measure of reinforcement learning, obtained by embedding the planning criterion into the dynamics through a resetting planning process. Its stationary measure, which we term visitation measure, is the object on which the information geometry of decision making is most naturally expressed. The achievable visitation measures form a dually flat statistical manifold whose two affine charts are the visitation probabilities and the log-policies, dual under the conditional entropy. This structure makes planning-as-inference generalize from linear rewards to nonlinear functionals of the visitation, each iterate solved by one natural-gradient step, and gives the temporal-difference error the interpretation of a marginal-utility estimate. We develop the geometry and its consequences for reinforcement learning and theoretical neuroscience.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a novel information-geometric framework for reinforcement learning using visitation measures and dual flat statistical manifolds, enabling natural gradient planning for nonlinear functionals.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to develop a more natural information-geometric foundation for reinforcement learning and decision making, moving beyond linear reward functions to handle nonlinear functionals, and providing better mathematical structure for planning-as-inference approaches.
AI.method: The authors propose an alternative characterization of occupancy measures by embedding planning criteria into dynamics through a resetting planning process. They define visitation measures as stationary measures, construct dually flat statistical manifolds with visitation probabilities and log-policies as dual affine charts under conditional entropy, and develop natural gradient methods for planning.
AI.result: The framework enables planning-as-inference to generalize from linear rewards to nonlinear functionals of visitation measures, with each planning iteration solved by one natural-gradient step. It provides temporal-difference errors with marginal-utility interpretations and establishes a geometric foundation applicable to both RL and theoretical neuroscience.
AI.conclusion: The paper presents a principled information-geometric approach to reinforcement learning that unifies planning, inference, and optimization through dual flat manifolds, offering mathematical elegance and practical algorithmic advantages for handling complex objective functions beyond simple linear rewards.

title: Neural-Network Maxent: a general extension with learned nonlinearity, applied to time-series for Desert Locust distribution modelling
summary: Species Distribution Modelling (SDM) is essential for understanding how environmental conditions shape biodiversity, particularly for destructive pests such as the Desert Locust (Schistocerca gregaria), whose breeding dynamics are tightly coupled to rapidly evolving environmental conditions. Maxent has become the dominant method for presence-only data, but its reliance on a linear combination of hand chosen feature transforms limits its ability to capture the nonlinear, temporal relationships common in ecological monitoring, where covariates such as precipitation, soil moisture, and vegetation indices evolve meaningfully over time. Standard implementations flatten time-series covariates into independent features, discarding sequential structure that carries critical signal. We introduce RNN Maxent, an extension of the Maxent framework that replaces the fixed feature dictionary with a neural network, specifically a Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU), trained end to end via backpropagation. The approach preserves Maxent's presence only statistical foundations, background normalization, and probability calibration, differing only in that the nonlinearity is learned from data rather than fixed in advance. We apply RNN Maxent to map suitable habitat for the Desert Locust using 50 day environmental time series derived from ERA5 Land, MODIS, and Sentinel 3, maintaining a 7 day gap between covariates and presence records to yield forecasting behavior. Compared against standard Maxent, RNN Maxent improves performance across metrics (ROC AUC 0.862 std 0.036 vs. 0.792; F1 0.671 std 0.056 vs. 0.590).

AI.tldr: RNN Maxent extends traditional Maxent SDM by replacing hand-crafted features with a GRU neural network to better capture temporal patterns in environmental time-series data, significantly improving Desert Locust habitat prediction performance.
AI.motivation: Traditional Maxent has limitations for ecological monitoring of species like Desert Locusts because it uses linear combinations of hand-chosen features that can't capture complex nonlinear temporal relationships in environmental covariates (precipitation, soil moisture, vegetation indices) that evolve over time. Standard implementations discard sequential structure by flattening time-series data into independent features.
AI.method: RNN Maxent extends the Maxent framework by replacing the fixed feature dictionary with a neural network - specifically a Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) trained end-to-end via backpropagation. It preserves Maxent's presence-only statistical foundations, background normalization, and probability calibration, but learns nonlinearity from data rather than using predefined features. Applied to Desert Locust habitat mapping using 50-day environmental time series from ERA5 Land, MODIS, and Sentinel 3, with a 7-day gap for forecasting.
AI.result: RNN Maxent outperformed standard Maxent across metrics: ROC AUC improved from 0.792 to 0.862 (std 0.036), and F1 score improved from 0.590 to 0.671 (std 0.056).
AI.conclusion: The RNN Maxent framework successfully addresses temporal modeling limitations in species distribution modeling by incorporating recurrent neural networks while maintaining Maxent's statistical properties, demonstrating significant performance improvements for forecasting Desert Locust habitat suitability from environmental time-series data.

title: LLM4CKD: Large Language Models for Early Stage Chronic Kidney Disease Screening
summary: Early screening of chronic kidney disease (CKD) is critical for timely intervention, yet most machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) approaches require labeled data and model training, limiting their use in real-world screening settings. This study evaluates the effectiveness of large language models (LLMs) for CKD screening under zero-shot and few-shot in-context learning settings and compares them with traditional ML and DL methods. We propose a framework that uses clinically selected tabular features and structured prompt templates to enable LLM-based inference without task-specific training. LLM performance is evaluated across multiple prompt styles, feature configurations, and data settings, and compared with standard ML, DL, and tabular foundation model (TFM) baselines, and existing CKD screening tools. The results show that LLMs can achieve competitive performance using only a small number of examples, often matching or outperforming traditional approaches in low-data settings. However, their performance remains model-dependent and less stable as input complexity increases. In contrast, ML, DL, and TFM models show more consistent improvement with larger training data. Overall, the findings highlight a trade-off between data efficiency and stability, suggesting that LLMs may serve as a flexible complementary approach for CKD screening when labeled data are limited.

AI.tldr: LLMs can achieve competitive CKD screening performance with minimal data through zero/few-shot learning, offering a flexible alternative to traditional ML/DL approaches when labeled data is scarce, though with less stability than data-intensive methods.
AI.motivation: Early CKD screening is critical but current ML/DL approaches require labeled data and model training, limiting real-world deployment. There's a need for approaches that can work with limited labeled data.
AI.method: Proposed a framework using clinically selected tabular features and structured prompt templates for LLM-based inference without task-specific training. Evaluated LLMs under zero-shot and few-shot in-context learning settings across multiple prompt styles, feature configurations, and compared with ML, DL, tabular foundation models, and existing CKD screening tools.
AI.result: LLMs achieved competitive performance using only small numbers of examples, often matching or outperforming traditional approaches in low-data settings. However, performance was model-dependent and less stable with increased input complexity. ML/DL/TFM models showed more consistent improvement with larger training data.
AI.conclusion: There's a trade-off between data efficiency and stability: LLMs offer flexible CKD screening when labeled data is limited, serving as complementary approaches to traditional methods rather than replacements.

title: On the Interaction Between Model Compression and Test-Time Adaptation
summary: Deep neural networks deployed in the wild must be both efficient and adaptable, requiring model compression and test-time adaptation (TTA). While both are well studied in isolation, their interaction remains poorly understood. We systematically analyze how structured compression affects a model's ability to adapt under distribution shift. Using ResNet-18 and ViT-Base on CIFAR-10-C and ImageNet-C, we evaluate multiple compression methods combined with standard TTA techniques. We introduce a diagnostic framework that examines representational expressivity and adaptation subspace compatibility. Our results reveal a consistent gap: although compressed models retain high accuracy under supervised adaptation, their TTA performance degrades significantly with increasing compression. We show that this stems from reduced representational diversity and structural constraints that limit recoverability. These effects strongly depend on the compression method, highlighting the need to design compression strategies that preserve adaptability.

AI.tldr: Compressed neural networks maintain accuracy with supervised adaptation but fail at test-time adaptation due to reduced representational diversity and structural constraints limiting recoverability.
AI.motivation: While model compression and test-time adaptation (TTA) are both well-studied individually, their interaction remains poorly understood. Real-world deployment requires models to be both efficient (compressed) and adaptable (TTA), creating a need to systematically analyze how compression affects adaptability under distribution shift.
AI.method: Systematically analyzes how structured compression affects model adaptation under distribution shift using ResNet-18 and ViT-Base on CIFAR-10-C and ImageNet-C. Evaluates multiple compression methods combined with standard TTA techniques. Introduces a diagnostic framework examining representational expressivity and adaptation subspace compatibility.
AI.result: Reveals a consistent gap: compressed models retain high accuracy under supervised adaptation, but their TTA performance degrades significantly with increasing compression. Shows this stems from reduced representational diversity and structural constraints that limit recoverability. Effects strongly depend on the compression method used.
AI.conclusion: Compression methods need to be designed specifically to preserve adaptability, not just accuracy. There's a fundamental trade-off between efficiency and adaptability that depends on compression methodology, highlighting the need for compression strategies that maintain both representational diversity and structural flexibility for effective test-time adaptation.

title: InSituMeasure: Probing Situated Measurement Grounding in Industrial Scenes with Multimodal Large Language Models
summary: For trained operators, gauge reading requires little specialized knowledge, low cognitive effort, and high repeatability. Yet Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) remain unreliable in continuous-valued measurement despite strong results on general multimodal benchmarks. Existing benchmarks expose this weakness but isolate measurement from realistic, knowledge-grounded settings, with limited situated context, specialized instruments, real-world noise, and matched diagnostic annotations, reducing realism and constraining root-cause analysis. We introduce InSituMeasure to evaluate situated measurement grounding. It contains 2,922 real industrial monitoring scenes across eight functional categories of professional engineering instruments, with dense gauge-attribute annotations and noise tags for failure diagnosis. We define metrics for numerical accuracy under predefined tolerances and unit consistency, rejection of fake or unanswerable tasks, and alignment between model failures and annotated error factors. Across 24 state-of-the-art MLLMs, the best model reaches only 25.7\% joint value-unit accuracy and 51.8\% confidence-diagnosis F1, revealing a substantial gap between general multimodal competence and reliable situated measurement. Further analysis identifies failures from text-induced shortcuts, overconfident responses, and authentic industrial noise, including mixed disturbances, viewpoint deviation, occlusion, and environmental interference.

AI.tldr: MLLMs perform poorly on realistic industrial gauge reading tasks despite strong general multimodal capabilities, revealing a significant gap between general competence and reliable situated measurement.
AI.motivation: Current multimodal benchmarks don't adequately evaluate continuous-valued measurement in realistic industrial settings with specialized instruments, real-world noise, and proper diagnostic annotations, limiting understanding of MLLM failures in practical measurement tasks.
AI.method: Introduces InSituMeasure, a benchmark containing 2,922 real industrial monitoring scenes across 8 categories of professional engineering instruments, with dense gauge-attribute annotations and noise tags for failure diagnosis. Defines metrics for numerical accuracy, unit consistency, rejection of unanswerable tasks, and alignment between model failures and annotated error factors.
AI.result: Across 24 state-of-the-art MLLMs, the best model achieves only 25.7% joint value-unit accuracy and 51.8% confidence-diagnosis F1 score, showing substantial performance gap. Analysis identifies failures from text-induced shortcuts, overconfident responses, and various industrial noise types.
AI.conclusion: There's a significant gap between general multimodal capabilities and reliable situated measurement in industrial settings. The InSituMeasure benchmark enables better diagnosis of MLLM measurement failures and highlights the need for improved measurement grounding in realistic contexts.

title: Local Updates, Global Learning (LUGL): Playing Games with non-incremental Learners
summary: The dominance of Neural Networks (NNs) in RL is partially due to their incremental learning capability, which naturally suits the online, non-stationary nature of self-play training. However, gradient-boosted trees like LightGBM are widely recognised as the state of the art for tabular data in supervised learning, often outperforming NNs in accuracy and efficiency. Game states are inherently tabular---discrete actions, categorical card identities, structured board positions---which makes them an ideal candidate for tree-based methods. We introduce LUGL (Local Updates, Global Learning), a framework that decouples data collection from model fitting, enabling non-incremental learners such as GBTs to operate in RL settings where they would otherwise fail due to distributional shift. LUGL alternates between a local updates phase, where the agent plays self-play games and accumulates tabular updates (Q-values, V-values, policies, or regret values) in a finite table, and a global learning phase, where the table is used to train a function approximator that generalises to unseen states before the table is reset. We test our approach in four standard perfect-information games (Tic-tac-toe, Connect-4, Othello, and Hex) and five imperfect-information games (Kuhn's poker, Leduc Hold'em, Liar's Dice, Goofspiel, and Flop5 Hold'em), and show that our results are competitive with or superior to DQN and DeepCFR. Our experiments demonstrate that the community's strong bias towards NNs in game-playing may be unwarranted, since LightGBM-based agents achieve competitive or superior performance across all tested benchmarks.

AI.tldr: LUGL framework enables gradient-boosted trees (LightGBM) to work in RL for game playing by decoupling data collection from model fitting, achieving competitive or superior performance to neural networks in various perfect and imperfect-information games.
AI.motivation: Neural networks dominate RL for game playing due to their incremental learning capability suited to online self-play, but gradient-boosted trees are state-of-the-art for tabular data in supervised learning. Game states are inherently tabular, making them ideal for tree-based methods, yet current RL frameworks fail for non-incremental learners like GBTs due to distributional shift.
AI.method: LUGL (Local Updates, Global Learning) decouples data collection from model fitting. It alternates between: 1) Local updates phase - agent plays self-play games and accumulates tabular updates (Q-values, V-values, policies, or regret) in a finite table; 2) Global learning phase - the table is used to train a function approximator (LightGBM) that generalizes to unseen states, then the table is reset.
AI.result: The approach was tested in 4 perfect-information games (Tic-tac-toe, Connect-4, Othello, Hex) and 5 imperfect-information games (Kuhn's poker, Leduc Hold'em, Liar's Dice, Goofspiel, Flop5 Hold'em). Results show LUGL with LightGBM is competitive with or superior to DQN and DeepCFR across all benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: The community's strong bias towards neural networks in game-playing may be unwarranted, as LightGBM-based agents can achieve competitive or superior performance. LUGL enables non-incremental learners like gradient-boosted trees to operate effectively in RL settings where they would otherwise fail due to distributional shift.

title: FLY-EVAL++: An Evidence-Driven Evaluation Protocol for Safety-Constrained Flight Prediction with Large Language Models
comment: Published as a conference paper at COLM 2026
summary: Evaluating large language models (LLMs) in safety-critical, physics-governed environments requires more than accuracy-based metrics, because predictions that are numerically close to the ground truth can still violate operational constraints, combine fields in physically inconsistent ways, or fail to produce usable structured outputs. Existing evaluation protocols do not measure these failure modes reliably. We propose FLY-EVAL++, an evidence-driven evaluation protocol that combines deterministic verification of protocol compliance, physical feasibility, and safety constraints with fixed rubric-guided aggregation into interpretable multi-dimensional scores. We instantiate FLY-EVAL++ for Flight Trajectory and Attitude Prediction (FTAP) by extending the PilotBench setting with history-conditioned and multi-step prediction tasks. Across 66 LLMs, safety compliance is the most discriminative dimension of model behavior: models with comparable predictive performance differ by more than 28 points in safety score, and we observe recurrent failures including safety violations under physically plausible predictions and instability in multi-step rollouts. These results show that evaluation in safety-critical domains should measure constraint satisfaction and structured validity explicitly rather than rely on accuracy-centric reporting alone.

AI.tldr: FLY-EVAL++ is an evidence-driven evaluation protocol for LLMs in safety-critical physics-governed environments that combines deterministic verification of compliance, feasibility, and safety constraints with rubric-guided scoring, revealing safety compliance as the most discriminative dimension across models.
AI.motivation: Current evaluation protocols for LLMs in safety-critical physics environments don't reliably measure critical failure modes where predictions can be numerically accurate but still violate operational constraints, be physically inconsistent, or produce unusable structured outputs.
AI.method: FLY-EVAL++ combines deterministic verification of protocol compliance, physical feasibility, and safety constraints with fixed rubric-guided aggregation into interpretable multi-dimensional scores, instantiated for Flight Trajectory and Attitude Prediction by extending PilotBench with history-conditioned and multi-step prediction tasks.
AI.result: Across 66 LLMs, safety compliance was the most discriminative dimension: models with comparable predictive performance differed by more than 28 points in safety score, showing recurrent failures including safety violations under physically plausible predictions and instability in multi-step rollouts.
AI.conclusion: Evaluation in safety-critical domains should explicitly measure constraint satisfaction and structured validity rather than relying solely on accuracy-centric metrics, as FLY-EVAL++ demonstrates that safety compliance is a critical and highly variable dimension of model performance.

title: Extracting Forgotten Prompts from Targeted Unlearned Models
summary: Recent unlearning methods (e.g. NPO, DPO, LUNAR) make use of refusal alignment to suppress forgotten data. However, it has been shown that refusal responses might leave traces of unlearning, and recent attacks have been able to successfully recover some of the unlearned knowledge. In this paper, we uncover a new vulnerability. Existing attacks typically assume that the forgotten prompts are already known to the adversary and focus on recovering their answers. However, we show that the forgotten prompts themselves can be extracted by using the retained data and black-box access to the model. Our attack, Targeted Active Search (TAS), first identifies the forgotten entities by constructing canonical templates and entity pool, and selectively querying the model using the most informative template-entity pair under a limited query budget. Once the entities are identified, TAS instantiates prompt templates with those entities to probe the unlearned model and reconstruct the forgotten prompts. Experiments across three unlearning methods with three datasets and three LLMs shows that TAS recovers the forgotten entity with $100\%$ accuracy and reconstructs up to $95\%$ of forgotten prompts, all while using up to $99.7\%$ fewer queries than naive probing.

AI.tldr: A new attack called Targeted Active Search (TAS) that can extract forgotten prompts (not just answers) from unlearned LLMs using black-box access and retained data, achieving near-perfect recovery with significantly fewer queries than naive methods.
AI.motivation: Current unlearning methods rely on refusal alignment to suppress forgotten data, but these refusal responses leave traces that allow attackers to recover some unlearned knowledge. However, existing attacks focus only on recovering answers assuming the prompts are known, leaving a vulnerability where the forgotten prompts themselves could be extracted.
AI.method: TAS uses targeted active search: 1) identifies forgotten entities by constructing canonical templates and entity pools, 2) selectively queries the model using the most informative template-entity pairs under limited query budget, 3) once entities are identified, instantiates prompt templates with those entities to probe the unlearned model and reconstruct forgotten prompts.
AI.result: Experiments across three unlearning methods, three datasets, and three LLMs show TAS recovers forgotten entities with 100% accuracy, reconstructs up to 95% of forgotten prompts, while using up to 99.7% fewer queries than naive probing.
AI.conclusion: The paper uncovers a critical vulnerability in current LLM unlearning methods - forgotten prompts themselves can be extracted, not just their answers. This demonstrates that refusal-based unlearning leaves recoverable traces and highlights the need for more robust unlearning techniques that truly erase both prompts and responses.

title: Instruction Duplication as an Inference-Time Control Primitive
comment: 7 pages, 2 tables. Code and frozen reproduction artifacts: https://github.com/victorlavrenko/answer-engineering/releases/tag/instruction-duplication-arxiv-v1
summary: Procedural instruction following is a basic requirement for controllable language-model systems, especially when generated trajectories are inspected or repaired downstream. We introduce instruction duplication, a minimal black-box inference-time control that repeats only the procedural instruction, without retraining or decoding changes. Across seven instruction-tuned models, 300 medical multiple-choice questions, eight placement conditions, and 16,800 scheduled generations, moving from one to two copies raises the deterministic All-8 diagnostic--responses passing all eight observable tests--from 90.22% to 93.17% (+2.95 percentage points), eliminating 30.2% of the failures remaining after one copy. Pre-provisional TF-IDF recall rises from 73.44% to 74.81% (+1.38 points; Holm-adjusted p < .001), while final-answer accuracy remains exactly 60.21%. Premature commitment increases from 1.52% to 2.30% (p_Holm = .00536). A blinded challenge audit yields 10/30 directional confirmations, 20/30 perceptual ties, and no reversals; its prespecified 28/30 confirmation criterion is not met. Yet this distinction can matter operationally when a downstream system acts on the generated trajectory. In Answer Engineering (AE), where explicit trajectory state determines local repair, the published reason-first no-editing SSNHL endpoint was 25.1%; system-only AE was later reproduced at 84.2%, and the same trailing duplicate raised it to 97.1%. For conductive diagnostic branch preservation, the corresponding values are 58.9% published without editing, 78.6% with reproduced AE, and 73.8% with AE plus duplication--a within-AE decrease, but still 14.9 points above the no-editing baseline. Instruction duplication is therefore a low-complexity, placement-sensitive control whose practical value can emerge through the downstream system that consumes the exposed trajectory.

AI.tldr: Instruction duplication improves procedural instruction following by repeating instructions without model retraining, showing modest but statistically significant gains in diagnostic test performance.
AI.motivation: Procedural instruction following is crucial for controllable language-model systems, especially when generated trajectories are inspected or repaired downstream. Current methods may fail to properly follow procedural instructions, requiring inference-time controls.
AI.method: Instruction duplication - a black-box inference-time control that repeats procedural instructions without retraining or decoding changes. Tested across 7 instruction-tuned models, 300 medical multiple-choice questions, 8 placement conditions, and 16,800 scheduled generations.
AI.result: Moving from one to two copies raised the deterministic All-8 diagnostic from 90.22% to 93.17% (+2.95pp), eliminating 30.2% of failures. Pre-provisional TF-IDF recall rose from 73.44% to 74.81% (+1.38pp, p<.001). In Answer Engineering applications, duplication raised SSNHL endpoint from 84.2% to 97.1%, but decreased conductive diagnostic branch preservation from 78.6% to 73.8%.
AI.conclusion: Instruction duplication is a low-complexity, placement-sensitive control whose practical value emerges through downstream systems consuming exposed trajectories, though benefits vary by application and blind audit shows mixed evidence.

title: Out-of-Distribution Generalisation with Sequence Models in Offline Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
summary: Generalising to unseen tasks remains a fundamental challenge in offline multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL). In this work, we present a principled analysis of zero-shot task generalisation in the offline setting and conduct an extensive empirical investigation into the scaling behaviour governing task diversity, dataset size, and network capacity. To facilitate this study, we extend offline sequence modelling architectures to handle multi-task observation and action spaces alongside variable agent counts across tasks. Our primary finding is that scaling task diversity---rather than sheer dataset size is the dominant factor in achieving robust zero-shot transfer. Through large-scale experiments across four challenging environments (Connector, RWARE, SMAX, and LBF), we demonstrate that our multi-task approach achieves a mean improvement of 3.2x on held-out test tasks compared to single-task models and consistently outperforms strong behaviour cloning baselines. These results suggest that the development of generalisable MARL agents should prioritise the diversity of the training distribution with varying numbers of agents, providing a roadmap for scaling offline MARL effectively.

AI.tldr: Offline MARL approach shows that scaling task diversity (not dataset size) is key for zero-shot generalization to unseen tasks, achieving 3.2x improvement over single-task models.
AI.motivation: Generalizing to unseen tasks remains a fundamental challenge in offline multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL). There's a need to understand scaling behavior for task diversity, dataset size, and network capacity in zero-shot task generalization.
AI.method: Extended offline sequence modeling architectures to handle multi-task observation and action spaces with variable agent counts across tasks. Conducted large-scale experiments across four challenging environments (Connector, RWARE, SMAX, and LBF) with principled analysis of scaling behavior.
AI.result: Scaling task diversity rather than dataset size is the dominant factor for robust zero-shot transfer. The multi-task approach achieves mean 3.2x improvement on held-out test tasks compared to single-task models and consistently outperforms behavior cloning baselines.
AI.conclusion: Development of generalizable MARL agents should prioritize diversity of training distribution with varying numbers of agents, providing a roadmap for scaling offline MARL effectively.

title: IRWOZ 2.0: A Large Language Model-driven Dialogue Dataset for Industrial Robot Conversations
summary: IRWOZ has improved industrial human-robot interaction (HRI) dialogue systems through domain-specific annotations. However, its initial version contains substantial noise in dialogue states and utterances, limiting state-tracking accuracy. We introduce IRWOZ 2.0, which addresses these limitations through large language model (LLM) enhanced generation (Mistral/Claude-3.5) and quality refinements. Our improved dataset expands to 390 dialogues across 4 industrial domains (Assembly, Delivery, Position, Relocation), featuring manual corrections and automated typo removal. Benchmark experiments on dialogue state tracking demonstrate significant improvements, with GPT-2's BLEU-4 score increasing from 0.1651 to 0.5604 compared to original IRWOZ. To support industrial HRI research, we publicly released IRWOZ 2.0 dataset at https://ieee-dataport.org/documents/irwoz-20-large-language-model-driven-dialogue-dataset-industrial-robot-conversations

AI.tldr: IRWOZ 2.0 improves industrial HRI dialogue datasets through LLM-enhanced generation and quality refinements, expanding domains and boosting state-tracking performance significantly.
AI.motivation: The original IRWOZ dataset contained substantial noise in dialogue states and utterances, which limited state-tracking accuracy in industrial human-robot interaction systems.
AI.method: Used large language models (Mistral/Claude-3.5) for enhanced generation, manual corrections, automated typo removal, and expanded the dataset to 390 dialogues across 4 industrial domains (Assembly, Delivery, Position, Relocation).
AI.result: Significant improvements in dialogue state tracking benchmarks, with GPT-2's BLEU-4 score increasing from 0.1651 to 0.5604 compared to original IRWOZ, and the dataset was publicly released.
AI.conclusion: IRWOZ 2.0 successfully addresses noise limitations in industrial HRI datasets through LLM-enhanced generation, providing a higher-quality resource that significantly improves dialogue state tracking performance for industrial robot conversation research.

title: Resolution-Aware Experimental Design under Partial Identifiability
summary: Experimental design is commonly framed as choosing the experiment expected to provide the most information. Under partial identifiability however, persistent nuisance uncertainty can make the same observation carry different structural meanings. We introduce Resolution-Aware Experimental Design (RAED), which selects an experiment by the smallest expected nonempty structural candidate set achievable subject to false-exclusion control. We prove an exact cross-nuisance aliasing separation: an experiment can be preferred by structural and full-latent information gain, average classification, and nuisance-marginalized informativeness while having arbitrarily poorer valid structural resolution. RAED nevertheless preserves the expected ordering under a genuine composite Blackwell comparison. To make this criterion operational, we develop a learned score-based implementation with finite-sample nuisance-average and positive-tail calibration, and characterize a rare-tail sample-complexity obstruction. Under constrained sensing, two subsurface-flow benchmarks exhibit genuine RAED--expected-information-gain (EIG) experiment-selection disagreements, with the clearest and largest held-out resolution differences in WCA. In a fluvial benchmark, tail protection changes the selected physical experiment and replaces hard-region false exclusions primarily with explicit ambiguity. In a mechanistic methane-oxidation benchmark, a prospectively specified 5\% false-exclusion tolerance also yields a nontrivial finite-sample population guarantee for tail-sensitive nuisance risk, with 95\% joint confidence across all three structural families.

AI.tldr: RAED is a new experimental design method for partial identifiability that selects experiments based on smallest expected structural candidate set with false-exclusion control, rather than just maximizing information gain.
AI.motivation: Under partial identifiability, persistent nuisance uncertainty means the same observation can have different structural interpretations, making traditional information-based experimental design suboptimal for structural resolution.
AI.method: RAED selects experiments by the smallest expected nonempty structural candidate set subject to false-exclusion control, with a learned score-based implementation featuring finite-sample nuisance-average and positive-tail calibration.
AI.result: RAED exhibits genuine experiment-selection disagreements with expected information gain methods, showing clearest resolution differences in WCA benchmarks. Tail protection changes selected experiments and replaces false exclusions with explicit ambiguity, with 95% joint confidence across structural families.
AI.conclusion: RAED provides a principled approach to experimental design under partial identifiability that focuses on structural resolution rather than just information gain, with practical finite-sample guarantees and demonstrated improvements in benchmark applications.

title: Spurious Advantage Hidden in GRPO
summary: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) is widely studied for reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, where its advantage estimator assigns each rollout a magnitude from within-group reward statistics. In the common case, this magnitude rewards rollouts that reach the correct answer through reasoning. Yet, an overlooked case shares the same surface: a rollout may land on it by guessing, and the formula still assigns a high magnitude, which we identify as the spurious advantage. This arises in three cases: bounded-answer tasks with a small candidate set; open-answer sets hosting bounded sub-cases; and search agents whose budget opens many paths to the same answer. In all three, this misleads the policy toward guess-like behaviors. We propose SIGNBALANCE, whose magnitude is composition-free: it keeps the verifier sign, uses a global scale, and restores zero-mean balance via a stop-gradient per-class rescaling. Across math and search agent benchmarks at different scales, SIGNBALANCE matches GRPO on open-answer math and improves on bounded-answer math and search agents. Code will be released.

AI.tldr: SIGNBALANCE addresses spurious advantage in GRPO by using composition-free magnitude estimation with verifier sign preservation, global scaling, and per-class rescaling, improving performance on bounded-answer math and search agents while matching GRPO on open-answer tasks.
AI.motivation: Current Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has a flaw where it assigns high advantage magnitudes to rollouts that reach correct answers through guessing rather than reasoning, creating "spurious advantage" that misleads policies toward guess-like behaviors, especially in bounded-answer tasks, open-answer sets with bounded sub-cases, and search agents with multiple paths to the same answer.
AI.method: Proposes SIGNBALANCE with three key design principles: 1) composition-free magnitude estimation that preserves the verifier sign (correct vs incorrect), 2) uses a global scale rather than within-group statistics, and 3) restores zero-mean balance through stop-gradient per-class rescaling, preventing spurious advantage from guessing behaviors.
AI.result: Experimental results across math and search agent benchmarks at different scales show that SIGNBALANCE matches GRPO performance on open-answer math tasks while improving performance on bounded-answer math and search agents, demonstrating effectiveness in addressing the spurious advantage problem.
AI.conclusion: SIGNBALANCE successfully addresses the spurious advantage problem in GRPO by redesigning the advantage estimator to avoid rewarding guessing behaviors, making reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards more robust across different task types including bounded-answer, open-answer, and search agent scenarios.

title: Federated Causal Discovery via Regression-Directed Cumulants
comment: Accepted at the 12th International Conference on Probabilistic Graphical Models (PGM 2026)
summary:
In this paper we study linear non-Gaussian acyclic models (LiNGAM) when used in federated environments. These causal models allow one to go beyond Markov equivalence. However, in many domains data are scarce, and increasing the sample size by centralising data from different clients is not advisable due to regulations such as the GDPR. The federated environment offers an attractive option to balance privacy and causal discovery accuracy. Unfortunately, the standard centralised estimator in the LiNGAM setting, i.e., DirectLiNGAM, cannot be straightforwardly federated. Higher-order cumulant tensors offer a way around this obstacle: they depend only on the joint distribution of the variables involved and add exactly across independent sample groups, so a single communication round suffices in horizontal, vertical, and hybrid partitions.
  However, FedISHC, i.e., the current federated method along these lines, breaks down under near-symmetric noise. To overcome the above limitation, we introduce the FedRCD family of causal discovery algorithms, and investigate three variants that trade off communication rounds against algebraic noise; two of them are exact federated counterparts of the centralised high-order cumulant (HC) and HC-LiNGAM algorithms, and the single-round variants further effectively support exact unlearning at any granularity, from a single observation to a whole client. Numerical experiments show that at sample sizes typical of real deployments, the entire cumulant-based federated family does not actually rank variables by the population asymmetry that the scores encode at zero. It ranks them by a variance ladder induced by the DAG along its directed paths, the cumulant counterpart of varsortability. Marginal standardisation collapses every cumulant method to near-random ordering, while scale-invariant DirectLiNGAM, not federable under this protocol, is unaffected.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces FedRCD, a family of federated causal discovery algorithms for LiNGAM models that work across horizontal, vertical, and hybrid data partitions, with single-round communication and support for exact unlearning.
AI.motivation: Federated learning offers privacy-preserving causal discovery when data cannot be centralized due to regulations like GDPR. However, existing federated LiNGAM methods like FedISHC fail with near-symmetric noise, and DirectLiNGAM cannot be easily federated.
AI.method: Proposes FedRCD family using higher-order cumulant tensors that add exactly across independent sample groups. Three variants trade communication rounds for algebraic noise. Two variants are exact federated counterparts of centralised HC and HC-LiNGAM algorithms.
AI.result: FedRCD algorithms enable single-round communication for horizontal/vertical/hybrid partitions and support exact unlearning at any granularity. However, cumulant-based methods rank variables by variance ladder (cumulant counterpart of varsortability) rather than population asymmetry, and marginal standardization collapses them to near-random ordering.
AI.conclusion: While FedRCD addresses federated causal discovery needs, cumulant-based methods have inherent limitations in ranking variables. Scale-invariant DirectLiNGAM, though not federable under this protocol, remains unaffected by these issues, highlighting a trade-off between federatability and robustness to scaling.

title: DRACO: Fine-Grained Credit Assignment with Dynamic Rubrics for Long-Horizon Agent Training
summary: Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards works well when a task has a programmatic checker, but most long-horizon agent domains have none. We work in the outcome-blind setting, where ground-truth success signals are not available. Multi-criteria rubrics are a popular way to supply such a reward; they are scored once per trajectory, but a single scalar is a poor signal across tens of steps. We propose DRACO: Distributing Rubric-based Advantage for Credit Optimization. It generates rubrics dynamically during training to track the policy's evolving capability, scores those rubrics once per completed trajectory, and redistributes that judgment over the steps responsible for annotated rubrics to produce differentiated per-step advantages in GRPO. The redistribution is closed-form and does not introduce any trained attribution module. On AppWorld, DRACO gains 15.9 points over the base model and 5.3 points over GRPO trained with a sparse ground-truth reward, despite not using any verifiers itself. On out-of-domain Tau-Bench, it gains 5.3 points over the base model even without a frontier judge, beating both ground-truth-reward training and other rubric-based training settings. The code for DRACO is available at https://github.com/IBM/draco.

AI.tldr: DRACO is a novel reinforcement learning method that dynamically generates rubrics during training to distribute credit across time steps, improving performance in outcome-blind settings without requiring verifiable rewards.
AI.motivation: Most long-horizon agent domains lack programmatic checkers for verifiable rewards, and existing multi-criteria rubrics provide poor signal across many time steps since they're only scored once per trajectory in outcome-blind settings.
AI.method: DRACO (Distributing Rubric-based Advantage for Credit Optimization) generates rubrics dynamically during training to track the policy's evolving capability, scores rubrics once per completed trajectory, then redistributes that judgment over relevant steps using closed-form redistribution to produce differentiated per-step advantages in GRPO without requiring a trained attribution module.
AI.result: On AppWorld, DRACO gained 15.9 points over the base model and 5.3 points over GRPO trained with sparse ground-truth reward. On out-of-domain Tau-Bench, it gained 5.3 points over the base model without a frontier judge, beating both ground-truth-reward training and other rubric-based methods.
AI.conclusion: DRACO effectively addresses the credit assignment problem in outcome-blind reinforcement learning by dynamically generating and distributing rubric-based advantages, demonstrating strong performance improvements over baseline methods across different domains.

title: Projected Riemannian Gradient Descent for the Bures-Wasserstein Barycenter: Dimension-Independent Linear Convergence at Unit Step Size
summary: The computation of the Bures-Wasserstein (BW) barycenter of an ensemble of positive definite matrices arises throughout machine learning, optimal transport, and quantum information. Riemannian gradient descent (RGD) at unit step size -- the fixed-point iteration used in practice -- converges rapidly, yet existing analyses present a dichotomy: unit-step guarantees carry worst-case exponential dependence on the dimension, while dimension-independent guarantees require small step sizes that forfeit the empirical speed. We resolve this dichotomy, not by improving the guarantees for unit-step RGD, but by proposing a Projected RGD algorithm that achieves dimension-independent linear convergence at unit step size. The achieved rate, $(1 - κ^{-3/2})$, where $κ$ is the condition number of the ensemble, also polynomially improves on the best small-step guarantee ($κ^{3/2}$ versus $κ^{5/2}$ iteration complexity). The crux is a novel Projection Lemma: clipping the eigenvalues of a positive matrix to an interval $[α, β]$ is the closed-form, non-expansive (1-Lipschitz) BW-metric projection onto the set $\{S : αI \leq S \leq βI\}$ -- a statement which, unlike its known one-sided counterpart, does not follow from convexity. The projection is moreover free: it reuses an eigendecomposition the next iteration must perform in any case, so the projected and unprojected iterations cost the same per step. The same analysis covers the invariant matrix projection problem of Brahmachari et al. (2025), whose fixed-point algorithm we identify as unit-step RGD on a totally geodesic submanifold, thereby extending the dimension-independent guarantee to that setting verbatim.

AI.tldr: Projected Riemannian Gradient Descent (RGD) algorithm achieves dimension-independent linear convergence at unit step size for computing Bures-Wasserstein barycenters, with improved condition number dependence compared to existing methods.
AI.motivation: Current methods for computing Bures-Wasserstein barycenters face a dichotomy: unit-step RGD converges fast in practice but has worst-case exponential dependence on dimension in theoretical guarantees, while dimension-independent methods require small step sizes that sacrifice empirical speed. There's a need for an algorithm that combines the practical speed of unit-step methods with dimension-independent theoretical guarantees.
AI.method: The authors propose a Projected RGD algorithm that uses eigenvalue clipping as a projection operator. The key innovation is a Projection Lemma showing that clipping eigenvalues of a positive matrix to an interval [α, β] is the closed-form, non-expansive Bures-Wasserstein metric projection onto the set {S : αI ≤ S ≤ βI}. This projection is computationally free as it reuses the eigendecomposition needed for the next iteration anyway.
AI.result: Projected RGD achieves dimension-independent linear convergence at unit step size with rate (1 - κ^{-3/2}), where κ is the condition number of the ensemble. This improves the iteration complexity from κ^{5/2} (best small-step guarantee) to κ^{3/2}. The analysis also extends to the invariant matrix projection problem, showing the existing fixed-point algorithm is unit-step RGD on a geodesic submanifold.
AI.conclusion: The proposed Projected RGD algorithm resolves the dichotomy between empirical speed and theoretical guarantees for Bures-Wasserstein barycenter computation. It achieves practical unit-step convergence with dimension-independent theoretical guarantees, significantly improving both theoretical bounds and practical performance. The method also provides new insights connecting optimization geometry and projection operators.

title: Why Gated DeltaNet Survives 4-Bit Quantization: NVFP4 W4A4 for the Recurrent Half of a Hybrid 27B LLM
summary: Hybrid LLMs pair softmax attention with linear-attention layers such as Gated DeltaNet (GDN), whose recurrent state summarizes the context in fixed size. Early community 4-bit quantizations of Qwen3.8-27B (48 GDN layers, 16 attention layers) left the GDN block in 8- or 16-bit precision -- especially its decay and write-strength gates -- on the intuition that errors in a recurrence accumulate over long contexts. We test that intuition by building Minima: NVFP4 W4A4 on all 496 linear layers, GDN included. Across perplexity at 4K/32K, MMLU-Pro, GSM8K, AIME'25, GPQA-Diamond, LiveCodeBench, and RULER retrieval to 64K, Minima matches BF16 within seed noise (5-task average -0.52) while being the smallest (17.5 GiB) and fastest-prefill (+14-19%) recipe we compare, and its 32K perplexity gap shrinks with position. A four-part mechanism study explains why: (i) NVFP4's 16-element block scaling localizes the residual stream's extreme outliers, equalizing activation error across layer roles; (ii) the supposedly fragile gate projections are the least sensitive -- softplus/exponential and sigmoid parameterizations compress ~11% GEMM error to ~2% output error; (iii) the delta-rule recurrence holds injected noise at a flat plateau over 32K tokens and forgets a state impulse within hundreds of steps, because each write overwrites the state along the current key direction; (iv) the per-token quantization cost washes out with context instead of compounding. We also repair a global-scale mismatch that arises when per-module-calibrated NVFP4 checkpoints are served by kernels that fuse those modules into one GEMM, and show calibrated FP8 KV-cache scales are performance-free. The result: a practical recipe -- quantize everything, ship KV scales -- and a mechanistic account of why the recurrent half of a hybrid LLM is the easy half to quantize. Checkpoint: https://huggingface.co/minima-ai/mnma_qwen3.8_27b_nvfp4

AI.tldr: 4-bit quantization of hybrid LLMs (Qwen3.8-27B) works well on all layers including recurrent GDN blocks, achieving BF16-level performance while being smaller and faster.
AI.motivation: Previous 4-bit quantizations left GDN (Gated DeltaNet) layers in higher precision (8- or 16-bit) due to concerns that errors in recurrent components would accumulate over long contexts, but this intuition was untested.
AI.method: Created Minima: used NVFP4 W4A4 quantization on all 496 linear layers including GDN blocks in Qwen3.8-27B (48 GDN layers, 16 attention layers), with mechanism studies to understand why it works.
AI.result: Minima matches BF16 performance within seed noise (-0.52 average on 5 tasks), is the smallest (17.5 GiB) and fastest-prefill (+14-19%) quantization method, with 32K perplexity gap shrinking with position.
AI.conclusion: The recurrent half of hybrid LLMs is actually easier to quantize than intuition suggests, leading to practical recipe: quantize everything, ship KV scales, with mechanistic explanations for why recurrence doesn't compound errors.

title: From Nowcasting to Forecasting: Adapting a Reanalysis-Trained
summary: Accurate cloud-cover forecasts are important for temperature prediction, radiation forecasting, and solar-power operations. Short-range forecasting methods can preserve observed cloud placement during the first forecast hours, but their skill decreases when cloud fields evolve through formation, dissipation and deformation. Longer lead times require accounting for atmospheric evolution, but operational numerical weather prediction (NWP) forecasts may not accurately represent the satellite-observed cloud state at initialization. We develop CloudCast v2, a machine-learning model for 12-hour cloud-cover forecasting from observation-based initial conditions. The model is first trained on the Copernicus European Regional Reanalysis (Ridal2024) to learn cloud-evolution dynamics, and is then adapted to satellite-derived cloud fields using conditional flow matching (Lipman2023), a generative method that transforms noise into cloud-cover forecasts conditioned on the observed initial cloud fields and NWP inputs. CloudCast v2 reduces mean absolute error by 10% relative to its predecessor, CloudCast v1 (Partio2025), over the 1-12 h range. It also overtakes CloudCast v1 in fractions skill score, a neighborhood-based measure of spatial agreement, after approximately 3-6 h, depending on the cloudiness category. These results show that observation-initialized machine-learning forecasts can extend beyond the usual 1-3-hour nowcasting range while retaining spatial detail from satellite cloud fields.

AI.tldr: CloudCast v2 is a machine learning model that extends cloud-cover forecasting to 12 hours by using satellite observations as initial conditions and combining reanalysis training with conditional flow matching adaptation.
AI.motivation: Current cloud-cover forecasting methods have limitations: short-range methods lose skill when clouds evolve (formation, dissipation, deformation), while longer-range NWP forecasts may not accurately capture the observed cloud state at initialization. Accurate cloud forecasts are crucial for temperature prediction, radiation forecasting, and solar-power operations.
AI.method: Two-stage approach: 1) Train on Copernicus European Regional Reanalysis (Ridal2024) to learn cloud-evolution dynamics, 2) Adapt to satellite-derived cloud fields using conditional flow matching (Lipman2023), a generative method that transforms noise into cloud-cover forecasts conditioned on observed initial cloud fields and NWP inputs.
AI.result: CloudCast v2 reduces mean absolute error by 10% relative to CloudCast v1 over the 1-12 hour range. It also overtakes CloudCast v1 in fractions skill score (neighborhood-based spatial agreement measure) after approximately 3-6 hours, depending on cloudiness category.
AI.conclusion: Observation-initialized machine-learning forecasts can successfully extend beyond the typical 1-3-hour nowcasting range while retaining spatial detail from satellite cloud fields, representing a significant advancement in cloud-cover forecasting capability.

title: Epistemic Warrant for LLM Recommendations: Characterizing the Basis for Reliance When Ground Truth Is Unavailable
summary: Large language models are increasingly used to support organizational decisions, yet users often lack a principled basis for assessing whether to rely on a specific recommendation. Existing approaches typically evaluate broad model properties, such as reliability, uncertainty, or robustness, or focus on user trust, rather than the underlying basis for relying on an individual recommendation. Adapting theoretical foundations from epistemology, we introduce epistemic warrant, a decision-level construct that characterizes the stability of a model's preference and the scope over which that preference holds. We operationalize this construct through a four-tier reliance certificate for pairwise recommendations, distinguishing among unstable, context-dependent, locally supported, and broadly supported recommendations. We validate the construct using contemporary methodologies: known-groups tests successfully recover expert-prespecified warrant orderings, and stronger warrants systematically align with independent consensus from crowd workers. Furthermore, we demonstrate that epistemic warrant provides information distinct from verbalized confidence and is not readily explained by decision difficulty. Ultimately, this framework offers a theoretically grounded, implementable approach for characterizing the warrant of individual LLM recommendations when objective ground truth is unavailable.

AI.tldr: Introduces "epistemic warrant" - a decision-level construct for assessing reliability of individual LLM recommendations using stability and scope metrics, validated through empirical tests showing it provides distinct information beyond verbalized confidence.
AI.motivation: Large language models are increasingly used for organizational decision support, but users lack principled ways to assess whether to rely on specific recommendations. Existing approaches evaluate broad model properties or focus on user trust rather than the basis for relying on individual recommendations.
AI.method: Adapted theoretical foundations from epistemology to create the epistemic warrant construct, operationalized through a four-tier reliance certificate for pairwise recommendations (unstable, context-dependent, locally supported, broadly supported). Validated using known-groups tests and comparison with independent consensus from crowd workers.
AI.result: Known-groups tests successfully recovered expert-prespecified warrant orderings, stronger warrants systematically aligned with independent crowd consensus, and epistemic warrant provided information distinct from verbalized confidence and not explained by decision difficulty.
AI.conclusion: Epistemic warrant offers a theoretically grounded, implementable framework for characterizing the warrant of individual LLM recommendations when objective ground truth is unavailable, addressing a critical gap in organizational decision support.

title: OBER+: Continuity-Aware Reporting and Traceable Continuous Improvement in Outcome-Based Education
comment: 14 pages, 6 figures, 7 tables. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Learning Technologies
summary: Institutions practising outcome-based education compute learning outcome attainment routinely, while reviews of curriculum analytics report an absence of evidence on how that computation informs decisions. This paper presents OBER+, an extension of a deployed institutional attainment platform that computes the step from a measured shortfall to an evaluated corrective action. Five connected stages accumulate attainment across deliveries of a course, signal a shortfall and a persistent shortfall, grade it on cutoffs the regulator already uses, record the decision against a catalogue of practices annotated with their evidence, log the change, and quantify the subsequent movement in the shortfall. A further rule compares successive statements of an outcome, so attainment is never read as a series across a point at which the outcome changed. Applying the rules to the live record of two real courses produced three results. Every outcome of a core course was substantively redefined between consecutive deliveries, with subject matter moving between outcome numbers, so a naive reading would have reported a twenty-five point collapse between quantities that do not refer to the same learning. Recomputing the platform's figures from its documented rule showed six of ten differing by more than rounding explains, in a pattern that identified a defect since reported to the institution. Across fifteen statement pairs from three transitions, five were identical character for character, and among the ten that were not, the outcome carrying a given number was nearest to a differently numbered earlier outcome in six, a result resting on an ordering of similarities and requiring no threshold and no labelling. The contribution is a computational design for outcome-based reporting, stated as rules any attainment platform can implement, with evidence of what they make visible in a live institutional record.

AI.tldr: OBER+ extends institutional attainment platforms to compute corrective actions for learning outcome shortfalls, revealing hidden issues like outcome redefinition and computational defects through rule-based analysis.
AI.motivation: Institutions compute learning outcome attainment but lack evidence on how these computations inform decisions. There's an absence of systematic connection between measured shortfalls and evaluated corrective actions.
AI.method: Develops OBER+ as an extension of existing attainment platforms with five connected stages: accumulate attainment across course deliveries, signal shortfalls, grade them using regulatory cutoffs, record decisions against evidence-annotated practices, log changes, and quantify subsequent movement. Also compares successive outcome statements to prevent misreading attainment across outcome changes.
AI.result: Application to two real courses revealed: 1) All outcomes in a core course were substantively redefined between deliveries (content moved between outcome numbers), making naive readings misleading. 2) 6 of 10 recomputed figures differed significantly from original, identifying a platform defect. 3) Across 15 outcome statement pairs, 5 were identical, while 6 of 10 non-identical ones showed outcomes numbered differently than their nearest semantic match.
AI.conclusion: Provides a computational design for outcome-based reporting as implementable rules that make previously invisible institutional practices visible, revealing issues like outcome redefinition and computational errors that undermine accurate attainment analysis.

title: Environment Evolution for Terminal Agents
summary: Scaling interactive and verifiable environments is critical for training terminal agents. As frontier models become more capable, environments synthesized from scratch become less challenging and thus provide limited learning signals. Recent co-evolution methods iteratively synthesize environments near the model's learnable frontier based on weaknesses exposed during rollouts. However, their dependence on on-policy rollouts limits generalization and the continuous provision of learning signals as the model becomes stronger. In this paper, we propose environment evolution, which incrementally increases environment difficulty off-policy and schedules the evolved environments generation by generation during training to provide continuous learning signals. We derive three evolution directions that influence environment difficulty from the multi-turn learning objective and then implement evolution along these directions through a loop-engineered multi-agent harness. Quantitative rollout experiments with Hy4 preview, Claude Opus 5, and GPT-5.6 Sol show that environment evolution consistently produces more difficult environments. We validate its effectiveness on Qwen3.6-27B and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B through simple long-horizon RL training, improving their performance by 14.4 and 18.0 percentage points on Terminal-Bench 2.1, respectively.

AI.tldr: Environment Evolution: A method for automatically generating increasingly difficult interactive environments for training terminal agents through off-policy difficulty scaling and scheduled environment evolution.
AI.motivation: Current co-evolution methods for training terminal agents rely on on-policy rollouts which limit generalization and fail to provide continuous learning signals as models become stronger. Environments synthesized from scratch become less challenging for frontier models, limiting their learning potential.
AI.method: Proposed environment evolution approach that: 1) Incrementally increases environment difficulty off-policy, 2) Schedules evolved environments generation by generation during training, 3) Derives three evolution directions from multi-turn learning objective, 4) Implements evolution through a loop-engineered multi-agent harness.
AI.result: Environment evolution consistently produces more difficult environments (validated with Hy4 preview, Claude Opus 5, and GPT-5.6 Sol). RL training with Qwen3.6-27B and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B showed performance improvements of 14.4 and 18.0 percentage points respectively on Terminal-Bench 2.1.
AI.conclusion: Environment evolution effectively addresses limitations of existing co-evolution methods by providing continuous learning signals through systematically evolved environments, significantly improving terminal agent performance without reliance on on-policy rollouts.

title: Landmark-Based Discrimination of Injury-Associated Athlete-Sessions from Minute-Resolution Multimodal Football Monitoring Data
summary:
Athlete monitoring data may be recorded minute by minute throughout a match or training session, while injury information may only indicate whether the entire session was injury-associated.
  This creates a modelling problem: assigning the same session-level label to every minute would imply that injury status is known at each exact time, even though within-session injury onset is unknown.
  Our novelty is a fixed-landmark, one-representation-per-athlete-session formulation that directly addresses this mismatch. Instead of labelling every minute, we construct one representation per athlete-session at each landmark using information observed up to that point. This keeps the target at the session level and avoids unsupported minute-level injury supervision.
  A landmark is a fixed time point within the same session, such as 10, 20, or 30 minutes. At each landmark, we assess whether the whole session is injury-associated or non-injury-associated and examine how discrimination changes as more within-session information becomes available.
  Using 2020 SoccerMon data, we analyse 3,743 athlete-sessions from 48 elite women's football athletes, including 22 injury-associated sessions from five athletes. We evaluate pre-session, cumulative, dynamic, and combined representations with athlete-disjoint validation, athlete-cluster bootstrap uncertainty, common-cohort sensitivity analysis, alternative negative-athlete fold allocations, equal-athlete weighting, and Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and XGBoost benchmarks.
  Primary CUM+DYN Logistic Regression yields ROC-AUC 0.367-0.607 and PR-AUC 0.0080-0.0150 across landmarks, with wide uncertainty. PRE-containing representations show higher point estimates at several landmarks but remain uncertain.

AI.tldr: Proposes fixed-landmark modeling for athlete monitoring where only session-level injury labels are available, avoiding unsupported minute-level supervision by creating one representation per athlete-session at each time landmark.
AI.motivation: There's a mismatch between high-frequency minute-by-minute athlete monitoring data and only available session-level injury labels. Traditional approaches would incorrectly assign the same injury label to every minute, implying knowledge of exact injury onset time within sessions when this information is actually unknown.
AI.method: Develops fixed-landmark, one-representation-per-athlete-session formulation using SoccerMon data (3,743 athlete-sessions from 48 elite women's football athletes). Creates representations at each landmark time (e.g., 10, 20, 30 minutes) using only information observed up to that point. Evaluates pre-session, cumulative, dynamic, and combined representations with comprehensive validation including athlete-disjoint validation, athlete-cluster bootstrap uncertainty, sensitivity analysis, and multiple ML benchmarks.
AI.result: Primary CUM+DYN Logistic Regression yields modest performance: ROC-AUC 0.367-0.607 and PR-AUC 0.0080-0.0150 across landmarks, with wide uncertainty. PRE-containing representations show higher point estimates at several landmarks but remain statistically uncertain. The approach successfully addresses the session-level labeling problem but shows limited predictive power.
